### [47] [LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17685)
*Jingyue Cong,Estrid He,Zhuang Li,Nan Wu,Li Shen,Yameng Peng,Xinshu Li,Andy Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available at this https URL .

### [48] [Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17747)
*Tianyang Xu,Jing Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. Real observations motivate these tests: on three benchmarks, simple predictors match or beat GPT-4.1. In two Who&When Pro systems, a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps, motivating input restriction. In one of them, error injection leaves no reasoning after the faulty step; judges fine-tuned on its labels beat GPT-4.1 by 41 points. Adding task-related reasoning after that step moves this cue: fine-tuned judges lose 31-99 points, but zero-shot judges lose at most 9, motivating cue following. On Aegis, blaming every agent matches GPT-4.1 on micro-F1 but trails by 19 points in exact-set accuracy, motivating aggregation. We recommend reporting these tests when developing failure-attribution benchmarks.

### [49] [Efficiently Learning To Reason or Not to Reason: Root-token Policy Optimization for Adaptive Thinking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17767)
*Taehyeon Kim,Hyunsoo Lee,Youngsoo Jang,Moontae Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by externalizing explicit reasoning traces before producing the answer, yet suffer from overthinking challenge that allocates uniformly heavy computation to queries of varying difficulty. While proprietary models mitigate this via opaque routing, open-source LRMs still lack an efficient mechanism to internalize adaptive reasoning due to both expensive training cost and limited disclosure of training recipes. In response, we introduce RPO (Root-token Policy Optimization), a framework that enables LRMs to self-determine when to reason by training only the initial root token (e.g., whether to invoke the <think> tag) via group relative reward and group-wise advantages. By focusing on this pivotal branching point, RPO drastically reduces training overhead and VRAM usage. Across multiple model families and scales, RPO learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at just ~2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods.

### [50] [Cross-Lingual Transfer of Evil Vectors Is Directionally Asymmetric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17880)
*Juann Kim,Minku Kang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Persona vectors are linear directions in the residual-stream activations of LLMs that encode behavioral traits and enable fine-grained control over model behavior. Among them, the evil persona vector is particularly relevant to understanding harmful behavior, jailbreak vulnerabilities, and the unlearning of harmful knowledge. Yet whether this vector reflects a genuinely cross-lingual concept, rather than an artifact of its extraction language, remains untested. We conduct a systematic evil-vector transfer study across two high-resource languages (English, Spanish) and two low-resource languages (Swahili, Telugu) on four open-source instruction-tuned LLMs, and find that transfer is directionally asymmetric. Evil vectors are harder to obtain reliably from low-resource languages, and the resulting vectors are largely ineffective at steering, even within their own language. In contrast, vectors extracted from high-resource languages transfer effectively to low-resource inputs while largely preserving general knowledge, as measured by MMLU. Geometric analysis further supports this pattern: evil vectors from the two high-resource languages are closely aligned, whereas low-resource vectors align only weakly with this shared direction. These results suggest that a shared cross-lingual evil direction exists and, once reliably extracted from a high-resource language, can be reused to steer behavior in low-resource languages without additional per-language data collection.

### [51] [Virtual Head Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17959)
*Xibo Ding,Guoxia Wang,Jinle Zeng,Jiabin Yang,Sirui Tao,Chao Yang,Dianhai Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.

### [52] [Seeing Through the Forgery Is Not Enough: Regressive Sycophancy under Fabricated Evidence in Medical Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17989)
*Sadif Ahmed,Soumya Swagata Biswas,Rifat Shahriyar,Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A medical vision-language model may analyze a given CT scan and correctly detect both kidneys in view. Continuing this conversation, if a user provides a prescription with an opposite direction, medical VLMs often sycophantically choose to realign their diagnosis. In this work, we study regressive sycophancy under fabricated evidence, where a model abandons a correct answer when pushback comes with a fake document. We test four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions in 19,200 multi-turn conversations, with and without a fabricated prescription. Without a disclosure that documents are synthetic, the models abandon 80.1% of 6,488 correct answers. Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%. A model rejected the prescription while still preserving the correct answer in 915 of 3,232 conversations with the prescription (28.3%), and 40% of these flipped in later turns. System-prompt sentences that disclose the documents as synthetic lower one model's flip rate from 77.8% to 47.3%. Thus, we conclude that awareness about a forgery does not prevent a model from adopting its answer.

Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%. A model rejected the prescription while still preserving the correct answer in 915 of 3,232 conversations with the prescription (28.3%), and 40% of these flipped in later turns. System-prompt sentences that disclose the documents as synthetic lower one model's flip rate from 77.8% to 47.3%. Thus, we conclude that awareness about a forgery does not prevent a model from adopting its answer.

### [53] [LatentRemedy: Efficient Remedy For Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18014)
*Zhiwei Chen,Zhongtao Rao,Waikit Xiu,Yuxiang Zhang,Shuting Cui,Jian Chen,Tianxiang Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Non-prefix KV cache reuse is a promising approach for improving inference efficiency in multi-agent systems as agents share the same context blocks. However, when agents have conflicting tasks, directly reusing non-prefix KV caches across agents can severely degrade model performance, causing up to a 90% drop. Existing remedies, including selective recomputation and offset-based calibration, recover a limited fraction of this loss. We argue that the problem lies not only in contaminated KV representations but also in the agent's difficulty interpreting reused context under its own instructions. To this end, we introduce LatentRemedy, which uses a few task-conditioned latent tokens to help the target agent leverage reused context without recomputing the shared block. Specifically, we use an MLP to map the last hidden state of the target prefix into a small number of latent tokens, which are placed after the reused KV block to interact with the shared context. To guide subsequent predictions toward the target task, we train the MLP through full-prefill distillation. Experiments show that LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks while maintaining TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size grows. Code and data are available at this https URL .

### [54] [Fan Out or Relay? Ownership-Aware Routing for LLM Agents Querying Siloed Tables](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18157)
*Zhexi Feng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Inside organizations, a question's data often sit with several owners, who query their own tables but never hand them over. An LLM coordinator can fan out, sending the question to every owner at once, or relay, querying owners in turn and reusing earlier rows. We show that neither is safe in advance, because data ownership decides which one is right. Across thirteen settings on PeopleJoin and BIRD with three model families, fan-out is more accurate in twelve on questions one owner can answer, yet answers at most 4.3% of those joining two owners' tables. The flip follows ownership, not query shape: on BIRD two-table joins, fan-out answers 32-44% when one owner holds both and 1-4% otherwise. Relay wins by conditioning on returned rows, and hiding them from an otherwise identical planner cuts two-owner accuracy from 23.2% to 5.1%. Since ownership is public, we propose Ownership-Aware Routing (OAR), which drafts a schema-only SQL query, counts the owners whose tables it joins, and routes the question before any private row is read. In ten settings OAR is never significantly less accurate than the best fixed protocol, and beats every fixed protocol on PeopleJoin, by up to 9.3 points on held-out organizations.

### [55] [Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18159)
*Jean Seo,Pepa Atanasova,Isabelle Augenstein*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.

### [56] [TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18216)
*Tianyu Huai,Jie Zhou,Bo Mao,Qin Chen,Liang He,Xipeng Qiu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.

### [57] [JevGPT: Thinking Fast and Slow in Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18272)
*Yasheng Sun,Yanning Dai,Yimeng Chen,Nanbo Li,Firas Laakom,Yifan Xu,Piotr Piękos,Mateusz Ostaszewski,Wenyi Wang,Cheng Luo,Yuhui Wang,Jürgen Schmidhuber*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Autonomous research agents must acquire and reason over evidence within a limited budget. Yet relevant sources can remain uninspected or unused, leaving a gap between retrieval coverage and the evidence that informs research. The challenge is to align fast local judgments with changing evidence needs and feed their findings back into research decisions. We introduce JevGPT, a dual-system architecture for autonomous research that couples fast evidence processing with deliberative research planning. System Two sets evidence objectives and integrates findings, while System One locates support, assesses relevance, and guides further inspection. Independent source judgments run in parallel; selected original passages inform the next research step. Experiments on fixed-corpus question answering and document ranking show that JevGPT achieves leading task performance, with faster completion and lower cost than comparably effective research agents. Evidence analysis shows broader source inspection and greater coverage of supporting documents in the research loop, highlighting efficient evidence processing as a route to more capable autonomous research.

### [58] [SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based Profile Enrichment for Conversational Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18308)
*Erfan Shahabi,Amirhossein Roshandel,Mohammad Sadegh Sadeghi,Azadeh Shakery*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) require reliable user simulators for cost-effective evaluation. LLM-based simulators have made realistic simulation possible but typically condition on profiles derived from explicit ratings, demographics, and static sources capturing surface preferences while omitting implicit behavioral characteristics such as decision-making style, aspect-level preferences, and domain expertise. We propose SimInter, a pipeline that elicits these attributes via synthetic interviews between two LLM agents, grounded in the user's statistical profile and historical conversational evidence. Before profile enrichment, an audit agent explicitly flags potential fabrication and stereotyping at the turn level. We instantiate and evaluate SimInter on movie recommendation. We simulate 300 ReDial users and, on a matched subset of 100 users, compare SimInter with a statistics-only baseline: SimInter significantly increases the diversity of expressed preference aspects (filtered aspect entropy: 1.619 vs. 0.859; paired d = 0.96, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). This gain persists when the simulator converses with two trained recommenders, KBRD and UniCRS, under two independent evaluation judges (+0.28 to +0.56 nats; all p < 0.001). Human evaluation finds 94.3% of enriched-attribute claims supported or partially supported, while human judgments agree with 95.2% of the auditor's binary filtering decisions on a stratified sample.

### [59] [Lightweight but Linguistically Fair? Quantisation Robustness across Bavarian, German, and English](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18343)
*Jophin John,Michael Hoffmann,Piroska Lendvai,Florent Dufour*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.

### [60] [Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18415)
*Pratuat Amatya,Vinay Setty,V Venktesh,Avishek Anand*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.

### [61] [Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18420)
*Ramchand Kumaresan,Madhusudhanan G,Kaushik Kezendirane*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files for this http URL , at this https URL code at this https URL

### [62] [Aligning Faithfulness for Theory-Scale Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18498)
*Yuming Feng,Tadd Mao,Dhruva Arekar,Tianjun Zhong,Jiani Huang,Xujie Si,Ziyang Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Autoformalization (AF) requires more than compilation: formal statements must preserve the meaning of their informal sources, a property known as faithfulness. An emerging frontier is the automated evaluation of this property, yet most existing methods operate at the statement level and produce whole-item verdicts, failing to reveal how individual expressions correspond or which contextual interpretations support the judgment. This omission is consequential because AF is inherently theory-scale: target statements derive their meaning from surrounding mathematical material and unstated conventions. We formulate faithfulness evaluation as a context-aware align-then-label problem: identifying phrase-level correspondences between informal and formal statements and assigning a faithfulness label to each under explicitly specified contextual interpretations and assumptions. We also introduce FaithAlign, the first theory-scale faithfulness benchmark comprising 460 items and 4,982 annotated phrase-level links, alongside FaithAlign-Gap, a companion set of 146 items with informal context and assumptions withheld. Each FaithAlign item includes the target statement pair, relevant context, formal dependencies, and, where needed, assumptions specifying one given interpretation. Across 8 models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest defect F1 at 47.8% and identifies all defects in only 4.5% of items with two or more defects. On FaithAlign-Gap, Astra identifies only 28.2% of undecidable items as such. These results show the difficulty of recovering context-dependent correspondences, establishing FaithAlign as a testbed for fine-grained, context-aware faithfulness evaluation.

On FaithAlign-Gap, Astra identifies only 28.2% of undecidable items as such. These results show the difficulty of recovering context-dependent correspondences, establishing FaithAlign as a testbed for fine-grained, context-aware faithfulness evaluation.

</details>


### [63] [The Geometry of Language Model Logits: Generic Structure and Learned Departures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18520)
*Swathi Shree Narashiman,Aravind Ramana Venkatramanan,Nambi Seshadri*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Autoregressive language models produce, at every prediction step, a vocabulary-sized logit vector whose structure determines the conditional next-token distribution. We empirically identify that the ordered vocabulary-head logits follow a remarkably consistent log-linear relation \[ z_{(r)} \approx \mu - \alpha \log r. \] across prediction contexts, architectures, and scales, emerging progressively during pretraining. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of the logit geometry underlying the distributional assumptions used in the prior decoding work. While controlled order-statistic baselines spanning bounded, light-tailed, and heavier-tailed distributions can largely explain the observed log-linear geometry, they do not explain the systematic shift in the slope $\alpha$: trained language models exhibit $\alpha \approx 1.4$--$1.7$, sitting well above the initialization baseline ($\alpha \approx 0.2$) . Moreover, $\alpha$ correlates with predictive performance, suggesting that it captures learned structure beyond generic extreme-value effects.

### [64] [The Many Morals of AI: The cautionary bias of North American news narratives in global perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18573)
*Andrew Piper,Edie Pearman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The stories told about artificial intelligence (AI) play a central role in shaping public understanding, policy debates, and expectations about technological change. News media are especially influential in this process. Using a cross-regional corpus of 12,924 English-language news articles about AI published since 2022, we examine how storytelling about AI varies across media systems in four regions: North America, China, India, and the Middle East. Leveraging large language models, we extract the implicit narrative lessons conveyed by each article---commonly known as story morals---capturing value-laden interpretations that extend beyond thematic content or sentiment. We find that North American AI coverage is uniquely characterized by narratives of caution, while under-emphasizing narratives of innovation and collaboration that are more prevalent elsewhere. However, this pattern is largely explained by a broader regional negativity bias in North American news sentiment, rather than by heightened concern about AI itself. Our findings bring into view the culturally conditioned nature of AI news narratives.

### [65] [Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18610)
*Kawai Chung,Chunkit Chan,Yuxuan Liu,Yauwai Yim,Xi Yang,Wenbin Hu,Huihao Jing,Chiu Yeung Tang,Changxuan Fan,Ki Sen Hung,Tsun On Kwok,Haoran Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.

### [66] [Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18616)
*Yuyang Bai,Yu Wang,Yu Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at this https URL .

### [67] [Known-Voice Cloning and the Limits of Personality Transfer for Character Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18669)
*Johanna Magdalena Kuch,Maud van Lier,Daksitha Senel Withanage Don,Patrick Gebhard,Tanja Schneeberger,Elisabeth André*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Recent advances in zero-shot voice cloning systems make it possible to reproduce a recognizable voice from a short recording and attach it to arbitrary virtual characters. Prior work suggests that familiar vocal identity can carry over associated personality impressions to new targets such as robots or virtual characters. However, these works have mainly examined familiarity and personalization effects rather than directly testing whether a cloned familiar voice systematically transfers personality impressions to an embodied virtual character. Such transference raises the concern that cloned voices could be used to manipulate people into engaging with virtual characters as capable social actors. Across two studies, we investigated whether personality impressions transfer when a virtual character speaks with the cloned voice of a familiar person. Study 1 examined this question in a real-world university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer familiar to the participating students. Study 2 examined the same question online using voices of social media content creators and members of their communities. Drawing on the concepts of identity activation, trait transfer, and person reconstruction, we show that evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies. Observed effects were selective and did not generalize across traits or study contexts. In the online study in particular, recognizable voice identity cues activated expectations about the speaker but did not reconstruct the broader person impression. Qualitative responses further indicated that judgments were frequently shaped by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together. Our findings moderate common concerns that cloned voices straightforwardly manipulate people into perceiving artificial characters as capable social actors.

### [68] [SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18672)
*Ziyang Song,Lia Shen,Yixuan Li,Qincheng Lu,Weihao Li,Haoran Xu,He Zhu,Xinyu Wang,Yue Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Biomedical language models (LMs) provide strong representations for clinical tasks, but they often fail to capture the hierarchical structure among medical concepts. This limitation is especially pronounced for rare and fine-grained clinical codes in long-tailed vocabularies, where hierarchy-agnostic LM representations become less informative as concept frequency decreases. We introduce Semantic Medical Identifier (SMI), a training-free framework for constructing ontology-grounded Semantic IDs and hierarchy-aware medical concept representations. For each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept, SMI defines its Semantic ID as the coarse-to-fine path through an expert-defined medical ontology. SMI then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the corresponding ontology levels to form hierarchy-aware medical concept representations that preserve coarse-to-fine clinical semantics. The base SMI uses uniform aggregation across ontology levels, while a level-weighted variant selects global level weights on validation data. Our theoretical analysis shows that SMI yields more informative medical concept representations than hierarchy-agnostic LM embeddings, particularly for rare and fine-grained clinical concepts. Experiments show that SMI captures meaningful hierarchical structure and improves clinical relation prediction. On MIMIC-IV, SMI improves mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction. On eICU, SMI yields more robust patient representations under cross-hospital distribution shift.

### [69] [From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18674)
*Jinghan Zheng,Jiajun Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

### [70] [Where Do LLM Ensemble Gains Come From? Decomposing Candidate Value, Diversity, and Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18786)
*Donghwan Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM ensemble gains are often measured against a single baseline, but the value attributed to additional candidates can change with the comparison used. We study an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions: Direct (no candidates), Single-slot (one candidate in a multi-slot interface), Duplicate (one candidate repeated), and Multi-candidate (separately generated candidates). Under either non-diverse control, overall candidate gain (CIV) splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast (DSV) and a candidate-context contrast (CCV); the split, but not CIV, depends on the chosen control. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2), the repetition gap Rep=-8.33 pp [-13.25, -3.75] quantifies the difference between gains measured against Duplicate and Single-slot. On a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200, k=3, aggregator output limit 4096), paired Delta Rep=+9.67 pp [+6.00, +13.50]; within panels, Rep changes sign (original -6.33; stronger +3.33). In FRAMES evidence aggregation, candidate-context contrasts remain strongly negative under both non-diverse controls. Our results show why ensemble evaluations should state the reference control before attributing gains to additional candidates.

### [71] [Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18818)
*Divyanshu Bathla,Parag Singla,Jitin Singla*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.

### [72] [Hybrid Reasoning Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18861)
*Jiaru Zou,Yunzhe Qi,Sirui Chen,Federico Bianchi,Shang Zhu,Pan Lu,Jingrui He,James Zou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL .

### [73] [DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18862)
*Minghao Luo,Liang Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at this https URL .

It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at this https URL .

</details>


### [74] [Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18868)
*Wenbo Hu,Shraman Pramanick,Krishna Kumar Singh,Nanyun Peng,Kai-Wei Chang,Yong Jae Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.

### [75] [SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16870)
*Zhiqing Zhong,Mingyu Chen,Aoyang Fang,Yuzhong Zhang,Haoye Tian,Lionel Briand,Boxi Yu,Pinjia He*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.

### [76] [Mira-Embeddings-V1: Domain-Adapted Semantic Reranking for Recruitment via LLM-Synthesized Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17738)
*Zhaohua Liang,Zhilin Wang,Renjie Cao,Yining Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Candidate sourcing for recruiters is best viewed as a two-stage retrieval and reranking pipeline with recall as the primary objective under a limited review budget. An upstream production retriever first returns a candidate shortlist for each job description (JD), and our goal is to rerank that shortlist so that qualified candidates appear as high as possible. We present mira-embeddings-v1, a semantic reranking system for the recruitment domain that reshapes the embedding space with LLM-synthesized training data and corrects boundary confusions with a lightweight reranking head. Starting from real JDs, we build a five-stage prompt pipeline to generate diverse positive and hard negative samples that sculpt the semantic space from multiple angles. We then apply a two-round LoRA adaptation: JD--JD contrastive training followed by JD--CV triplet alignment on a heterogeneous text dataset. Importantly, these gains require no large-scale manually labeled industrial training pairs: a modest set of real JDs is expanded into supervision through LLM synthesis. Finally, a BoundaryHead MLP reranks the Top-K results to distinguish between roles that share the same title but differ in scope. On a local pool of 300 real JDs with candidates from an upstream production retriever, mira-embeddings-v1 improves Recall@50 from 68.89% (baseline) to 77.55% while lifting Precision@10 from 35.77% to 39.62%. On a supportive global pool over 44,138 candidates judged by a Qwen3-32B rubric, it achieves Recall@200 of 0.7047 versus 0.5969 for the baseline. These results show that LLM-synthesized supervision with boundary-aware reranking yields robust gains without a heavy cross-encoder.

### [77] [PsyBer-Agent: A Psychology-Driven User Agent for Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13989)
*Chong Zhang,Qijie Shen,Haichao Zhang,Can Wang,Xiaobo Jin,Jia Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Evaluating recommender systems before deployment requires simulators that remain realistic over long, closed-loop interaction cycles. Current LLM-based agents generally function as surface imitators that generate realistic short-term responses but fail to capture the underlying user dynamics such as fatigue, affect, and shifting preferences. We propose PsyBer-Agent, a psychology-inspired simulator that models these dynamics through its Psy-Engine. This engine represents each user with three evolving, model-defined latent states. To calibrate simulated behavior against real interaction logs, we align log-conditioned reference trajectories with simulator-generated latent-state trajectories via Unbalanced Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport. This approach provides structured supervision for a lightweight policy without the computational burden of fine-tuning the backbone LLM. We also introduce WebSim and the PsyBer Benchmark, which encompass multimodal scenarios and seven recommender backbones. Our framework evaluates behavioral fidelity, latent-state consistency, robustness, and responses to social-cue perturbations. On the tested horizons, PsyBer-Agent shows lower behavioral discrepancy than the prompt-only simulators while maintaining stable performance under large-scale concurrent simulation for up to 5M queued simulation tasks under bounded concurrency. Code is available in the supplementary material and at: PsyBer-Agent: this https URL , WebSim Platform: this https URL .

### [78] [Does System One Transfer? Calibrated Typed-Decision Models, Label Budgets, and Translation for Indonesian Regional Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14112)
*Romi Fadli,Rusdah,Wahyu Ramadani Putri Utami,Zulfa Malika Amana*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Calibrated typed-decision ("System One") models return a label and a probability in a single forward pass at a small fraction of the cost of large language models (LLMs), yet their evaluation has been almost entirely English. We report a pre-registered evaluation of the commercial Jev model and the open Laya-multilingual model on Indonesian regional languages, using the parallel NusaX sentiment (12 languages) and NusaTranslation sentiment and emotion (7 languages) test sets. Jev is more often correct on sentences that are lexically closer to Indonesian in all three datasets, and presenting the human Indonesian translation instead raises its accuracy by up to 37.2 points, most in languages distant from Indonesian. Its expected calibration error does not grow on regional languages, but its ability to rank its own errors degrades in all three datasets. Retrained classifiers need more than 500 labels per language to match zero-shot Jev in 9 of 10 NusaX regional languages. A confidence-gated cascade that sends Jev's 10-30% least confident decisions to a local IndoBERT classifier matches or exceeds the better of the two systems, and routing to an LLM instead matches that LLM at 24-77% lower API cost. Of six further commercial LLMs (three Claude and three GPT models), five are 4-14 points more accurate than Jev, at several hundred times the API cost where it is reported, while the smallest (Claude Haiku) is less accurate. We release the pre-registration, code and all predictions.

### [79] [Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14423)
*Aditi Khandelwal,Ayush K. Tarun,Yixuan Xu,Imanol Schlag,Golnoosh Farnadi,Siva Reddy,Luke Zettlemoyer,Antoine Bosselut*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

### [80] [Dependency Reasoning for Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14873)
*Shima Esfandyar,Seywan Soleymanbaigi,Fardin Akhlaghian Tab,Fatemeh Daneshfar,Mourad Oussalah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction (ASQP) is fundamentally a relational reasoning problem: identifying aspect-opinion-category-sentiment quadruples requires modeling structured dependencies, not merely sequential co-occurrence. Existing LLM-based approaches incorporate syntactic information indirectly, via retrieval-based demonstration selection or multi-stage training, rather than as unified, single-pass generation-time context. We present DRIFT, which linearizes dependency parse trees and injects them directly into LLM prompts as explicit relational context, enabling the model to reason over aspect-opinion dependencies rather than infer them from token proximity alone. DRIFT further integrates retrieval-augmented in-context learning and a syntax-aware LLM-based adjudication mechanism that complements exact-match evaluation under span-boundary variation. On SemEval Rest15, Rest16, and ACOS, DRIFT achieves the strongest performance among compared generative ASQP methods, reaching 54.47% and 64.10% F1 on Rest15 and Rest16, with consistent gains across short- and medium-distance aspect-opinion configurations; adjudication further shows exact-match metrics systematically underestimate semantically correct predictions.

### [81] [Sanzaru: Benchmarking Protocol Formation under Epistemic & Communication Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15163)
*Yiping Li,Zhiyu An,Wan Du*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A language model's ability to solve a task individually does not ensure that a team can solve it under unequal access to information and communication. SANZARU examines this gap through cooperative bomb-defusal puzzles adapted from BOMBANANA! (Lefto Studio, 2026). Task information and action authority are divided among three agents: one cannot hear, another cannot speak, and the third cannot see. The benchmark contains 120 puzzle instances across seven families, each targeting a distinct coordination ability. Across 1512 episodes, 7 models achieve an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86% under the evaluated configurations. Teams develop or adopt diverse communication protocols, from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals. Yet trace analysis attributes about 60% of 771 team losses to communication, and agents attempt to use channels unavailable to their teammates despite explicit role instructions. Together, task outcomes and interaction traces enable evaluation of both collaborative performance and perspective taking throughout cooperation. The benchmark is available at this https URL .

### [82] [SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15186)
*Xingjian Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.

### [83] [AlphaPilot: Multi-Turn Tool-Using LLM Agents for Adaptive Alpha Mining with Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15488)
*Peiqi Jiang,Fan Zhang,Xin Xu,Tianhao Chen,Can Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.

### [84] [Enhancing Zero-Shot Domain Transfer in Low-Resource Sentiment Analysis: A Case Study in Marathi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15757)
*Tanvi Somani,Aryan Babare,Samyak Bora,Raviraj Joshi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Sentiment analysis is a key task in Natural Language Processing that determines the polarity of opinions in text. For low-resource languages like Marathi--where limited data prevents the direct use of standard statistical methods--models are often trained on single-domain datasets. While this yields strong in-domain performance, it leads to poor generalization to unseen domains. Recent studies highlight the need for domain-robust systems that can handle diverse real-world content through multi-domain modeling. This study investigates how multi-domain training improves sentiment classification for unseen Marathi domains. Models are trained using single-domain, two-domain, and three-domain dataset combinations. Results show that two-domain training improves accuracy on unseen domains by about 8\% compared to single-domain training. Adding a third domain provides further improvement, though the gain is smaller, averaging around 2\% for some domains. These results suggest that training with data from multiple domains helps build more robust sentiment analysis models for low-resource languages, though the benefits reduce as more domains are added.

### [85] [Robust Marathi Sentiment Analysis using Domain-Adaptive Pre-training and Data Augmentation Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15761)
*Tanvi Somani,Aryan Babare,Samyak Bora,Raviraj Joshi,Abhinay Dhamankar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: For languages with limited resources, Sentiment Analysis remains a challenging problem due to limited annotated data and strong domain variability across textual sources. Marathi, despite being widely spoken, lacks extensive multi-domain sentiment analysis studies. Recent efforts by L3Cube have introduced multi-domain datasets in Marathi, enabling a better study of domain-aware sentiment classification. This study uses the pretrained MahaBERT model to improve sentiment classification for Marathi across different domains. Models are trained on individual domain datasets and domain-adaptive pretraining is applied using masked language modeling to help the model better understand domain-specific language. In addition, back-translation is used as a method of data augmentation to increase the diversity of training data. Results show that these methods lead to consistent improvements in accuracy across all domains. The improvements range from a minimum of about 0.12% to a maximum of about 1.74%, depending on the dataset. These results demonstrate that domain-adaptive pretraining and data augmentation are effective strategies for improving sentiment analysis models. This helps achieve more robust performance across different domains and makes the approach more suitable for low-resource languages like Marathi.

### [86] [Latent Taxonomies: How Property Induction Develops in Language Model Pre-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15836)
*Jan Sobotka,Ekaterina Goliakova,Marcin Detyniecki,Antoine Bosselut,Xavier Renard*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. To shed light on this, we construct a hierarchical taxonomy of synthetic entities grouped by the properties they share. We then inject facts from this latent taxonomy into the continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models from 70M to 7B parameters, and track the development of inductive behaviors. We find that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone: a property learned for one entity transfers more strongly within its taxonomic category than across categories. Internally, entities that share a deeper category become more similar in activation space, and clustering recovers the full taxonomic tree from entity representations. Contrary to the usual expectation that scale helps, we find that induction weakens with model size when the data budget is fixed, suggesting that larger models memorize individual facts rather than compress them into shared structure. Induction also strengthens with more pre-training before the taxonomy injection, transfers to novel in-context properties, and can be overridden by a latent taxonomy implied by the prompt. Together, these results show that a model's inductive generalization reflects the latent organization of its training data, with implications for data curation and for predicting how far a learned fact will spread.

### [87] [Improving the Evaluation of Biomedical Question Answering with Few Human Preference Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16008)
*Shakila Mahjabin Tonni,Xiang Dai,Sarvnaz Karimi,Xiaomei Li,Samuel C. Andrew,Stephen Wan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly used for biomedical Question Answering (QA). However, evaluating their effectiveness remains challenging due to the lack of reliable reference resources and the frequent misalignment between automatic evaluation metrics and human judgments. One practical question is how evaluation results should be used to guide development decisions, especially when they correlate weakly with human judgments and may even lead to different conclusions. We explore how to use a small amount of human preference signals to calibrate direct assessment evaluation metrics, and show that calibrated metrics consistently outperform baselines that either treat all metrics equally or rely on a single best metric across multiple datasets.

### [88] [Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16165)
*Rishi Khare*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.

### [89] [Deep Speech Representations Track Word Timing along a Low-Dimensional Circular Trajectory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16273)
*Burin Naowarat,Hao Tang,Sharon Goldwater*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Speech timing is fundamental for speech models to recognize words accurately, but how word-timing information is represented in speech models remains underexplored. We study this question using the framework of representational geometry, which investigates whether and how concepts are represented in low-dimensional subspaces of the representation space. Prior work in cognitive neuroscience has shown that when HuBERT feature sequences are averaged across words of the same duration, they form near-circular trajectories from word onset to word offset in a two-dimensional "temporal subspace." Here we show that this circular structure of word timing is a general property of deep speech representations, by demonstrating its emergence in nine additional speech models covering both supervised and self-supervised. We then move beyond averaged word segments and show that in HuBERT, the circular trajectories are consistent enough at the level of individual words to perform word segmentation. Our approach, Rotary Segmentation (RoSeg), achieves 64.3% boundary F-score on Librispeech by detecting word boundaries when cycles complete in the temporal subspace. Although supervision is needed to identify a good subspace, nevertheless this result demonstrates much stronger implicit word knowledge in HuBERT than has previously been shown.

### [90] [RIFT: Token Influence Follows the Path of Least Resistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16349)
*Tingan Jin,Shuhang Dong,Haosong Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Which context tokens drive a language model's answer? Graph-based tools such as attention rollout and attention flow answer this from a single forward pass, yet their faithfulness in decoder-only models is rarely tested against interventions. We view the layers of a decoder as a causal network whose conductances are attention weights, and read a token's influence on the answer from the resistance between them. We propose RIFT (Resistance-based Information Flow in Transformers), which scores a token by the series resistance of its path of least resistance to the answer, found exactly by a classic shortest-path dynamic program. On synthetic in-context retrieval tasks and extractive question answering over Wikipedia paragraphs, RIFT predicts the effect of replacing a token with a Spearman correlation of 0.52-0.68; predicting a single replacement, it reaches 77-96% of the agreement between two different random replacements. It needs no gradients and no extra forward passes, scoring every token of a prompt in 0.9-3.4 ms on one CPU thread, whereas the replacement experiment needs a forward pass per token. On 576 held-out prompts from four models of two families (Qwen3 and Llama 3.2), it outperforms token distance, attention rollout and attention flow in every pre-specified comparison, by 0.23 to 0.88 in mean Spearman correlation, and it is the best or tied-best of all attention-based scores we test. Aggregates that add up all routes (attention flow, effective resistance and rollout) instead mostly encode token position: as a simple proposition shows, early tokens have many more parallel routes to the answer.

### [91] [Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16533)
*Zhipeng Chen,Wayne Xin Zhao,Ji-Rong Wen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at this https URL .

### [92] [Know Yourself and Know Your Neighbour: A Syntactically Informed Self-Supervised Compositional Sentence Representation Learning Framework using a Recursive Hypernetwork](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16547)
*Vasudevan Nedumpozhimana,John Kelleher*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Sentence representation learning is still an open challenge in Natural Language Processing. In this work, we propose a new self-supervised framework for learning sentence representations, using a special type of neural network called a recursive hypernetwork. Our proposed model composes the representation of a sentence from representations of words by applying a recursive composition through the parse tree. We maintain a separate syntactic and semantic representation, and the semantic composition is guided by the information from the syntactic representation. To train this model, we introduce a novel set of six self-supervised tasks. By analysing the performance on 7 probing tasks, we validate that the generated sentence representation encodes richer linguistic information than both averaging baselines and state-of-the-art alternatives. Furthermore, we assess the impact of the six proposed self-supervised training tasks through ablation studies. We also demonstrate that the representations generated by our model are stable for sentences of varying length and that the semantic composition operators adapt to different syntactic categories\footnote{Code available: this https URL }.

### [93] [A Bethe-Ansatz Source of Early Token Correlations: A marginal-preserving construction for parallel proposals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16781)
*Abraham Chachamovits*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Parallel token proposals in language-model decoding need a joint law, not merely accurate token marginals. We construct a family of coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain and compare each with its maximum-entropy pairwise projection at identical one- and two-site moments. In the eight-site, three-excitation sector, symmetry makes their entire probability-law difference one-dimensional, determined by a contiguous three-site moment. Along the Bethe branch, this gap varies with anisotropy, changes sign, and vanishes exactly at $\Delta=(3+\sqrt{3})/2$, where the eigenstate law becomes exactly pairwise. A nonlinear readout transfers a nonzero gap into the first two token positions while preserving their separate marginals. At $\Delta=1.5$ the deterministic binary token laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation. Exact speculative verification then gives a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and a neighborhood within targets sharing its first-token marginal. This is a mathematical existence result. It does not establish a language-model gain or wall-clock speedup.

### [94] [Predicting Mental Health Help-Seeking Behaviour on Reddit: A Survival Analysis of Linguistic and Behavioural Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16983)
*Nisar Ahmed,Ammara Kazmi,Irtaza Bashir Raja,Didier Devaurs*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Most prior work on predicting mental health help-seeking treats it as post-hoc classification of users already active in clinical communities, which cannot tell whether someone approaching a transition can be identified in advance. We instead frame help-seeking as a time-to-event problem and ask which Reddit users will eventually seek mental health support, and how imminent that transition is. We build a two-arm cohort: a control frame of 6,337 ordinary users with genuine right-censoring (12.1% transition rate) to answer who will transition, and a clinical frame of 5,023 eventual transitioners to answer how soon. Features come only from posts written before any clinical activity, and user-grouped five-fold cross-validation plus a four-year temporal holdout guard against leakage. We compare TF-IDF, MentalBERT embeddings and behavioural activity features using Cox proportional hazards models, Random Survival Forests and an LSTM sequential model. Behavioural features alone outperform text for predicting who will seek help (C-index 0.797 vs. 0.763), and combining both is best (0.823 under cross-validation, 0.856 on the holdout). The pattern reverses for predicting how soon a known transition will happen: text remains a stable predictor (C-index 0.698) while behavioural features become unstable. Structural engagement patterns therefore carry information about future help-seeking beyond linguistic content, and separating who from when yields a cleaner analysis.
