Our experiments indicate that the associative ability of VLMs depends on the cue concepts provided in the text and does not universally extend to visual puzzles.

</details>


### [240] [Decomposing and Predicting Annotation Disagreement in Harmful Content Across Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18588)
*Irem Ecem Yelkanat,Faeze Ghorbanpour,Alexander Fraser*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Annotator disagreement is increasingly recognized as a meaningful property of subjective tasks, rather than merely noise to be removed. Predicting which items are likely to be contested could help allocate annotation effort and route difficult cases to human review. We propose predicting disagreement from interpretable semantic properties of the text. An LLM answers a set of binary questions covering harmful-content characteristics, disagreement-related cues such as borderline severity and missing context, and language-sensitive cues such as local slurs. A classifier predicts disagreement from these answers, and we analyze which questions contribute most to the predictions. Across four datasets in English, German, and Turkish and three open-weight LLMs, our structured question features outperform direct prompting by 10.5 ROC-AUC points and the strongest text-based baselines by 5.0 points. A compact subset of eight questions performs within 1.5 ROC-AUC points of the full twenty-question set. In leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, models retain roughly 90-95% of their in-domain ROC-AUC. Across models and datasets, questions about derogation, missing context, and decision boundaries serve as the strongest predictors, suggesting that what makes harmful content contested is partly observable in the text.

### [241] [From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18605)
*Ziyang Ling*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Large language models (LLMs) often diagnose full sight, static clinical cases well yet struggle in foresight, dynamic diagnosis. Prior work has improved this limitation by quantifying the information models acquire and by developing stronger follow-up strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, we introduce a distinctive hindsight to systematically dissect why LLMs fail to acquire diagnostically critical evidence, tracing the failure from evidence identification, utilization and downstream diagnostic updating through not only diagnostic accuracy, but also evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, and elicited probability and information entropy. Starting experiments from the breakdown at the level of capabilities, to the diagnosis of the pre-event state before the evidence arrives, and to the post-event state transition after the evidence arrives, our research has revealed the profound limitations and internal causes existing in the dynamic diagnostic process. At the same time, we have also conducted sufficient verification and generalization experiments to prove that these limitations are widespread. Together, these findings shift the central challenge from whether LLMs possess relevant clinical knowledge to whether they can identify, acquire, and effectively use the right evidence under clinical diagnosis and conduct a more detailed mechanism analysis to identify the exact location of the capability gap.

### [242] [Legal-R1: Agentic Retrieval for Evidence-Based Legal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18611)
*Huaiwen Pang,Jiale Han,Junying Chen,Wenjun Xiao,Benyou Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Legal question answering requires answers that are not only plausible, but also grounded in legally valid and citable evidence. Standard retrieval-augmented generation often relies on one-shot semantic matching, which is insufficient when legal evidence must be selected according to authority, applicability, and diversity across heterogeneous sources. We introduce Legal-R1, an agentic retrieval framework for evidence-based legal reasoning. Legal-R1 decomposes legal reasoning into a multi-agent workflow, where a Lawyer agent learns when to retrieve, which legal source to query, what evidence to seek, and when the collected evidence is sufficient. A Legal Assistant agent retrieves from normative legal sources and precedent cases with authority-aware and diversity-aware selection, while a Judge agent generates the final answer from the complete evidence trajectory. We post-train only the Lawyer agent with masked supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-aware reinforcement learning. Experiments on multiple Chinese legal benchmarks show that Legal-R1 improves over general-purpose, legal-specific, and retrieval-augmented baselines.

### [243] [Breakdown of Conversational Involvement: A Joint Multi-Modal Analysis of Conversation Floors and F-formation Detection with Multiple Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18627)
*Zonghuan Li,Chirag Raman,Hayley Hung*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Interactions happen universally and spontaneously in daily lives. Studying involvement in interactions helps us analyze who can influence who and has a wide potential in applications. Specifically, we consider conversational involvement in free-standing conversations. We study two operationalizations of an FCG: F-formations and conversation floors, and propose that current assumption that F-formations capture single conversations is insufficient. To illustrate how different implementations could impact the detected F-formations, we employ three analyses. First, we propose that speaking status can be used for estimating conversation floors, and leveraged it to analyze floors within F-formations. Second, we analyze spatial characteristics of the detection results by applying different feature sets on chosen baselines, and find that groups resulting from head features are more likely to be subsumed by groups detected using other features. Finally, we do a joint analysis which combines the spatial features and floor patterns in the conversation. We observe that certain pipelines can detect groups with single floors from upper body features, while retaining F-formations with lower body features. We conclude that a more detailed theory and framework is needed to holistically demonstrate conversational involvement within interactions.

### [244] [Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18726)
*Jie Chi,Zakaria Aldeneh,Masha Fedzechkina,Maureen de Seyssel,Natalie Schluter*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of $0.798$ across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with $0.776$ for a CNN and $0.751$ for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora.

### [245] [Looking Complete Is Not Being Grounded: Evaluating LLM Sitreps Against Human-Authored Situation Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18762)
*Sachin Kumar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Evaluation for automatic crisis reporting should measure what practitioners need, not what is convenient to compare. Through LLM-assisted, author-approved content analysis, we derive a 15-slot information schema from professional humanitarian situation reports using qualitative content analysis, then evaluate 121 human and 261 LLM-generated reports across five disasters and three hazard types. Under google/gemini-3.7-flash on Cyclone Idai, the best machine arm is nominally above the empirical human ceiling (0.827 vs. 0.821), but the difference is statistically indistinguishable from zero (95\% bootstrap CI $[-.049,.059]$; permutation $p=.852$), and the ordering does not replicate under openai/gpt-5.6-luna. On a blind 100-item Idai sample, the author agrees with the Gemini judge at 0.910 accuracy and unweighted Cohen's $\kappa=.799$. All four judges clear the plan's raw-agreement criterion of .7; only Gemini reaches .7 on chance-corrected $\kappa$. Across the three primary events, machine reports reproduce 5.4-11.0% of same-day official figures. Across those same events, raw exact-number matching links 14.3-19.6% of official figures and 85.4-90.1% of machine figures to the social stream; manual audit confirms 45/50 declared absences, 4/25 official matches, and 24/25 machine matches semantically. The issuing-provenance gap is positive in all 12 observed event-judge cells: report date, organisation, series, and authority were not supplied at professional-report coverage in any cell. On the three primary events, ROUGE-L is uninformative, BERTScore is negatively associated with completeness after multiplicity correction, and a generic LLM judge changes sign.

### [246] [Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18766)
*Tianci Liu,Haoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Rubric-based reward models (RMs) evaluate responses against explicit criteria. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability. Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone, and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization. We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher's outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization. We further find that generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and that higher preference accuracy does not necessarily translate into better downstream policies. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research.

### [247] [Almost Lossless Transfer for Cuttable Distributed Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15596)
*Wojciech Wawrzyniak*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We study constant-round LOCAL approximation for additive local vertex-subset minimization problems. Given a $k$-uniform $\alpha$-approximation on a hereditary source class closed under disjoint union, Bonamy, Das, Gavoille, Picavet, Suomela, and Wesolek obtained ratio $\alpha(d+1)+1$ on locally nice target classes of asymptotic dimension $d$. We prove two transfers with ratios $\alpha+1+\eta$ and $\alpha+\eta$ for every $\eta>0$. These bounds require the stronger local niceness assumption at a larger scale that depends on $\eta$. The first algorithm keeps their repair construction and increases the radius used to detect errors. We average over partitions of the graph to bound the retained cost without the factor $d+1$. These partitions are used only in the analysis. The second algorithm tests several deletion widths around the errors. In each component of the repair zone, it chooses a smallest union of retained choices and an exact repair. Averaging over the widths bounds the cost counted twice and yields ratio $\alpha+\eta$. Both transfers are deterministic and computable, use arbitrary distinct numerical identifiers, and need no knowledge of the graph size. Their outputs also satisfy local uniformity guarantees. For 2-domination on graphs of bounded Euler genus, the same planar source gives ratio $19$ through the earlier transfer and $6+\eta$ through ours. For minimum dominating set, our transfer gives ratio $7+\varepsilon$ on graphs formed by attaching a clique of arbitrary size at one vertex of a planar graph, using the source algorithm of Amiri and Siebertz. This class satisfies our target assumptions and allows nonempty error sets. Its Euler genus is unbounded, so their guarantee for graphs of bounded Euler genus does not cover the whole class.

### [248] [Distributed $(Δ+1)$-Coloring in $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ Rounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16575)
*Marc Fuchs,Fabian Kuhn*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We give a deterministic distributed algorithm for $(\Delta+1)$-coloring an $n$-node graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ in $O(\sqrt\Delta+\log^* n)$ rounds in both the LOCAL and CONGEST models. More generally, $(°+1)$-list coloring with lists from a color space of size $C\geq\Delta+1$ can be solved in $O(\sqrt\Delta\log(1+C/\Delta)+\log^* n)$ rounds; in CONGEST, we assume $C\leq n^{O(1)}$. The algorithm combines Barenboim's polynomial coloring procedure with arbdefective decompositions, degree reduction, and a short family of hash functions. Using the polynomial procedure in the degree-reduction framework already gives an $O(\sqrt\Delta\log\Delta+\log^* n)$-round algorithm when $C=O(\Delta)$. Hashing adapts the color space to the current degree and removes the logarithmic factor. We prove the existence of the hash family by the probabilistic method and compute it by deterministic exhaustive search, using unrestricted local computation. We also give an explicit variant based on lossless expanders that avoids this search and achieves $O(\sqrt\Delta+\log^* n)$ rounds for $C=O(\Delta)$.

### [249] [No Truly Sublogarithmic-Round Algorithm for Distributed MIS in the LOCAL Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18215)
*Seri Khoury,Aaron Schild*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We prove that $o(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})$-round randomized LOCAL algorithms find a maximal independent set (MIS) with subconstant probability on some input. This shows that the 40-year-old $O(\log n)$-round randomized CONGEST algorithm of Luby and Alon, Babai, and Itai is nearly optimal. Our lower bound improves upon the $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$-round lower bound of Khoury and Schild and nearly closes the 20+ year-old gap between the $O(\log n)$-round algorithm and the $\Omega(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}})$-round lower bound of Kuhn, Moscibroda, and Wattenhofer. To close this gap, one must show a lower bound for a graph that is not locally treelike. We do this by starting with a $D$-regular, $\Theta(\log_D n)$-girth graph, with $D = \Theta(\log n)$. Crucially, this is not our final graph. We obtain our hard instance by \emph{replacing} each vertex of this treelike graph with a clique on $n^c$ vertices for some constant $c \in (0,1)$. We then replace each edge with a bipartite Erdős--Rényi graph between the corresponding cliques, with each edge present independently with probability $1/2$. We analyze arbitrary LOCAL algorithms on our non-treelike hard instance with a novel round elimination approach. We describe algorithms that output a set of vertices in this graph using two metrics: their \emph{occupancy probability} and their \emph{conflict probability}. Our round elimination framework takes an $r$-round algorithm and produces an $(r-1)$-round algorithm where occupancy and conflict probabilities collectively slightly degrade, but individually can significantly improve or degrade. This round elimination result is obtained by exploiting the lack of large biclique complements in dense bipartite Erdős--Rényi graphs, which in turn allows us to bound the entropy of the output distribution for any independent set algorithm.

### [250] [Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16144)
*Muntaser Syed,Ameerah Alsulami,Marius Silaghi*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure. We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). Against the radix matcher on a live vLLM stack serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M on four A100 GPUs, Hashrope identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20x faster, at a context length the dense engine cannot even prefill.

Abstract: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. ### [251] [Grover Search for a Threshold-Fraction Variant of the Travelling Salesman Problem: A Circuit-Level Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14062)
*Aayra Dhindsa Sawkmie*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: The Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) is a classic combinatorial optimisation problem which is NP-hard in optimisation form and NP-complete as a decision problem. The standard question asks for the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the origin. This paper studies a threshold-fraction variant, which we call the robust TSP, formulated as a promise problem: given a distance threshold $K$ and a promised fraction $p$, decide whether at least a fraction $p$ of all tours have total length at most $K$, or whether no such tour exists. We show that Grover's quantum search algorithm decides this problem using $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ oracle queries, independent of the number of cities $N$, with each query implemented by a quantum circuit of polynomial size in $N$. For any fixed robustness level $p$, the total runtime is therefore polynomial in $N$. Measured in oracle queries, the quantum algorithm offers a quadratic improvement in the dependence on $1/p$ over classical random sampling, which needs $\Theta(1/p)$ samples; because each quantum query is costly, however, it is faster in total running time only when $p$ is very small (roughly below $N^{-4}$), where the number of queries is no longer constant. We describe the problem formulation, detail the oracle construction (edge-length loading, sequential quantum addition, and threshold comparison), and analyse the query complexity to achieve the required result.

### [252] [Many Scores Force Many Reads: An Optimality Proof for Score of Parentheses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14213)
*Andrew Au*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: LeetCode Problem 856, Score of Parentheses, admits a one-pass algorithm using $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary registers. Its correctness follows from a local interpretation: every occurrence of () contributes a power of two determined by its nesting depth. The space bound is immediately optimal in the usual programming-challenge model, but the linear-time bound is less obvious. In particular, a direct adversary that forces an algorithm to inspect every character is difficult to maintain under the promise that the input is balanced. We instead prove a counting lower bound. For every $k$, we construct $2^k$ balanced parenthesis strings of the same length $4k+2$, all having distinct scores. The construction encodes each bit using one of two operations, changing a current score $v$ to either $2v+1$ or $2v+2$. Consequently, any deterministic character-query decision tree computing the score must have depth at least $k$. A two-character padding argument extends the result to every even input length, proving an $\Omega(n)$ worst-case time lower bound. The one-pass algorithm is therefore asymptotically optimal in the unit-cost RAM model.

### [253] [Faster Deterministic Approximation for Counting Knapsack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14595)
*Ce Jin,Jaewoo Park,Barna Saha*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Given $n$ nonnegative integer weights $w_1, \ldots, w_n$ and an integer knapsack capacity $T$, the $\#$Knapsack problem asks to count the number of subsets $I \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ such that $\sum_{i \in I} w_i \le T$. A long line of research has been devoted to designing faster $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for this \#P-hard problem. Until very recently, the best-known time complexity was $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{2.5}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$, achieved by the randomized algorithm of [Dyer, STOC 2003] and the deterministic algorithm of [Gawrychowski, Markin, and Weimann, ICALP 2018]. The recent work by [Feng and Jin, SODA 2025] improved the randomized complexity to $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{1.5}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$, leaving open the question whether this $n^{2.5}$ barrier could also be broken by a \emph{deterministic} algorithm. In this work, we answer this question in the affirmative by presenting a deterministic $(1 + \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for \#Knapsack in $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{2.4}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$ time. Our key technical innovation is to deterministically simulate the balancing technique, which was previously used in the literature of knapsack-type problems via random partitions and seemed to require randomization.

### [254] [The Matching Number Characterizes the Query Complexity of Edge Counting and Degree Moment Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14604)
*Chenglin Fan,Wonseok Shin*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Consider an unknown graph $G = (V,E)$ with vertex degrees $d_v$, accessed only by sampling uniformly random edges and querying the degrees of their endpoints. We study the query complexity of estimating the number of edges $m$ and the degree moments $M_s = \sum_{v \in V} (d_v)^s$ for fixed integers $s \ge 2$. In this model, [Beretta and Tětek, TALG 2024] estimate $m$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ using $O(\log n/\varepsilon^2+\sqrt n/\varepsilon)$ expected queries without knowing the number of vertices $n$, and [Bhattacharya and Pradhan, CIAC 2025] estimate $M_s$ using $O(n^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^2)$ queries when $n$ is given. We show that the query complexity of both problems is governed by the matching number $\nu$ of $G$ (the maximum number of pairwise disjoint edges) rather than the number of vertices $n$, and that the dependence on $\varepsilon$ for degree moments can be polynomially improved. Our algorithms rest on a simple observation: the endpoints of a maximum matching cover every edge, so a random endpoint of a random edge falls on this set of $2\nu$ vertices with probability at least $1/2$. For every $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$, we give advice-free algorithms that estimate $m$ and $M_s$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $2/3$, without knowledge of $n$, $\nu$, or other graph parameters. Specifically, our algorithms use $O(\min\{\nu/\varepsilon, 1/\varepsilon^2+\sqrt\nu/\varepsilon\})$ expected queries for $m$ and $O(\min\{\nu^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^{2/s}, \nu^{1-1/(2s-1)}/\varepsilon^{2/(2s-1)}\})$ for $M_s$. Finally, our lower bounds show that for every $k \ge 2$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, these query complexities are optimal up to constant factors over graphs with matching number at most $k$.

### [255] [A Fixed Parameter Sublinear Time Approximation Scheme for Metric Min-Sum Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15148)
*Karthik C. S.,Euiwoong Lee,Yuval Rabani,Chris Schwiegelshohn,Samson Zhou*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Metric $k$-minsum clustering is a simple, natural, appealing density-based clustering criterion whose computational complexity remains poorly understood, despite the progress achieved fornother clustering criteria in the past three decades. In this paper we give an efficient approximation scheme for this problem that runs in sublinear time for mildly increasing $k$, and thus is fixed parameter tractable with respect to the parameter $k$. We complement this result by showing that similar algorithms are unlikely to exist for the closely related problems $k$-median and balanced $k$-median, assuming popular fine-grained complexity conjectures. Specifically, we show that no sublinear time algorithm with small approximation factors can exist even for $2$-median and balanced $2$-median. It was previously known that no efficient PTAS can exist for $k$-median and our results show a strong and perhaps surprising separation between the $k$-minsum clustering problem and $k$-median even in the sublinear regime. Our upper bounds improve qualitatively upon decades old results. Our lower bounds establish the first use of the Distributed PCP framework to clustering problems.

### [256] [A Fast Greedy Algorithm with a 0.45 Approximation Guarantee for the Airplane Refueling Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15222)
*Oleg Lomachenko,Arnold Enikeev*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We study a natural greedy algorithm for the Airplane Refueling Problem (ARP), based on a well-known priority rule. We show that this algorithm achieves an approximation guarantee of $9/20$, noticeably improving the previously known $1/12$ guarantee for a fast algorithm. We also show that the same priority rule can be implemented in $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space using a dynamic convex-hull data structure. These results provide a worst-case approximation guarantee for an existing greedy priority rule and establish an efficient implementation. In the real-RAM model, the running-time bound is independent of the magnitude of the processing times. The resulting method is also suitable as a fast primal routine inside more complex exact and approximation algorithms for large instances. These results narrow the gap between theoretically strong but complex approximation schemes and lightweight algorithms that can be used directly in computational pipelines. The algorithm combines a simple selection rule with a provable performance bound, making it a useful baseline for further algorithmic studies of ARP.

### [257] [Cascade: GPU-Accelerated Out-of-Core Suffix Array Construction for LLM Corpora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15254)
*Jamshed Khan,Prashant Pandey*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Suffix arrays over LLM (pre)training corpora underpin deduplication, contamination testing, n-gram statistics, and training-data attribution, and every new corpus or tokenizer needs a new one. GPU constructors are fast but bounded by device memory, and out-of-core pipelines run at CPU speed, reaching trillions of tokens by building sharded indexes. Reach is bounded not by the size of the data but by what must stay resident, and in a partitioned construction that is the coupling between partitions. We present Cascade, which requires none of it to stay resident. Splitter K-grams sampled from the corpus fix every partition's range of the final suffix array before any sorting, so the GPU sorts and ranks partitions independently and never merges them. The partitions are still coupled: every round of the method needs ranks that other partitions hold, classically kept in a global rank array (the inverse suffix array) that must stay resident. We instead send each rank to the one partition that needs it, and maintain an invariant ensuring ranks are only ever compared within one partition, so no global rank array is needed. The text and a compact partition map, the only structures read at random, then stay in host memory by choice rather than necessity, one at a time when memory is short; every other structure becomes a stream that can be placed across device memory, host memory, and disk as it is written. On a single GPU node, Cascade builds exact suffix arrays of up to 238B tokens, 2.4-6.8x faster than infini-gram's pipeline and 5.9-10.9x faster than libsais.

### [258] [Solving Restricted Versions of #SAT Faster than $2^m$: Algorithms and Lower Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15426)
*Sanjay Jain,Junqiang Peng,Frank Stephan,Mingyu Xiao*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$, the #SAT problem (counting the number of satisfying assignments of a CNF formula) cannot be solved in $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^n)$ or $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^m)$ time, where $n$ is the number of variables and $m$ is the number of clauses. On the other hand, simple exhaustive search and the standard inclusion-exclusion give $\mathcal{O}^*(2^n)$-time and $\mathcal{O}^*(2^m)$-time algorithms, respectively. A natural line of research is to beat these SETH-based barriers for restricted versions, such as #$k$-SAT (where each clause contains at most $k$ literals) or #$d$-occ-SAT (where each variable appears in at most $d$ clauses). It is known that the $2^n$-barrier can be broken when $k$ or $d$ is any constant; yet, whether the $2^m$-barrier can also be broken in these cases remains unknown. We present two simple algorithms that overcome the $2^m$-barrier. First, for #$k$-SAT, we give an $\mathcal{O}^*(2^{m(1-1/O(k))})$-time algorithm, thereby breaking the $2^m$-barrier for any constant $k$. Second, for #$2$-occ-SAT (which also includes the problem of counting the number of edge covers in a graph as a special case), we provide an algorithm with runtime $\mathcal{O}^*(2^{m\omega/3})$, where $\omega < 2.3714$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both algorithms generalize to the weighted counting setting while preserving the same runtime bounds. On the hardness side, we present a reduction from #Max-$d$-SAT to #$d$-occ-SAT, showing that for any $d\ge 3$, #$d$-occ-SAT admits no $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^m)$-time algorithm for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, even on positive formulas, under the hypothesis that #Max-3-SAT on $n$ variables admits no $\mathcal{O}^*((2-\varepsilon)^n)$-time algorithm for any such $\varepsilon$.

### [259] [Optimal High Probability Bounds for Random Order Online Sorting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15438)
*Chenglin Fan,Mingyu Kang*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: In random order online sorting, a fixed multiset of $n$ real numbers arrives in a uniformly random order. Each value must be placed immediately and irrevocably into an empty position of an array with exactly $n$ positions. The objective is to minimize the sum of the absolute differences between consecutive entries. If the entire input were known in advance, sorting the values would be optimal and would have cost equal to the range of the input. We prove that the optimal worst case competitive ratio in this model is $\Theta(\log n)$ with high probability. In particular, we give a single online algorithm that achieves an $O(\log n)$ competitive ratio with high probability for every fixed input, and we show that every randomized online algorithm has some fixed input on which an $\Omega(\log n)$ ratio is unavoidable with high probability. The same upper bound also holds for independent samples from an arbitrary unknown distribution on the real line. The algorithm uses the random arrival order to learn the relative positions of future values from the values seen so far. It maintains a hierarchy of small regions of the input order and allows an arriving value to use nearby space when its preferred region is full. This flexibility avoids the need to reserve large amounts of space for unlikely local fluctuations. The analysis shows that large displacements become rapidly less likely as their scale grows, leading to the $O(\log n)$ high probability bound. A matching lower bound shows that no randomized online algorithm can improve the logarithmic dependence in the worst case.

### [260] [FirstFit coloring process of random bipartite graphs and an online coloring lower bound in the random order model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15468)
*Yaqiao Li,Xin Li*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: FirstFit colors each arriving vertex with the smallest positive integer absent from its previously colored neighborhood. We prove that this rule can require $n^{\Omega(1)}$ many colors on certain bipartite graph of $n$ vertices even when the vertices arrive in a uniformly random order. This refutes the conjecture of Bosek, Gutowski, Lasoń, and Przybyło [BGLP24] that FirstFit uses a polylogarithmic expected number of colors on every bipartite graph in the random order model. We obtain the lower bound by analyzing the FirstFit coloring process on random bipartite graphs, where vertices arrive to either side with equal probability, and with an independent edge density $n^{-x}$ for some $0 < x < 1$. Our result can also be viewed as a qualitative strengthening of Kučera [Kuč91], who showed that, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there are graphs with chromatic number at most $n^{\epsilon}$ on which FirstFit uses $\Omega(n/\log n)$ colors in expectation under a uniformly random order. Our result shows that such poor behavior of FirstFit already occurs for $\chi(G) = 2$.

### [261] [Approximation Algorithms for Dual-Memory Request Scheduling in Disaggregated LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15579)
*Xin Wang,Hong Shen,Hui Tian,Ye Tao*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Disaggregated LLM inference executes the prefill and decode phases on separate resource pools, reducing interference between the two phases. However, this architecture introduces a coupled scheduling problem because a request that completes prefill retains its prompt KV cache in prefill memory until it is admitted to the decode pool. Prefill and decode admission decisions therefore jointly determine memory occupancy and request completion times. To the best of our knowledge, this problem lacks a formal formulation, and no approximation guarantees are known for request scheduling in disaggregated LLM inference. We formalize this setting as the dual-memory request scheduling (DMRS) problem, whose objective is to minimize the sum of request completion times, and prove that it is strongly NP-hard. We develop two deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithms. The first applies to instances satisfying $\alpha<1$ and $\beta<1$ and achieves an approximation ratio of $8+\frac{4}{1-\alpha}+\frac{8}{1-\beta}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the maximum normalized prefill and peak decode memory demands among all requests, respectively. In particular, it yields a $32$-approximation when $\alpha,\beta\leq 1/2$. The second algorithm applies to all feasible instances and achieves a uniform $36$-approximation. Finally, evaluations on two H100 GPUs using trace-derived offline workloads show that the proposed algorithms reduce the sum of request completion times relative to multiple vLLM deployment baselines.

### [262] [Metric Planarity Testing is Hard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15682)
*Anubhav Dhar,Debajyoti Kar,Sándor Kisfaludi-Bak,Hung Le,Bartłomiej Lewandowski,Karol Węgrzycki*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: A key milestone in algorithmic graph theory is Hopcroft and Tarjan's 1974 linear-time algorithm for graph planarity testing. At a workshop in 2002, Linial and Rabinovich asked for either a polynomial-time algorithm or an NP-hardness proof for metric planarity testing: given a metric space $(X,d_X)$, determine whether there exists an edge-weighted planar graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $X\subseteq V$ that realizes the distances in $X$, meaning that $d_G(x,y)=d_X(x,y)$ for every $x,y\in X$. This question arose in the context of research on metric embeddings and their applications in computer science since the mid-1990s. Over the past few decades, polynomial-time algorithms have been developed for several special cases. In this work, we show that metric planarity testing is NP-hard, in sharp contrast to graph planarity testing. Our reduction yields a stronger result: under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), no $2^{o(n)}$-time algorithm for metric planarity testing exists, where $n$ is the number of points in the metric. To complement our ETH lower bound, we give two algorithmic results: (i) an algorithm for computing a metric planar embedding in $2^{\tilde{O}(n^2)}$ time and (ii) a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm in $2^{\tilde{O}(n)}$ time for any fixed $\epsilon\in(0,1)$. The second algorithm produces a planar graph that preserves the input metric up to a factor of $(1+\epsilon)$.

### [263] [Exact and Asymptotic Analysis of Greedy Online Facility Assignment on Cycle Metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15776)
*Md. Tanzeem Rahat,Md. Rawha Siddiqi Riad,Md. Manzurul Hasan*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We identify the free-facility gaps of greedy online assignment on a cycle with the discrete additive coalescent and use this connection to determine the exact expected assignment cost. The cycle has circumference $n$, with one unit-capacity facility at each integer point and $n$ independent uniform arrivals. Each request is assigned immediately to a nearest free facility. The conditional one-step cost is the sum of squared gap lengths divided by $4n$. A uniform cyclic-order argument identifies the unordered gap process with additive coalescence. The classical Cayley-tree representation then reduces the accumulated cost to a two-vertex distance functional, yielding \[ G_n=\frac n4\sum_{d=0}^{n-1}\prod_{j=1}^{d}\left(1-\frac jn\right) \sim\frac14\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,n^{3/2}. \] The formula requires a linear number of scalar recurrence steps to evaluate. We also obtain an asymptotic upper bound of $\pi\sqrt3/2$ on the ratio of expected greedy cost to expected offline optimum under this arrival model. An exact rational Bellman calculation shows that greedy is optimal for three facilities but exceeds the optimal online expected cost by $1/512$ for four facilities. Independent exact recurrences and finite tree enumeration provide reproducible checks of the analysis.

### [264] [Adaptive Sorting, also in the BST Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15828)
*Ivor van der Hoog,Eva Rotenberg,Daniel Rutschmann*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Sorting is one of the most basic algorithmic problems. Adaptive sorting algorithms exploit features that make an input easier to sort, often captured by entropy measures. Many such measures have been studied, raising two natural questions: how do they relate to one another, and are there algorithms that are adaptive to them? We complete a hierarchy of relations between previously studied entropy measures and show that the classical measure Reg is a source of this hierarchy. We prove that an existing data structure yields a Reg-adaptive sorting algorithm, thereby achieving the adaptive bounds of every measure in the hierarchy. Following McIlroy's observation that Reg has a mathematically inconvenient definition, we study a slightly weaker but simpler measure, reg. For inputs without duplicates, we show that O(n + log reg) = O(n + log Reg), so this simplification preserves the adaptive bound. Finally, we do algorithms design and introduce SproutSort, a reg-adaptive algorithm in the offline binary search tree (BST) model. SproutSort achieves an access cost of O(n + log reg), making it the most adaptive algorithm in this model to date. We also introduce SkeletonSort, a simple randomised pointer-machine algorithm that sorts distinct keys in expected O(n + log reg) time, offering a considerably simpler implementation of a sorting algorithm this high in the adaptive hierarchy.

### [265] [Social Learning of Ranking: Getting the Top Right despite Local Herding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15896)
*Shahrzad Haddadan,Jie Gao*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: In sequential learning, a group of agents sequentially receives a noisy private signal and observes the predictions of prior agents to estimate a hidden ground truth. While extensively studied for binary signals, we formalize and analyze sequential learning when the hidden ground truth is an ordering of $n$ items, and both private signals and inferences involve pairwise comparisons. A key focus in sequential learning is herding, where agents disregard their private signals to follow the crowd. We show that, while local herding in our model may lead agents to make incorrect pairwise inferences, the global hidden order can still be approximated. Specifically, by aggregating all pairwise comparison outputs, the highest-ranked items can be retrieved. We investigate top-$k$ retrieval across three scenarios: (1) passive aggregation, where information is gathered from the social learning process without intervention; (2) strategic selection, where agents choose their pairwise comparisons dynamically; and (3) aggregation with stubborn nodes, where a very small set of stubborn agents, who base their inferences solely on their private signals, join the mechanism. With query complexity as the number of agents needed for a high-probability estimation, we propose top-$k$ retrieval algorithms with query complexities sublinear in $O(n^2)$, the total number of pairs.

### [266] [Online Batching with Lookahead: Adversarial Limits and Stochastic Gains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16013)
*Dimitris Christou,Jiayi Chen,Nihal Sharma,Aditya Akella,Shuchi Chawla,Sanjay Shakkottai*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Modern inference systems rely on batching to exploit parallel execution and amortize serial execution overheads, but batching creates a fundamental online scheduling tradeoff: serving requests immediately reduces request queuing delay, while waiting can form larger batches that better utilize parallel hardware and improve serving efficiency. We study this tradeoff in a single-server online batching model with bounded batch capacity, fixed batch processing time, and the objective of minimizing total flow time. Our focus is on the value of finite lookahead into future arrivals over a purely online setting for scheduling. We show that the benefits of lookahead depend on the arrival model. In the adversarial setting, finite perfect lookahead has inherent limitations: for any bounded lookahead window, every online algorithm remains separated from the offline optimum by a constant factor. Thus, worst-case arrival sequences can prevent perfect knowledge of future events from fully overcoming online uncertainty. In contrast, under Poisson arrivals in the stable regime, finite lookahead is much more powerful. Although the best distribution-aware online algorithm has a nonzero asymptotic gap from the offline optimum, lookahead closes this gap exponentially fast in the window length. We prove matching upper and lower bounds up to constants in the exponent. Together, these results give a tight characterization of when lookahead can close the online--offline gap, incorporating insights from the competitive analysis of online algorithms into queueing-theoretic steady-state bounds. We also study imperfect predictions, showing that the benefit of lookahead degrades gracefully with prediction error. Simulations on synthetic arrivals and experiments on real request traces support the theory: modest lookahead substantially reduces flow time and brings online batching close to the offline benchmark.

### [267] [QPTAS for Max Weight Independent Set in Graphs with Strongly Edge-Sublinear Separators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16025)
*Édouard Bonnet,Yeonsu Chang*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: A hereditary graph class has strongly edge-sublinear separators if, for some constant $0 \leqslant b < 1$, every graph in the class with $m$ edges admits a balanced separator of size $\mathcal O(m^b)$. We show that Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) admits a deterministic quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) on every such class. In particular, this applies to graphs excluding any fixed graph as an induced minor, by a separator theorem of Korhonen and Lokshtanov [SODA 2024]. Our theorem generalizes the QPTASes for axis-parallel rectangles [Adamaszek and Wiese, FOCS 2013] and polygons [Adamaszek, Har-Peled, and Wiese, JACM 2019], or equivalently for packing connected subgraphs of a planar graph [Pilipczuk, van Leeuwen, and Wiese, Algorithmica 2020]. It also generalizes the QPTAS for MWIS on hereditary classes with strongly sublinear separators measured in vertices [Dvořák, EJC 2018; Dvořák and Lahiri, ESA 2021], as well as the QPTASes for graphs excluding particular induced minors [Chudnovsky et al., arXiv 2025; Bonnet et al., SWAT 2026; Czyżewska et al., arXiv 2026].

### [268] [Stochastic Weighted Caching with Per-Request Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16045)
*Shuchi Chawla,Dimitris Christou*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Both the unweighted and weighted variants of caching are cornerstone problems in competitive analysis, with tight randomized competitive ratios of $\Theta(\log k)$, where $k$ is the cache size. We study weighted caching with per-request predictions, where each page request is accompanied by a prediction of the next arrival time of the same page. For unweighted caching, such perfect predictions suffice to implement Belady's offline optimal rule. For weighted caching, however, previous work shows that a logarithmic lower bound persists even with perfect predictions on adversarial request sequences. Stochastic assumptions alone are also insufficient: the classical caching lower bounds already apply to uniform independent requests. In this work, we ask whether combining these two sources of additional information can overcome this barrier, and answer this question affirmatively. Specifically, we develop an efficient, deterministic cache eviction policy that achieves a competitive ratio of $15.75$ using perfect per-request predictions when page requests are drawn independently from an arbitrary, known static distribution in every step, and page costs are arbitrary. Our algorithm's performance degrades gracefully under erroneous predictions: we prove a bound of $O(\min\{1+E,\log k\})$ on the competitive ratio, where $E$ aggregates each page's average prediction error, and may be unknown to the algorithm.

### [269] [Online Submodular Welfare Maximization: Computation is not the Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16060)
*Rajan Udwani,David Wajc*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We revisit the online submodular welfare maximization problem (OSW), a vast generalization of numerous well-studied online allocation problems, including online bipartite matching, display ads and AdWords. A natural greedy OSW algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of $1/2$ [LLN06], and $1-1/e$ under i.i.d. arrivals [KPV13]. Both bounds are tight for polynomial-time algorithms unless NP=RP [KPV13]. The information-theoretic limits for OSW, in contrast, remained open. This prompted researchers to ask for tighter upper bounds [Mehta13] or conjecture the existence of better-competitive (slow) algorithms [Huang23, LTX+23, CHS24, Huang2024, HTW24}. We resolve Mehta's question and refute the subsequent conjectures, proving that the greedy algorithm is in fact tight for both adversarial and i.i.d. arrivals, regardless of computation time. Seemingly contradicting recent $(1-1/e)$-competitive fractional algorithms for OSW [HJP+24,Patton26], we show that this impossibility even holds for fractional algorithms, provided their outputs correspond to marginals that are roundable in hindsight. Conceptually, our proofs can be seen as identifying that a bottleneck for OSW, even under (deterministic) adversarial arrivals, is the inherently random notion of correlation gap [ADSY12].

### [270] [Improved Approximations for Coflow Scheduling via Iterated Rounding and Stable Matchings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16068)
*Mikhail Cherniavskii,Arseni Fedorovich,Mikhail Koshelev,Andrey Kupavskii,Stanislav Moiseev,Fedor Ozhegov,Alexander Shekhovtsov*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We study Coflow Scheduling, introduced by Chowdhury, Zhong, and Stoica (2014). We give deterministic polynomial-time algorithms achieving a $2.77$-approximation without release dates and a $3.17$-approximation with integer release dates. These improve the $3.42$ and $4.36$ guarantees of Rohwedder and Schnaars (2025). Our approach combines two ideas: (1) a novel iterated rounding scheme, and (2) Galvin's list edge coloring method, which is based on the Gale--Shapley stable matching algorithm.

Our approach combines two ideas: (1) a novel iterated rounding scheme, and (2) Galvin's list edge coloring method, which is based on the Gale--Shapley stable matching algorithm.

</details>


### [271] [Approximation algorithms via discrepancy with hard constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16079)
*Mikhail Cherniavskii,Andrey Kupavskii,Stanislav Moiseev,Alexander Shekhovtsov*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: In this paper, we present a discrepancy-based approach to cost-preserving rounding under hard constraints. Starting from a feasible fractional solution, our rounding procedure preserves the designated hard constraints, never increases the linear objective, and bounds the error in the remaining constraints by the discrepancy of a suitable column-difference matrix. Our second discrepancy-theoretic result bounds the discrepancy of a matrix in terms of a novel column parameter, called mountain distance. This notion captures ordered structural features of a matrix which are invisible to the classical Beck--Fiala and Komlós column-norm parameters. We show a variety of applications of these two results. In particular, we obtain new results for min-cost unsplittable flows, bounded-turn routing in grids and tori, rainbow prefix hypergraph decomposition, and $2$-multicast scheduling.

### [272] [Ramsey Meets Simultaneous Planarity: Vertex Integrity and Pathwidth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16392)
*Thomas Depian,Simon D. Fink,Alexander Firbas,Robert Ganian,Matthias Pfretzschner,Ignaz Rutter*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We study the following simultaneous embedding problem: Given k graphs on the same vertex set with the same pairwise intersection, do they admit planar drawings that coincide on their shared graph? We establish fixed-parameter tractability with respect to the vertex integrity of the union graph (that is, the union of the input graphs) plus k, resolving an open question and generalizing the known algorithm parameterized by vertex cover number plus k. Our main technical contribution on the way towards this result is the extension of the recently introduced Ramsey pruning technique beyond ordering problems. Finally, we complement our tractability result with a lower bound that establishes NP-hardness when both k and the pathwidth of the union graph are bounded by constants, ruling out a generalization of our main result to path- or treewidth.

### [273] [Dynamic Maximal Independent Set using Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16637)
*Shahbaz Khan,Anshul Kumar*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We present the first dynamic maximal independent set (MIS) of a graph with $n$ vertices and up to $m$ edges under edge updates in the prediction model, where a predicted update sequence is available for offline preprocessing before the real updates arrive online. We consider the incremental (insertion-only), decremental (deletions-only), and fully dynamic (insertions and deletions) models. Without predictions, deterministic algorithms need worst-case update time of $O(n)$ for decremental and $O(m)$ for incremental and fully dynamic settings. Bernstein et al.~[SODA26] proved under the combinatorial BMM conjecture, combinatorial incremental algorithms against an adaptive adversary require $\Omega(n^{1-o(1)})$ amortized update time. We present deterministic incremental, decremental, and fully dynamic algorithms whose update times depend on the prediction error. This error is measured by the number $\eta_e$ of mispredicted updates, and by the number $\eta_v$ and total degree $\eta_v^*$ of vertices whose MIS membership was mispredicted. With $O(mn)$ preprocessing, our decremental and incremental algorithms achieve worst-case update times $O(\eta_v)$ and $O(\eta_e+\eta_v^*)$, respectively. Our fully dynamic algorithm achieves $O(\eta_e+\eta_v^*)$ worst-case update time with $O(un)$ preprocessing for $u$ updates. We also give space-efficient variants using $O(m)$ space for the decremental and $O(m\sqrt{m})$ for the incremental setting, at the cost of a logarithmic overhead in worst-case update time. Our algorithms satisfy consistency, robustness, and smooth degradation, the required properties of algorithms with predictions. They can also utilize the general error correction framework of Khan et al.~[Arxiv26], relaxing the error measures from first point of difference to prefix matching (for partially dynamic) and set edit distance (for fully dynamic), maintaining the same bounds.

### [274] [Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part I: Glauber Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16705)
*Aniket Das,Tselil Schramm*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: In the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem, we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\{\pm1\}^N$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. We show that Glauber dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization, demonstrating that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.

### [275] [The Online Steinitz Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16715)
*Matteo Russo,Jiaye Wei*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Inspired by Steinitz's celebrated result (1913) and recent online vector-balancing results of Kulkarni et al. (2024) and Aden-Ali (2026), we introduce the online Steinitz problem: $T$ vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, each of $\ell_2$-norm at most $1$ and with total sum zero, arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably to unused positions of an array. The goal is to keep every prefix sum of the resulting order small. We first obtain deterministic prefix-discrepancy bounds of $O(\log T)$ for $d=1$ and $O(\sqrt T)$ for $d\ge2$. Our main contribution is a general reduction that converts deterministic and randomized online vector-balancing algorithms, which assign signs to arriving vectors, into online ordering algorithms. Combined with recent vector-balancing results, this yields a randomized algorithm with prefix discrepancy $O(\log T+\sqrt{d\log T})$ and running time $O(dT\log T)$. The guarantee holds with high probability against an oblivious adversary. The reduction also gives bounds for sparse vectors and extends to inputs in arbitrary compact convex bodies. Finally, we prove matching lower bounds in both the deterministic and randomized cases.

### [276] [A Deterministic $0.401$-Approximation for Non-monotone Submodular Maximization under Matroid Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16785)
*Shengminjie Chen,Kaifeng Lin,Xiaoming Sun,Jialin Zhang*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Submodular maximization arises in a wide range of combinatorial optimization problems and has been extensively studied from the perspective of approximation algorithms. For maximizing nonnegative, non-monotone submodular functions subject to a matroid constraint, randomized algorithms achieve a $0.401$-approximation, whereas obtaining comparable deterministic guarantees remains challenging. In this paper, we present a deterministic $0.401$-approximation algorithm in the exact value and independence oracle model, improving upon the previous deterministic guarantee of $(0.385-\varepsilon)$ \cite{ChenGLSZ2026}. Our algorithm builds on the extended multilinear extension and provides a deterministic implementation of the recursive guided framework underlying the randomized $0.401$-approximation algorithm. The main technical ingredient is a direction oracle supported on at most two partitioned matroid bases. This oracle simultaneously satisfies the growth condition required by the extended-multilinear update and an approximate stationarity condition needed to construct the recursive guides. The resulting finite-support representation enables exact evaluation of the relevant expectations and marginal values without random sampling. The algorithm uses polynomially many value- and independence-oracle queries.

### [277] [Tight Approximations for Fixed-Order Vehicle Routing with Stochastic Demands](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16802)
*Jingyang Zhao,Mingyu Xiao*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We study the vehicle routing problem (VRP) with stochastic demands, where each client has an independent demand with a known distribution, and its realized demand is observed only on the first visit. We consider a priori and restocking policies that fix the client order before observing demands and serve each client's entire demand before first visiting the next. Gupta, Nagarajan, and Ravi (Oper. Res., 2012) developed randomized a priori $(\alpha+1)$-approximation and $(\alpha+2)$-approximation algorithms for splittable and unsplittable deliveries, respectively, where $\alpha$ is the approximation ratio of a metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) algorithm. We improve these approximation ratios to $2$ and $3$ by using their replenishment rules with a TSP tour constructed via matroid parity. We also obtain deterministic a priori $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation and $(3+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms by compressing the distributions of cumulative demands to select an initial stock in polynomial time. All guarantees are relative to the general adaptive optimum. We then establish matching lower bounds of $2$ and $3$ that hold even for the more general class of randomized restocking policies. Finally, we apply our matroid-parity construction to improve approximation ratios for several VRP variants with deterministic demands.

### [278] [The Communication Complexity of the Coin Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16830)
*Adithya Diddapur,Pachara Sawettamalya*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We study the two-player communication complexity of the \textsf{Coin} problem. Here, two players, denoted Alice and Bob, are given up to $n$ individual i.i.d. random coins, and asked to output whether there are more heads or tails. An immediate approach is for Alice to send Bob her exact numbers of heads and tails, yielding a deterministic protocol with one-way communication cost $O(\log n)$ bits. Indeed, this is provably optimal in the related multi-player and streaming settings [Braverman, Garg, Woodruff, FOCS'20]. Our contribution is to show that this is not the right answer in the one-way two-player setting. Instead, we prove a $\Omega(\log\log n)$ bit lower bound for the constant error-rate regime, and a $\Omega(\log(1/\delta))$ bit lower bound for arbitrarily small error rates, $\delta \geq n^{-0.1}$. We also complement these with a tight one-way protocol using $O(\log\log n + \log(1/\delta))$ bits of communication. Unlike the previous works, our lower bounds avoid intricate direct information-theoretic arguments. Instead, our $\Omega(\log(1/\delta))$ bound is via a standard fooling-set style argument, whilst our $\Omega(\log\log n)$ bound is via a novel yet simple reduction from the \textsf{Gap-Greater-Than} problem. This reduction is our main technical contribution, and can be seen as loosely inspired by the \emph{Robust Communication Complexity} arguments of [Chakrabarti, Cormode, McGregor, STOC'08]. Finally, we also show that our constant-error lower bound and protocol can be adapted to the multi-round setting: up to polynomial factors in $r$, the $r$-round communication complexity of the coin problem is $\Theta\left((\log\log n)^{1/r}\right)$ bits.

### [279] [Tractability of Hard Digraph Cut Problems on Eulerian Instances: Treewidth Reduction and Reducing CMSO to Unbreakable Eulerian Instances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16869)
*Esther Galby,Roohani Sharma,Bart van der Steenhoven*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Eulerian digraphs retain the directional structure of general digraphs while exhibiting a symmetry of cuts reminiscent of undirected graphs. We show that this symmetry extends beyond individual cuts to two fundamental techniques in parameterized algorithms for undirected cut problems: treewidth reduction and recursive understanding and randomized contractions. Both of these techniques have proved useful for dealing with undirected graph cut problems as each of them reduces the problem at hand on general undirected instances to ones that have bounded treewidth or that are highly connected, respectively. In this work we prove an edge-cut analogue of the treewidth-reduction theorem of Marx, O'Sullivan, and Razgon [ACM TALG 2013], and an Eulerian analogue of the reduction of CMSO model checking to unbreakable instances due to Lokshtanov, Ramanujan, Saurabh, and Zehavi [ICALP 2018]. Both these results allow us to reduce several problems on general Eulerian digraphs to Eulerian digraphs whose underlying undirected graph has bounded treewidth, or to Eulerian instances that are highly connected, thus bringing to Eulerian digraphs two fundamental tools from the undirected parameterized cut toolkit for which no counterparts are known on arbitrary digraphs. Beyond their structural significance, these results have substantial algorithmic consequences: they yield FPT algorithms for several directed cut problems that are W[1]-hard in general. We show that Directed Multicut and Directed Edge Odd Cycle Transversal are FPT on Eulerian digraphs when parameterized by the solution size and the number of terminal pairs, and just the solution size, respectively. This is in sharp contrast to general digraphs, where the first problem is W[1]-hard even for 4 terminal pairs, and the second is W[1]-hard in general. We also obtain FPT algorithms for Directed Edge Multiway Cut-Uncut and Directed Steiner Cut.

### [280] [Approximation Algorithms for Graphic Multi-Depot TSP and Graphic Multi-Path TSP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16893)
*Niklas Dahlmeier,Raoul Luqué,Philipp Pabst,Laura Vargas Koch*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We give improved approximation algorithms for two graphic TSP variants. First, we consider Multi-Depot TSP on graphic instances. In this variant, we are given an undirected graph with a set of depot vertices, and we are tasked with finding an Eulerian multi-edge set that connects each non-depot vertex to at least one depot. For this problem, Deppert, Kaul and Mnich (ESA 2023) presented a 3/2-approximation algorithm with running time exponential in the number of depots. We improve this result to a fully polynomial 3/2-approximation. Our algorithm is a variant of the classic Christofides-Serdyukov algorithm with an improved and simple analysis. On subcubic instances, we improve the approximation guarantee to 4/3 using the technique of removable pairings introduced by Mömke and Svensson (J. ACM 2016). We use a removable pairing to construct a set of disjoint cycles that can be completed to a cheap feasible solution. Second, we consider the Graphic Multi-Path TSP, which was previously considered by Alimi, Dahlmeier, Mömke, Pabst and Vargas Koch (SOSA 2026) who give a 2-approximation for this problem. Additionally, the authors present a reduction that shows that any better-than-two approximation for Graphic Multi-Depot TSP immediately leads to an improvement for Graphic Multi-Path TSP. We give an improved algorithm and analysis that yield an approximation guarantee of 1.9304.

### [281] [Exponential Local Search in Bounded-Occurrence MAX-CSP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16898)
*Sophia Heimann,Hung P. Hoang,Stefan Hougardy*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We study the number of improving steps that local search may require for $(2,2,r)$-MCA (Maximum Constraint Assignment), a bounded-occurrence version of MAX-CSP with valued constraints in which every constraint involves at most two variables, every variable occurs in at most two constraints, and every variable takes one of $r$ values. We consider the flip neighborhood, where two assignments are neighbors if they differ in the value of exactly one variable; moving to such a neighbor is called a flip. Local search repeatedly performs improving flips, that is, flips that strictly increase the objective value, until a local optimum is reached. Our main result is that $(2,2,5)$-MCA has the all-exp property: there is an infinite family of instances with initial assignments for which every sequence of improving flips ending in a local optimum has length exponential in the number of variables. Thus, on these instances, local search requires exponentially many steps regardless of which improving flip is chosen at each step. This is the first all-exp result for $(2,2,r)$-MCA for any value of $r$, and our result extends to every $r\ge 5$. In contrast, for $(2,2,2)$-MCA every sequence of improving flips has length at most quadratic in the number of variables~\cite{Kaz2020,KCJ2020}. We give a short, direct proof of this result.

Abstract: We study the number of improving steps that local search may require for $(2,2,r)$-MCA (Maximum Constraint Assignment), a bounded-occurrence version of MAX-CSP with valued constraints in which every constraint involves at most two variables, every variable occurs in at most two constraints, and every variable takes one of $r$ values. We consider the flip neighborhood, where two assignments are neighbors if they differ in the value of exactly one variable; moving to such a neighbor is called a flip. Local search repeatedly performs improving flips, that is, flips that strictly increase the objective value, until a local optimum is reached. Our main result is that $(2,2,5)$-MCA has the all-exp property: there is an infinite family of instances with initial assignments for which every sequence of improving flips ending in a local optimum has length exponential in the number of variables. Thus, on these instances, local search requires exponentially many steps regardless of which improving flip is chosen at each step. This is the first all-exp result for $(2,2,r)$-MCA for any value of $r$, and our result extends to every $r\ge 5$. In contrast, for $(2,2,2)$-MCA every sequence of improving flips has length at most quadratic in the number of variables~\cite{Kaz2020,KCJ2020}. We give a short, direct proof of this result.

</details>


### [282] [LOCAL LLL in $\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n)$ Rounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17133)
*Maxime Flin,Mohsen Ghaffari,Magnús M. Halldórsson,Yannic Maus,Alexandre Nolin*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We provide a $\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n)$-round randomized LOCAL algorithm for the constructive Lovász Local Lemma with polynomial criterion $pd^{c} < 1$, for a sufficiently large constant $c$. The best previous general round complexity was $\widetilde O(\log n)$. The key ingredient is a local reduction that amplifies the LLL probability exponent quadratically, while increasing the dependency radius only by a constant factor.

### [283] [Parameterized algorithms for representing graphs as intersections of threshold graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17152)
*L. Sunil Chandran,Suraj Kumar Sahoo*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: A graph is called a threshold graph if there is an assignment of real valued weights to its vertices such that two vertices have an edge between them if and only if the sum of the weights of the two vertices is above a certain `threshold value'. We will denote the class of all threshold graphs as $TH$. For a graph $G=(V,E)$, if for some integer $t\geq 0$, there are $t$ many threshold graphs $\{G_i=(V,E_i)\}_{i\in [t]}$ such that we have $E=E_1\cap E_2\cap \cdots \cap E_t$, then we say that the collection of threshold graphs $\{G_i=(V,E_i)\}_{i\in [t]}$ forms a $TH$-representation of $G$ of size $t$. \emph{The intersection dimension of $G$ with respect to threshold graphs} (denoted as $dim_{TH}(G)$) is the smallest non-negative integer $t$ such that there is a $TH$-representation of $G$ of size $t$. It is known that for a graph $G$ and integer $t>0$, the problem of deciding whether $dim_{TH}(G)\leq t$ is NP-complete even for $t=3$. In this paper, we study this problem in the framework of parameterized algorithms. We consider the vertex cover number and the cluster vertex deletion number as our parameters. We give a FPT algorithm for determining an optimal $TH$-representation of a graph when parameterized by its vertex cover number. Our main result is an efficient parameterized approximation scheme for this problem when parameterized by the cluster vertex deletion number of $G$.

### [284] [A Better-than-$2$ Approximation for $k$-Median Part II: Stable Instances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17172)
*Rares-Darius Buhai,Vincent Cohen-Addad,Henry Fleischmann,Anupam Gupta,Antoni Jubés Monforte,Madhusudhan Reddy Pittu,Miltiadis Stouras,Ola Svensson,Lukas Vogl*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We consider the $k$-median problem on general metric spaces, subject to the condition that the instances are $\beta$-stable (i.e., the optimal solution using $k-1$ centers has a cost at least $(1+\beta)$ times that of the optimal solution with $k$ centers). We give a $(1.89+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for such instances running in time $\exp(1/(\beta \times \mathrm{poly}(\epsilon)))\cdot \mathrm{poly}_{\epsilon}(n)$. In particular, for $\beta =\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon)/\log n$ and $\epsilon$ a tiny constant, this is a polynomial-time algorithm. This improves on previous work showing a $(2 + \epsilon)$-approximation algorithm with similar running time [CGL+25]. Combined with the pseudo-approximation algorithm in our companion work, this results in a better-than-$2$ approximation algorithm for general $k$-median instances. Our main technical contribution is a novel nuanced analysis of local search that allows us to isolate a subset of clients on which we lose essentially nothing compared to the optimal solution, while losing an approximation factor of $3$ on the rest of the clients. We complement this with an algorithm based on sampling and partial enumeration, achieving a better-than-$2$ approximation on the rest of the clients. Trading off these two algorithms yields our final approximation.

### [285] [Greedy Region Growing: Improved Approximations for Cutwidth, Pathwidth, Flow-Expander Decomposition, and More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17237)
*Aditya Anand*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: We give a new rounding technique for spreading-metric linear programs, called Greedy Region Growing, which adapts the classical technique of region growing to min-max graph layout problems and flow-expander decomposition. Using this technique, we obtain state-of-the-art approximation algorithms for several fundamental problems. (1) An $O(\log n)$-approximation for Cutwidth and Pathwidth, improving upon the previous bound of $O(\log n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})))$ due to Bansal, Katzelnick, and Schwartz (FOCS 2024). This matches the $\Omega(\log n)$ integrality gap of the standard LP relaxations. (2) An $O(\log n)$-approximation for their directed analogues, Minimum Storage and Minimum Register Sufficiency on directed acyclic graphs, improving the previous bound of $O(\log^{3/2} n)$. (3) A $\phi$-flow-expander decomposition that cuts at most an $O(\phi\log n\log\log n)$ fraction of the edges. This improves the $O(\phi\log n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})))$ bound of Bansal, Jambulapati, and Saranurak (ICALP 2026), and is within an $O(\log\log n)$ factor of the graph-theoretic lower bound. The vertex version of our algorithm also gives an $O(\log n)$-approximation for Treedepth. In particular, our results answer several open problems of Bansal, Katzelnick, and Schwartz (FOCS 2024). Technically, we also solve the conceptual question raised by their work: our technique shows how to adapt Seymour recursion to min-max objectives, and constructs $O(1)$-weak local partitions in spreading metrics.

### [286] [Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17406)
*Daniel Lemire*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In this http URL 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with this http URL 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

### [287] [Thin matrix products up to D <= N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, with 3SUM over abelian groups and a dichotomy for coordinatewise problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17420)
*Ruhollah Majdoddin*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: Alman and Vassilevska Williams ( arXiv:2610.06783 ) gave the first polynomial improvements over the textbook algorithms for 3SUM and APSP: deterministic algorithms with exponents 1.9992 for 3SUM, 2.9983 for Exact Triangle and 2.99942 for APSP. Their algorithm has two steps: a matrix theorem, computing N^2/sqrt(D) prescribed entries of the product of an N x D and a D x N integer matrix in time N^2/D^gamma, gamma > 0, when D <= N^eps, for every eps < 0.1204; and reductions from the three problems to the lopsided sparse triangle problem. We improve both. With Schönhage's five-term partial-product tensor, the matrix theorem holds for every eps < 0.172. The preprint's reductions keep a quarter of the matrix theorem's saving for 3SUM and a half for Exact Triangle and APSP; ours keep all of it, by calling the counting version of the triangle problem adaptively and building composite moduli one prime at a time. Together this gives deterministic 3SUM in n^{1.9945+o(1)}, and Exact Triangle, (min,+)-product and APSP in n^{2.9945+o(1)}. We also improve on the preprint's proof sketch for 3XOR and solve it deterministically in O(n^{1.99451}). Which other problems on three lists does the method make truly subquadratic? It solves 3SUM over F_p^d for every fixed prime p with 3XOR's exponents, and over every finite abelian group of exponent p^2, such as Z_4^d, in O(n^{1.99726}). For coordinatewise problems with a fixed relation P on every coordinate triple, a certified exhaustive computation shows that every Boolean P, and every functional P over three letters, either is the solution set of an equation over Z, F_2 or F_3, and the problem is then truly subquadratic, or has a gadget for Orthogonal Vectors, and the problem is then hard under the Orthogonal Vectors hypothesis. Over four letters, just four functional relations, up to symmetry, satisfy neither condition.

### [288] [Certifying Capacity and Gaps of the Rank-Dependent Gain-Sharing Framework for Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17545)
*Pan Xu*

Main category: cs.DS

TL;DR: The randomized primal-dual framework of Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg (SODA 2013) splits each unit matching gain between endpoint dual variables according to the matched offline rank. The gain-sharing function affects the certificate but not Ranking's decisions. Keeping the splitting rule and expected edgewise feasibility criterion fixed, we define certifying capacity as the strongest uniform guarantee obtainable by functional optimization over a prescribed function class. Its shortfall from Ranking's actual competitiveness is the certifying gap. We study unweighted online bipartite matching under adversarial arrivals on graphs with online degree at most $d$ and on $d$-regular graphs. The optimized protocol is tight on both degree-one classes and in the unrestricted setting, but has a strictly positive gap on both degree-two classes, even over all measurable nonnegative complementary splits. In both degree-two settings, we determine Ranking's exact competitiveness and the exact certifying capacity over nondecreasing gain-sharing functions. For general $d$, we optimize over nondecreasing, right-continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $f(1)=1$, using their probability-measure representation. Both the certifying capacity and actual competitiveness converge to $1-1/e$ in both instance families as $d\to\infty$. The resulting gap is at most $1/(2ed)+O(d^{-2})$ for online degree at most $d$; on $d$-regular graphs, it vanishes but is at least $(1/(2e)-o(1))/d$. These results distinguish function-class restrictions from limitations of the fixed protocol and motivate tighter randomized primal-dual frameworks.
