### [417] [Predict Before You Modify: Learning Improvement Dynamics for Self-Evolving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13991)
*Zixuan Xie,Chang Xu,Yuhua Jiang,Li Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. We introduce predictive self-evolution through an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM). Before evaluation, the IDM predicts task-level outcomes of a proposed modification and guides an optional revision. After evaluation, past modifications and their observed outcomes are used to improve the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations. The system can thus improve how it solves tasks, proposes modifications, and predicts their effects. Building on HyperAgents, we evaluate this approach across multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level mathematical grading. Our approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with up to 46% higher average performance over generations. Gains also persist under matched token budgets that include both agent evolution and task evaluation, and extend to held-out tasks. Forecast accuracy improves as the IDM evolves, and the learned predictive knowledge transfers to improve evolution in a new domain.

### [418] [Posterior Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13994)
*Chenrui Ma,Xi Xiao,Lin Zhao,Xinru Jiang,Tianyang Wang,Yanning Shen,Ferdinando Fioretto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Flow matching learns how to transport noise toward data, but its mean prediction does not directly report the endpoint uncertainty remaining at an intermediate state. This paper introduces Posterior Flow Matching (PFM), a general generative modeling framework that learns conditional velocity means and componentwise variances with a Gaussian posterior model. The same model evaluation supplies both a transport prediction and endpoint uncertainty, making posterior diagnostics available throughout generation. These learned moments support a mean-driven ordinary differential equation (ODE) and a posterior-driven stochastic differential equation (SDE), whose local noise scales adapt to the predicted uncertainty. Across image, point-cloud, molecular, and action generation, PFM improves generation quality and provides endpoint-posterior readouts throughout generation.

### [419] [GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13995)
*Weixian Waylon Li,Jiaxin Zhang,Han Zhou,Chengzu Li,Ke Wang,Fengxiang He,Yiwen Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.

### [420] [Splicing Hints into Reasoning Traces: Learning from Demonstrator Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13996)
*Hamed Mahdavi,Pouria Mahdavinia,Majid Farhadi,Vasant Honavar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.

### [421] [Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13998)

TL;DR: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. ### [422] [SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13999)
*Jincheng Gao,Wei Ding,Shuo Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.

### [423] [VH-GPO: Verified Handoff for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14000)
*Haoze Li,Peng Zhou,Peiyuan Wu,Weijie Zhao,Yinan Xin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Group-relative reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO train large language model (LLM) agents by comparing rollouts for the same task. When every trajectory in a group fails with the same reward, relative advantages collapse toward zero, leaving no useful learning signal. A frozen teacher can recover from a student-visited state, but letting it complete the task makes the recovered suffix entirely teacher-generated. We ask: after repairing a student failure, when should control return to the student? We propose outcome-verified teacher-student handoff, instantiated in Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). The teacher provides enough support to reach a state from which the student can succeed, then returns control so that successful experience is again student-generated. Given an environment-verified teacher recovery, VH-GPO selects the earliest independently confirmed handoff point found within a bounded search budget. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, VH-GPO increases success rates over GRPO from 59.38% to 94.79% on ALFWorld and from 71.62% to 77.34% on WebShop. Improvements also hold with the 7B student, for which additional teacher and student output tokens amount to 1.77% and 2.61% of regular student rollout output tokens on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the key components. These results support using verified teacher assistance to repair failures while reinforcing the student's ability to complete tasks independently.

### [424] [PreSO: Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14001)
*Yuhang Yang,Mingxuan Xia,Chao Ye,Shuai Zhu,Shouqing Yang,Haobo Wang,Shenzhi Yang,Zhengqing Zang,Chenglong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses a self-teacher conditioned on privileged information to turn the sparse outcome signal of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) into dense token-level supervision. Yet the teacher's advantage may depend on information unavailable to the student at inference, raising a central question: which privileged changes are worth distilling? We use cross-problem recurrence as an empirical cue for potentially reusable guidance. Comparing the representation shifts induced by full solutions and compact hints, we find that hint-induced shifts are more concentrated and directionally consistent across problems, and yield more sustained downstream gains despite revealing less information. Motivated by this association, we propose Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation (PreSO). At the source, PreSO uses compact hints to limit the solution-specific detail entering the privileged shift. At the target, it estimates a leading low-rank subspace from shifts pooled across related problems, projects the privilege-induced correction onto this subspace, and adds it to the student's unprivileged representation to form the representation-level distillation target. The selected subspace serves as an operational proxy for recurring structure, rather than a guaranteed separation of transferable and instance-specific information. On five competition-level mathematics benchmarks, PreSO consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, improving average accuracy over the base model by 6.8, 9.0, and 10.0 points. Beyond peak accuracy, PreSO attains the highest final-checkpoint average at every model scale, with improvements that persist through the end of training.

### [425] [Showing versus Doing: Teaching by Demonstration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14004)
*Mark K. Ho,Michael L. Littman,James MacGlashan,Fiery Cushman,Joseph L. Austerweil*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.

### [426] [Coding LLMs Can Be Harnessed to Learn Interpretable Models from Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14006)
*Aditya Kumar,Cassandra A. Cohen,William W. Cohen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Since compact, interpretable classifiers correspond to simple programs, it is natural to ask if LLM-based coding agents can be used to learn interpretable models from data. In this paper we present a simple harness that repeatedly prompts a coding LLM to produce the next rule in a rule set, given a sample of labeled examples. We show that this approach is competitive with, and often superior to, state-of-the-art rule-learning methods on tabular data, especially with small training sets, and wins by large margins on text, including against another LLM-based rule learner; that this approach outperforms standard harnesses, and that the approach immediately leads to new kinds of interpretable models, since coding agents are not restricted to search a highly restricted hypothesis space. In addition to the advances made in learning interpretable models, these results are of interest because they introduce a new class of coding benchmarks - construction of interpretable classifiers - which includes quantitative measurements of output quality (i.e., test-set error) and existing mature ``specialist coding algorithms'' (i.e., existing learning methods).

### [427] [What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction? Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14007)
*Luan Ozelim,Abicumaran Uthamacumaran,Hector Zenil*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory, universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so ``closer'' can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes certify even that: finite evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot see the constants that carry Solomonoff's guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of predictive success, so Solomonoff's predictor, which leaves part of it unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where it spends it; on mutually singular families this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper.

### [428] [When Log Parsing Removes What Matters: Detecting Failures in Distributed GPU Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14009)
*Boyuan Cui,Yuyang Zeng,Yifang Tian,Hans-Arno Jacobsen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large AI models increasingly rely on distributed GPU execution, yet it remains unclear whether established failure analysis methods transfer effectively to this setting. We introduce GF-Bench, a PyTorch-based framework and dataset for generating diverse failures in distributed GPU workloads. The framework supports extensible workload and fault-injection logic; based on this design, the current release targets failures visible in multi-GPU communication logs and provides 220 labeled two-GPU executions covering normal runs, CUDA out-of-memory fail-stop failures, and persistent straggler fail-slow failures. Using GF-Bench, we evaluate three sequence-based methods (DeepLog, LogAnomaly, and LogBERT) and the LLM-based LogPrompt on parsed logs, and additionally evaluate LogPrompt on raw logs. On parsed inputs, no method reliably detects both failure classes, and the highest overall F1 score is 0.667. Raw inputs raise the overall F1 score of in-context LogPrompt to 0.983, at 9.0x its average input-token usage and 8.7x its per-run cost. These results expose a substantial trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency: generic log parsing lowers operational cost but discards the distributed execution context required for accurate failure detection. GF-Bench provides a reproducible basis for studying cost-efficient analysis methods and can be extended to additional GPU workloads and failure types.

### [429] [Physics-Informed State Space Models for Day-Ahead Photovoltaic Power Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14014)
*Phil Aupke,Muhammad Hassan,Khalid Ali,Seema,Andreas Kassler,Andreas Theocharis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Accurate day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting requires both strong temporal modeling and adherence to physical PV system constraints. Purely data-driven models often ignore the underlying PV conversion process and may produce predictions that are outside the operational range of a PV system. In this paper, we propose a physics-informed state space framework that combines a differentiable PV conversion model with a selective state space backbone (PowerMamba). Our approach follows a physics-residual decomposition. The physics module provides a structured baseline based on solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits, while the state space model learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. Experiments on one year of utility-scale PV data show that the proposed method significantly improves forecasting accuracy, reducing RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% compared to a physics-only baseline, and outperforming a purely data-driven model. Results further show that incorporating system-level physics provides the largest performance gains, while additional refinements offer only marginal improvements. Beyond accuracy, the model improves robustness by constraining predictions toward physical feasibility, reducing unrealistic predictions under corrupted measurements.

### [430] [Barycentric Anchored Weight Search for Robust Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14017)
*Antoni Buades,Jose-Luis Lisani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We propose Barycentric Anchored Search, a post-hoc weight-space procedure for improving fine-tuned vision models under distribution shift without additional gradient training or increased inference cost. Given a pre-trained initialization and two checkpoints fine-tuned on a source dataset, the method constructs barycentric candidate weights and performs a small derivative-free search along directions connecting each candidate to the pre-trained model. Candidate weights are selected using a small validation subset of one or more out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets; the selected model is then evaluated on the held-out portions of those datasets, on additional OOD benchmarks, and on the ImageNet validation set to quantify the robustness-accuracy trade-off. The method is inspired by simplex-based derivative-free optimization, including Nelder-Mead and Torczon multidirectional search, but is specialized to the geometry of neural network weight merging. Unlike Model Soup, which typically benefits from many fine-tuned checkpoints, and unlike Model Stock, which applies a fixed geometric merge, our approach uses only two fine-tuned checkpoints and iteratively adapts the merge using validation feedback from OOD data. Experiments with CLIP ViT-B/32 show that the proposed search substantially improves performance on held-out OOD data, including ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Sketch, while keeping ImageNet accuracy competitive. The resulting weights also improve transfer to OOD datasets not used during candidate selection, outperforming the original fine-tuned checkpoints, naive model soups, and Model Stock in our evaluations. These results suggest that lightweight optimization in anchored weight space provides a practical alternative to fixed weight-averaging rules, geometric merging, or single-model selection.

### [431] [CoEvoke: Evoking Multi-Agent Collaboration for Trajectory Collection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14021)
*Lin Wu,Shu Yao,Yuheng Wang,Jingru Fan,Huatao Li,Yihan Li,Liu Yixuan,Cheng Liu,Jian Chang,Zeyu Zhao,Aohua Zhang,Huiying Zhao,Shuyuan Zhu,Chen Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training multi-agent collaboration requires trajectories of checking, feedback, and repair, yet task-solving rollouts may end in immediate approval or repeat unsuccessful attempts without useful correction. We introduce CoEvoke, a cross-domain framework that evokes these interactions during trajectory collection. Controlled perturbations create recoverable difficulties, while restricted reference-based guidance directs investigation. The resulting dataset contains 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, linking public interactions to evidence, decisions, and task-native outcomes. Separate experiments over 2,287 same-task pairs show feedback increases of 47.72-100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups; guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training improves ACPBench-Hard success from 35.38% to 42.12% (+6.73 points). SWE verifier training gains 7.60-9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references. Workflow and post-training evaluations preserve task-solving topology with unperturbed inputs and no private-reference guidance. These results support designing collection conditions to obtain corrective supervision that improves collaborative decisions with frozen solving agents.

### [432] [OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14022)
*Yingdong Shi,Zhihong Li,Changming Li,Jingyi Yu,Quan Li,Kan Ren*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream computation, then it internalizes these states from on-policy trajectories. OPMD achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher--student settings, and generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that mechanism supervision yields more effective reasoning and meaningfully alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies, supporting that it transfers information beyond output supervision alone. Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.

Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.

</details>


### [433] [Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14025)
*Alexandros Xenos,Manos Plitsis,Niki Foteinopoulou,Yannis Panagakis,Ioannis Patras*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations during inference. For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings. The largest relative improvement occurs on AxBench and Emotion where we outperform the next strongest steering baseline by $48$ to $70\%$ and $13$ to $27\%$, respectively. Furthermore, CCS outperforms naive difference-of-means steering by up to $151\%$, showcasing the importance of deconfounding concepts. A toy experiment verifies our motivation on why: planting a topic nuisance into the training data reduces unprojected steering by $46\%$, whereas CCS loses only $12\%$ and recovers most of the gap to an oracle that explicitly deletes the planted direction. A human study with $23$ raters on $296$ generations reproduces the LLM judge's ranking. Our extensive ablation verifies the importance of our method's components and robustness to the number of nuisance classes. Finally, we extend our method to multi-turn conversations, where CCS sustains both concept expression and fluency, matching system prompt performance as other steering methods drift.

### [434] [Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14028)
*Luyang Zhang,Jialu Wang,Bebei Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning faces two facts about real training: data pools draw from many distinct domains, and evaluation spans diverse tasks. As a result, the same sample helps different tasks differently, and samples interact during training so that a subset's value is not the sum of its parts. Current data-selection methods leave these realities largely unaddressed. We formalize them as Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates attribution (how samples are scored) from selection (which subset to pick) and models the non-additive interactions among samples. On a real instruction-tuning data pool, we find substantial cross-domain complementarity (joint utility exceeds the sum of singletons), alongside redundancy within domains. Inspired by this, we propose Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first decides how many samples to take from each domain, then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score. Theoretically, the gap to the optimal subset is linear in the selection size and independent of data pool size. Empirically, Mixture-then-Select outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%, is robust across attribution methods, and works across different models and data pool sizes. The framework also extends to the data purchasing problem under a budget constraint when sample prices vary. Our findings suggest that allocating selection across domains offers a promising path toward more efficient and effective data selection for modern LLMs.

### [435] [Can We Trust This Evaluation? Instance-Level Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14029)
*Yang Ba,Michelle V. Mancenido,Rong Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates multiple judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet this panel decision process does not guarantee that the evaluation of an individual item is reliable. We propose Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR), a label-free approach for estimating instance-level evaluation reliability based on the judge panel's behavior. A latent measurement model serves as the backbone for measurement system analysis, from which SCUR derives three complementary signals capturing panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity. These three sources of evidence are combined into a risk score. We evaluate the SCUR approach on five real-world benchmarks using majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification. Furthermore, we show our approach to be more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items, which are the blind spots for many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.

### [436] [Rotate the Loop: Blockwise Conformality for Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14030)
*Alexey Zemtsov,Albina Klepach,Vadim Lomshakov,Andrei Polubarov,Nikita Lyubaykin,Alexander Derevyagin,Vladislav Kurenkov,Alexander Nikulin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.

### [437] [PLDiv: Measuring Dataset Diversity and Semantic Collapse via Persistence Landscapes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14031)
*Yang Ba,Michelle V. Mancenido,Rong Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Modern data pipelines increasingly combine human-created and human-curated data with AI-generated data for model training and evaluation. As datasets grow, they often add semantically redundant samples rather than expanding semantic coverage, which deteriorates the quality of the whole dataset. Existing diversity metrics primarily summarize lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity, but provide limited characterization of the shape of the underlying data distribution. In this paper, we propose PLDiv, a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes that quantifies the structural organization of a dataset from its geometric representation. PLDiv summarizes how data neighborhoods evolve as nearby samples progressively connect, producing an interpretable scalar measure of structural diversity without requiring task-specific supervision. Whether measuring intrinsic diversity in text generations or image embeddings, or detecting semantic collapse in instruction datasets and reasoning trajectories, PLDiv performs competitively against evaluated baselines and aligns strongly with diversity labels during semantic collapse. Consequently, it effectively supports applications in synthetic data monitoring, dataset construction, data augmentation, and generative model evaluation.

### [438] [A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14041)
*Anish Diwan,Jan Peters,Oleg Arenz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.

### [439] [Auditing LLM Program Search for Bermudan Stopping with Primal--Dual Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14063)
*Yuhua Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM program-search agents are usually judged by the score that drives their search. We study LLM-driven search over Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, an optimal stopping problem where a trusted evaluator owns the simulation and a dual upper bound~$U$. For any policy, $0 \le V^\star - L_\pi \le U - L_\pi$; we report Monte Carlo estimates of both bounds with their sampling error. We audit 24 generation attempts from two pipelines, a six-pair feedback-representation ablation, and a holdout evaluated after selection was frozen. No selected generated program improves on Ridge LSMC consistently or by more than Monte Carlo uncertainty; holdout gap scores lie within $0.002$ of it. On six one-dimensional puts, a high-precision binomial reference places Ridge within Monte Carlo noise of optimal and attributes 99\% of the estimated gap to dual-bound looseness, so this dual audits validity but cannot certify progress at the search's scale. Structured memory showed no benefit over score-only memory in this ablation. Whether search ``worked'' depends on reporting rules: retaining the initial reference, freezing selection before holdout, and counting failures.

### [440] [One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14074)
*Yiyang Fu,Zihao Huang,Dongchen Han,Shukai Gong,Zhen Dong,Qiyang Min,Daquan Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.

### [441] [Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch for Effective Linear Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14219)
*Zongyue Qin,Haoran Deng,Jason Cong,Yizhou Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Softmax attention in Transformers suffers from quadratic complexity in sequence length, making it impractical for long-context applications. Linear attention alleviates this issue by replacing the exponential kernel with alternative functions that enable linear-time computation. Among existing linear attention approaches, recent studies have shown that polynomial kernels are particularly effective, as they exhibit sparse and spiky behavior similar to softmax attention, which emphasizes large dot products while suppressing irrelevant interactions. However, the exact computation of high-degree polynomial kernels is infeasible for high-dimensional representations. As a result, prior work relies on approximate polynomial kernels. This introduces a non-negligible approximation error. In this paper, we show that, from the perspective of polynomial kernel approximation, existing linear attention methods are still suboptimal. We propose \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{Lo}w-Rank \textbf{P}olynomial \textbf{S}ketch (LLoPS), a principled and flexible framework for approximating polynomial kernels with linear attention. Our method learns a low-rank polynomial sketch that provably achieves a strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches. Experiment results show that LLoPS achieves the highest performance across extensive benchmarks, comparing with various linear attention baselines.

### [442] [The RNN Homunculus: Learning to Gate Long-Term Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14279)
*Zeyu Fan,Alexandru-Dragos Manolache,Jan van Gemert*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Learning long-range dependencies with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) is difficult because of the vanishing gradient problem. Gated recurrent neural networks like GRUs and LSTMs address this problem and are commonly explained by their ability to create additive copy paths through time. This explanation is correct, but incomplete: useful RNN gate values must themselves be learned, which is typically done with another RNN. We study this gate-learning problem through carefully controlled sequence classification tasks. Our analysis shows that gated architectures struggle when all training samples require long-range memory and thus equally suffer from the vanishing gradient problem. We intervene by adding short-dependency samples which let gated models learn solutions that capture long-dependency samples, but also generalize across different class labels. When properly learned, gated RNNs match or even exceed the test accuracy of modern architectures like Mamba and xLSTM. Overall, our results highlight gate learning as a central part of learning long-range memory and show how training data can support this process by exposing the same task over shorter dependencies.

### [443] [Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14413)
*Shihua Yu,Yanzhi Wang,Tianchi Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.

### [444] [Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14440)
*Shayan Mohajer Hamidi,Kayhan Behdin,Wenhui Zhu,Aida Rahmattalabi,Jincheng Cao,Jelena Markovic-Voronov,Alborz Geramifard*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $\rho$ by $\rho^\alpha$ for a data-adaptive exponent $\alpha\in[0,1]$: $\alpha=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $\alpha=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $\alpha$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $\kappa$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$\alpha$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.

### [445] [KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14448)
*Sihwan Park,Sung-Yub Kim,Doohyuk Jang,Eunho Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.

### [446] [RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14474)
*Cong Wang,Jin Li,Shoujin Wang,Yishuo Li,Huilin Gu,Wenpeng Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: this https URL .

### [447] [Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14500)
*Zirui Peng,Heyi Zheng,Ziming Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Many widely used activation functions, including ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid, produce predominantly positive outputs, resulting in a nonzero post-activation mean that we term activation bias. Despite its ubiquity, the effect of activation bias on learning dynamics remains poorly understood. Using controlled models, we show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but is accompanied by overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape. This early advantage also coincides with the model's use of task-relevant information encoded in the activation bias component. In contrast, reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss. Experiments on larger vision and language models exhibit a similar pattern: smaller activation bias is associated with better late-stage performance. Thus, this seemingly minor property can substantially redirect learning and warrants explicit consideration in future activation function design.

### [448] [Active Neural Matter: A Finite-Window Response Framework for Physical Systems and Distributed AI Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14549)
*Tianchi Chen,Shihua Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physical systems and distributed AI workflows can retain past information, receive delayed feedback and combine conflicting signals. These features pose a common modeling problem: determining what information about past interactions a state must retain to account for future responses. Active Neural Matter (ANM) addresses this problem through a finite-window response framework. Forward analysis uses each system's dynamics to predict state and output responses to perturbations, separating propagation from output sensitivity. Inverse analysis tests whether a candidate state retains enough information for these responses. With the system and future inputs or interaction rules fixed, distinguishable responses from histories assigned the same state identify distinctions the representation must preserve. Their distributional separation gives a lower bound on the worst-case error of approximating behavior from that state. Uncertainty bounds distinguish rejection, support within a fixed tolerance on tested comparisons, and unresolved cases. Delayed-consensus simulations check analytical predictions of response amplitude and phase over a narrow range of delays; flocking illustrates dependence on the chosen observable. An exact delayed-return construction establishes a sufficient state for a specified program. The AI studies identify distinctions in interaction history and evidence order that a representation must preserve to reproduce observed response distributions. Tests on new histories in a controlled feedback task provide bounded support for a state specified by the task instructions; the instructed rule predicts every observed action. ANM connects response prediction to measurable information requirements, separating behavioral fidelity from task correctness and initial-state adequacy from a closed evolution law for that state.

### [449] [Integrating AIRL-Based Reward Estimation into a Control Method Using Fuzzy Inference and Policy Gradient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14723)
*Seiji Ishihara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A method integrating policy gradient with fuzzy inference has been proposed. This method, hereafter referred to as the base model, has high flexibility with respect to the configuration of fuzzy inference rules and fuzzy representation. It can also automatically adjust the rule weights and the membership functions in the antecedent and consequent parts using the same framework for learning. In methods that integrate reinforcement learning with fuzzy inference, however, the reward function must be designed in advance. It is therefore useful to add learning-based reward estimation to the base model. This paper proposes a fuzzy control method that integrates a reward estimation mechanism based on the adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL) framework into the base model. The generative adversarial nets (GAN) framework adopted in AIRL, however, tends to suffer from unstable learning. To address this, the proposed method treats the policy of the base model as the generator and also uses the set of membership functions in the policy as the cost function of the discriminator. This configuration allows the discriminator update for reward estimation and the generator update for policy estimation to be performed simultaneously on the parameters shared by both, without estimating a value function. In simulations of an illustrative vehicle speed control task, the proposed method acquired policies with high generalization performance through stable and efficient learning.

### [450] [PTGPO: Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14737)
*Ruolin Chen,Yang Li,Jihang Wang,Zhuoya Zhao,Yuchen Liu,Jiaming Xu,Qian Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training language agents on long-horizon interactive tasks is challenging because sparse terminal rewards provide weak credit signals for intermediate actions. Existing group-based methods either assign a shared trajectory-level advantage or estimate step-level advantages from state groups, which may conflate the current action with subsequent decisions. We propose Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization (PTGPO), a critic-free method that constructs prefix trees over trajectory suffixes within anchor-state groups. PTGPO assigns each tree edge a credit given by the difference between its child and parent empirical mean returns, capturing the conditional return change revealed by each additional action. These prefix-tree credits provide fine-grained learning signals without requiring a critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on interactive benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop and Sokoban show that PTGPO consistently improves over RL baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness.

### [451] [Prior-Fitted and Frozen Scorers for Multimodal Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14770)
*Tillmann Rheude,Roland Eils,Benjamin Wild*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multimodal contrastive learning typically relies on manually specified scoring functions, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the similarity between representations from different modalities. Several such functions have been recently proposed to extend contrastive learning beyond two modalities. In principle, however, any function that assigns high compatibility to matched samples and low compatibility to mismatched ones could serve as a scorer. Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.

### [452] [Probabilistic Multi-Source Data Selection via Learnable Categorical Priors: Variance Reduction and Guaranteed Derandomization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14942)
*Shizhan Cai,Qixin Zhang,Siyuan Ma,Siyuan Liang,Yongcheng Jing,Dacheng Tao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bilevel data selection is a fundamental task with numerous applications in machine learning and statistics. A common strategy for tackling this problem is to relax the original bilevel combinatorial optimization into a continuous one. However, existing methods, including 0-1 relaxation and probabilistic relaxation, still suffer from several limitations, such as unstable gradient estimation and infeasible rounding. To address these issues, this paper proposes a new probabilistic relaxation for the multi-source bilevel data selection problem. Our key idea is to introduce multiple learnable categorical priors to parameterize a probability distribution supported only on feasible data subsets, thus naturally yielding a lossless rounding scheme. We further show that our proposed relaxation admits an effective two-point gradient estimator, which can simultaneously avoid the inverse-Hessian computation required by existing 0-1 relaxation and the unbounded score term appearing in prior probabilistic relaxation. Furthermore, we develop a reducible representation of this estimator, which substantially reduces the number of lower-level retrainings required for gradient computation. Built upon this reducible two-point estimator, we then design a novel stochastic gradient algorithm, termed ReSGD, for multi-source bilevel data selection problem, and establish a rigorous approximation guarantee for the subset returned by ReSGD under weak submodularity. Finally, extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our proposed ReSGD.

### [453] [Counterfactual Rollouts for Offline Contrastive Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14953)
*Tingrui Huang,Ai Bo,Junzhe Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) learns goal-conditioned values by associating state--action pairs with the states subsequently reached, assuming that no unobserved variable jointly affects the recorded action and its outcome. When offline demonstrations come from a demonstrator with information hidden from the learner, this assumption fails and the critic absorbs spurious action--outcome associations. We formalize this setting with confounded Markov decision processes and introduce counterfactual transitions that separate what the data identify from what they do not; minimizing over all compatible transitions yields a worst-case occupancy that lower-bounds the true one. Causal Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CauCRL) learns a pessimistic counterfactual transition from positive and negative offline demonstrations and trains the critic on counterfactual rollouts, substantially improving success rates over standard CRL on confounded goal-reaching tasks.

### [454] [Fitting Every Hint Is Not Enough: Premature Floods in Recurrent Algorithmic Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14982)
*Amin Najafgholizadeh,Mohsen Afsharchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and run for many more steps on large ones. On breadth-first search in SALSA-CLRS, we find that a reasoner can reproduce every training hint and still fail on deep graphs: after some exact steps, it declares nodes reached before the search gets there. We call this a premature flood and trace two routes to it. In our GRU processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and set off when that input is in the tail of the training distribution. Setting the input higher at inference brings the flood sooner, and none of the six flooding models counts steps. Without the input, summing the neighbors' states instead of averaging them also breaks the processor. In the benchmark's own GIN and PGN, trained with its code, some seeds instead flood from a fixed step, on sparse and dense graphs alike. Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the GRU processor. Detaching the state between steps avoids the flood in that processor (0 of 23 seeds, against 6 under full backpropagation) but not with sums or a residual update, and two published remedies leave floods. None of the benchmark's test sets is both deep and dense, but its deepest one shows the second route: on its Delaunay graphs at 1,600 nodes, one GIN seed floods from step 18. We therefore recommend auditing the range of every input and aggregate, which catches the first route, and testing on deep graphs, which catches both.

### [455] [Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14988)
*Julien Roger,Sam Bodmer,Jian Qian,Benjamin Riviere*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because its Bellman operator is known to contract in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing. Whereas existing work typically assumes a contraction property, e.g., through environment mixing, we consider the setting where we are given a reward-agnostic $m$-step mixing policy, and we control the contraction and exploration properties of the learned policy by regularizing toward the mixing policy. We provide finite-time analysis of $Q$-learning algorithms that can be instantiated with multiple choices of regularization, with guarantees measured with respect to the regularized fixed point. Our framework exposes novel regularizer-dependent objects that control contraction, exploration, and operator bias. In the one-step setting, our rates match the best known rates for $Q$-iteration and synchronous $Q$-learning, and for $m$-step mixing we derive new rates. We also study $Q$-planning variants, and show that planning acts as time-localized learning, where the planning horizon $H$ trades off the bias from the boundary value against the sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, and its advantage increases with bottleneck severity and, (ii) our theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of regularizers from the $\alpha$-divergence family.

Abstract: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because its Bellman operator is known to contract in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing. Whereas existing work typically assumes a contraction property, e.g., through environment mixing, we consider the setting where we are given a reward-agnostic $m$-step mixing policy, and we control the contraction and exploration properties of the learned policy by regularizing toward the mixing policy. We provide finite-time analysis of $Q$-learning algorithms that can be instantiated with multiple choices of regularization, with guarantees measured with respect to the regularized fixed point. Our framework exposes novel regularizer-dependent objects that control contraction, exploration, and operator bias. In the one-step setting, our rates match the best known rates for $Q$-iteration and synchronous $Q$-learning, and for $m$-step mixing we derive new rates. We also study $Q$-planning variants, and show that planning acts as time-localized learning, where the planning horizon $H$ trades off the bias from the boundary value against the sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, and its advantage increases with bottleneck severity and, (ii) our theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of regularizers from the $\alpha$-divergence family.

### [456] [Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14998)
*Tejas Vaidhya,Gaurav Sahu,Irina Rish*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.

### [457] [InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15032)
*Łukasz Marcjan,Dorota Wilk-Kołodziejczyk,Roberto Corizzo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.

### [458] [scHFBiMamba: a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder for cardiac disease-state classification from single-nucleus RNA-seq data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15117)
*Ugo Lomoio,Pietro Hiram Guzzi,Pierangelo Veltri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: To evaluate whether a compact bidirectional state-space autoencoder improves joint classification of species, cell type, and disease state from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF), while yielding interpretable gene attributions. Building on the dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) and MLP framework of Ruz Jurado et al., we developed scHFBiMamba, combining a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (BiMambaAE) with an MLP head. BiMambaAE maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latent representations using 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the dense DAE (192.9M). We compared six encoder-classifier configurations on 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and assessed nine classifiers on frozen representations. Biological relevance was evaluated by comparing SHAP-derived differentially explained genes with differentially expressed genes against curated HF-related Gene Ontology keywords. BiMambaAE+MLP achieved the highest aggregate F1: pooled macro-F1 across 13 outputs was 0.966 versus 0.957 for DAE+MLP, and the mean category macro-F1 was 0.977 versus 0.970. It significantly improved cell-type and disease-state accuracy (adjusted p=7.1e-3 and p=4.8e-6, respectively), with species F1 of 1.000. SHAP-derived differentially explained genes achieved a pathway-enrichment benchmark F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes. Compact bidirectional state-space autoencoders can outperform substantially larger dense autoencoders for joint cardiac transcriptomic classification while reducing parameters. scHFBiMamba enables accurate multi-task prediction and hypothesis-generating gene-level interpretation. ### [459] [ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15124)
*Can Jin,Yan Kang,Yifan Gong,Chongjian Ge,Mingze Xu,Yuanjun Xiong,Dimitris N. Metaxas,Hongwu Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.

### [460] [To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15128)
*Vasileios Saketos,William Reveillard,Alexandre Proutiere,Sebastian Dalleiger,Ming Xiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.

### [461] [Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15207)
*Lass Najmuldeen,Seyedhamidreza Mousavi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at this https URL

### [462] [EvolvAttack: Backdooring self Evolving VLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15244)
*Chuan Zou,Yang Xiang,Zexin Li,Xiaonan Luo,Simin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-evolving mechanisms let vision-language model (VLM) agents continually adapt through evolving memory, but they also allow malicious behavior to emerge only after deployment. We introduce a new attack surface, the self-evolving backdoor, whose payload stays dormant in the initial agent and is progressively activated as the agent evolves. Unlike conventional backdoors, which can be exposed by testing triggered inputs on a static model, our attack requires both a visual trigger and a sufficiently evolved memory state; static scanning with clean memory thus yields near-zero attack success and may deem the agent benign. We realize this through memory-aware backdoor training, which couples trigger activation with the agent's evolving memory while preserving benign behavior unless the trigger co-occurs with payload-related memory. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, the attack preserves normal functionality and stays nearly inactive before evolution (0.5% attack success rate), yet exceeds 95% attack success within 100 interactions, revealing a stealthy threat unique to self-evolving agents.

### [463] [LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15267)
*Romina Yalovetzky,Randall Balestriero,Yann LeCun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models directly in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, LeHami substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model and empirically maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts. The learned flow also supports accurate integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.

### [464] [WisdomNet: trustable machine learning toward error-free classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15299)
*Truong X. Tran,Ramazan S. Aygun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Misclassification is a critical problem in many machine learning applications. Since even the classifier models with high accuracy (e.g., > 95%) still introduce some misclassification error, it may not be possible to rely on the output of a classifier. In this paper, we introduce trustable learning, which prompts the learning model to yield only the true output, thus avoiding misclassifications. Whenever the model cannot decide the output accurately, the learning model should indicate that there could be a misclassification error if it is forced to classify, and hence, it should reject to make a decision or defer it to a human expert. Therefore, we develop a methodology for trustable learning and apply it to artificial neural networks and show that it is possible to develop a classifier with 0% misclassification error. We propose a novel neural network architecture named WisdomNet that could provide zero prediction error by introducing an additional neuron named as conjugate neuron that would indicate whether the network is able to classify the data correctly or not. The WisdomNet architecture can be applied to any previously built model, and we have evaluated WisdomNet with several network architectures such as multilayer perceptron, convolutional neural network, and deep network on different data sets. The results show that the WisdomNet is able to reduce the classification error rate to 0%, while labeling the data is difficult to classify as `reject' at a low percentage of within around 10%.

### [465] [Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15314)
*Heng-Sheng Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.
