We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: this https URL .

</details>


### [653] [Understanding Hidden Spatial Preferences in Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14696)
*Maria Bånkestad,Jens Sjölund*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy. We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process' default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are reached. We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization. The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially affect optimization performance.

### [654] [Linear-Time Non-Local Codec Placement for Machine Learning Model Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14703)
*Matteo Spallanzani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, na\"ıve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to na\"ıve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.

### [655] [DeKoR: Decomposed Knowledge Routing for Efficient GNN--LLM Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14710)
*Peiyuan Li,Yongqi Huang,Jitao Zhao,Di Jin,Dongxiao He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for text-attributed graph learning by leveraging rich pre-trained knowledge and language understanding capabilities. Combining LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offers a promising paradigm for expanding the modeling capabilities of graph learning. However, LLMs and GNNs follow distinct learning paradigms, leading to a pronounced mismatch between their knowledge spaces. Such discrepancies make effective knowledge fusion nontrivial. Moreover, existing methods often incur substantial additional computation for only limited performance gains. To address these challenges, we propose DeKoR, an efficient framework for GNN and LLM knowledge fusion. To enable efficient knowledge transfer, DeKoR decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views and uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill them into lightweight experts. To enable selective knowledge fusion, an adaptive router learns how much each node should rely on each expert. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DeKoR outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification, achieving superior effectiveness and efficiency.

### [656] [Multi-Token Random-Walk Learning via Meeting-Triggered Information Exchange](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14716)
*Taichun Yeh,Xingran Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Random walk (RW)-based algorithms are widely used in decentralized learning due to their low communication overhead and scalability. While most existing methods rely on a single token, multiple tokens can explore the network in parallel and exchange information upon meeting. However, the fundamental benefits of such meeting-triggered interactions remain unclear. In this work, we investigate multi-token RW learning under two information exchange policies: \textsc{Average-Gradient} and \textsc{Average-Model}, which average stochastic gradients and updated models, respectively, when tokens meet. We establish iteration complexity lower bounds for non-convex, convex, and strongly convex objectives on complete graphs, which apply to both exchange policies. Compared with single-token RW learning, the scaling factor in these bounds is reduced by a factor of $m^2$ for non-convex and convex objectives, and by an exponentially in $m$ for strongly convex objectives, where $m$ denotes the number of tokens. Numerical experiments reveal distinct behaviors of the two policies under two performance criteria: mean-token loss (the average loss across all tokens) and best-token loss (the minimum loss across all tokens). \textsc{Average-Model} achieves lower mean-token loss and is relatively insensitive to the network-to-token ratio $N/m$, where $N$ is the number of nodes. In contrast, \textsc{Average-Gradient} achieves lower best-token loss but exhibits a trade-off between parallel exploration and gradient interference as $N/m$ decreases.

### [657] [VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14731)
*Muquan Yu,Dihan Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.

### [658] [More Domains, No Gains? FLO: Fast-Slow Reciprocal Learning for Multi-Domain Graph Pre-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14748)
*Yupeng Tong,Lianze Shan,Jitao Zhao,Di Jin,Dongxiao He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Inspired by the great success of foundation models in the development of artificial general intelligence, Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently attracted significant attention and have the potential to advance graph intelligence. Exhibiting such intelligence requires effectively learning knowledge from large-scale, multi-domain graph data during pre-training. Increasing domain diversity during pre-training is expected to yield richer and more generalizable knowledge. Most existing methods pursue this goal by designing domain alignment strategies that help a single graph model learn from multiple domains. However, we observe that existing methods struggle to benefit from increasing domain diversity. Through empirical and theoretical analysis, we reveal two key limitations. Firstly, pre-training in most GFMs is confined to a single message-passing paradigm. Since propagation flattens relations among neighboring nodes, the graph model can hardly perceive the knowledge beyond propagation, namely the attribute-predictable component of these relations. Secondly, domain alignment strategies often rely on randomly initialized parameters that are jointly updated with the graph model using immediate loss feedback, leaving early knowledge acquisition vulnerable to cross-domain interference. To address these issues, we propose FLO, a Fast--sLow reciprOcal approach for multi-domain graph pre-training. Specifically, a propagation-free attribute branch predicts the graph model's relations without message passing and returns these predictions to refine the model. We further stabilize knowledge acquisition by pairing a fast process that adapts to the current domain with a slow process that integrates knowledge across domains. On 12 datasets, FLO benefits from increasing domain diversity and achieves the best average performance in cross-domain and cross-task transfer.

### [659] [Random Fourier Features in Near-Linear Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14751)
*Sepideh Mahabadi,Sandeep Silwal,Tal Wagner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Random Fourier features approximate a shift-invariant kernel in $\mathbb{R}^d$, such as the Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2)$, using independent samples from its spectral measure to construct an unbiased estimator for the kernel value with subgaussian concentration. However, generating $m$ such features requires $O(md)$ time. A long line of work on structured random features has accelerated this computation for the Gaussian kernel and other radial kernels, albeit with weaker concentration guarantees. We close this gap by showing a random feature map that can be computed in near-linear time $O((d+m)\log d)$ and yields near-subgaussian concentration. We obtain it through a new and tighter analysis of the Fastfood feature map of Le, Sarlós and Smola (ICML 2013), using Brascamp-Lieb inequalities and the Schoenberg representation of radial kernels.

### [660] [CrossMean: Model Merging by Pairing Merged and Expert Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14762)
*Moshe Eliasof*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one network without retraining, and closed-form methods compute each merged layer from statistics of its input activations. However, these statistics are measured on a single expert, while in the merged model, each layer receives activations from the merged layers that precede it. Recent work re-measures these statistics in the merged model but still forms them from a single network. We formulate closed-form methods as a linear system and show that they use the same matrix on both sides. We then introduce CrossMean, which replaces this matrix on one side with a bilinear statistic that pairs merged and expert activations. From the same statistics, we also derive a label-free criterion that indicates the task sets in which accounting for the merged activations improves the merge more. Empirically, task sets with a lower criterion value show a larger improvement. On the eight-task benchmark of each vision backbone that we tested and on BERT encoders, CrossMean improves on merging with statistics measured on the experts, and with all linear layers merged, it also improves on re-measuring these statistics in the merged model. These results suggest that merging benefits from pairing merged and expert activations.

### [661] [Formalizing Forgetting: Theory of Forgetting for Online Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14787)
*Renjie Cao,Yifei Cheng,Li Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Online continual learning (OCL) requires a learner to acquire a sequence of tasks in a single pass over the data, and catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks remains its central challenge. Despite the many methods proposed to mitigate forgetting, the theoretical understanding of forgetting in OCL is still limited: existing analyses mostly focus on linear, overparameterized, or neural tangent kernel regimes, and it remains unclear which factors govern forgetting and how they affect it. To fill this gap, we analyze single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives and derive explicit upper bounds on the expected final forgetting. Further analysis of these bounds shows how the per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter them, and that their effects can differ across objective classes. Moreover, experiments with neural networks on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST show that the trends suggested by our theory also appear in practice, indicating that these insights extend beyond the convex setting.

### [662] [Groups Don't Move as One: A Bregman Clustering View of Linearized Group Influence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14809)
*Hyunho Choi,Jaeseung Heo,Youngbin Choi,MoonJeong Park,Dongwoo Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Influence functions provide an efficient alternative to retraining for assessing the effects of removing or reweighting training data. For groups, however, the standard first-order estimate reduces individual contributions to a sum that can conceal substantial differences among members, including opposing effects that cancel. We establish a Bregman centroid formulation of the linearized group influence objective, interpreting this aggregate as a single representative and using Bregman information (BI) to quantify the variation it omits. Extending this formulation to multiple clusters reveals distinct contributions whose sum recovers the original estimate. We further propose an estimator that jointly optimizes the weights of these cluster contributions, rather than simply summing them. Experiments uncover cluster-specific influence patterns and a positive association between target-specific BI and approximation error. The proposed estimator achieves higher $R^2$ than standard group influence in predicting target changes under the nonlinear proximal Bregman response function. Simplified clustering and correction variants reduce computational cost. The centroid view thus explains what additive group influence leaves out and provides a basis for using that information to improve estimation.

### [663] [Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Dengue Infection Using Clinical and Hematological Data from Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Benchmark and Extended Prediction Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14813)
*Neesha Naimeen,Victor Miranda Soberanis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV) and a major public health concern in Bangladesh, where symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses complicates early diagnosis. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost to predict dengue from clinical and hematological data using two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (2024, n=1,511; 2025, n=1,283) with SMOTE. Extended models outperformed benchmarks within 2024 (Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.640 to 0.661), with RDW-CV the most consistently influential added predictor. 2025 benchmark performance was higher (ROC-AUC 0.904), unexplained by class imbalance and possibly reflecting data quality. External validation is needed.

### [664] [Sequence-Structured Decision Learning for Branch-and-Bound in Mixed-Integer Linear Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14835)
*Tengfei Liu,Jinrun Liu,Bai Yan,Yuhui Shi,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Branch-and-bound (BnB) solves mixed-integer linear programs by constructing and exploring a search tree. Node selection and branching are two recurrent decisions that directly determine the tree. Learning-based approaches typically optimize either decision in isolation and condition on a mostly local view, leaving the coupled evolution of the search tree insufficiently modeled. This paper proposes Seq-BnB, a sequence-structured framework that learns branching and node selection from a shared global representation of the evolving BnB process. Seq-BnB serializes node creations, node updates, node-selection events, and branching events into typed tokens, producing a causal event sequence of the search trajectory. A self-attention encoder summarizes this global search history, a bipartite graph neural network encodes the current LP relaxation, and context-conditioned decision heads score branching variables and open nodes. To reduce distribution shift between expert demonstrations and learned policies, Seq-BnB is trained with DAgger-style data aggregation. On four MILP benchmark families, Seq-BnB consistently processes fewer BnB nodes than heuristic and learning-based baselines, with strong solution times on both standard and larger transfer instances. While this paper evaluates Seq-BnB instantiation for branching and node selection, it accommodates additional solver decisions, such as cut selection, by introducing new action tokens and decision heads.

To reduce distribution shift between expert demonstrations and learned policies, Seq-BnB is trained with DAgger-style data aggregation. On four MILP benchmark families, Seq-BnB consistently processes fewer BnB nodes than heuristic and learning-based baselines, with strong solution times on both standard and larger transfer instances. While this paper evaluates Seq-BnB instantiation for branching and node selection, it accommodates additional solver decisions, such as cut selection, by introducing new action tokens and decision heads.

</details>


### [665] [Disentangling Marginal Capacity from Geometry in Optimal-Transport Label Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14853)
*Ali Khodabandeh Yalabadi,Azim Dehghani Amirabad,Artem Moskalev,Yun-Ching Chen,Mehdi Pirooznia,Scott Oloff,Rui Liao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Optimal transport (OT) is widely used to align distributions and transfer labels between unpaired source and target data, but source-target composition shifts can cause rare classes to be systematically under-predicted even with high transport confidence. We identify a source of this failure in the transport marginal: under the standard uniform weighting of source points, each class has transport capacity proportional to its source frequency, which can be insufficient to meet its target demand even when separated well in the embedding space. We show that displaced mass is preferentially absorbed by high-capacity classes rather than geometrically similar classes, producing confident errors that are difficult to detect from the transport plan. Downstream read-outs, entropic smoothing, and marginal relaxation provide limited recovery, whereas matching the transport marginal to the target composition substantially improves label transfer. On single-cell data, the oracle composition-matched marginal raises macro-F1 from 0.322 to 0.623, and the best deployable estimator closes 69% of the oracle gap. Correcting the marginal also separates a coverage-dependent component of error from residual error associated with class separability, showing that transport capacity and representation geometry are distinct sources of transfer error.

### [666] [Terrarium: Growing Personal Assistants via Scalable Synthesis of App Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14860)
*Mengzhou Wu,Yuzhe Guo,Jiawen Tao,Xiaokun Yuan,Yuan Cao,Gang Cao,Yuetang Deng,Zhi Gong,Dezhi Ran,Linyi Li,Wei Yang,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought the vision of a general-purpose personal assistant closer to reality. Such assistants could provide a unified natural-language interface to a broad ecosystem of applications. However, real-world applications do not readily support training at scale because access is often restricted and their state is difficult to reset. To address this challenge, we introduce Terrarium, a framework that synthesizes executable App Worlds from real-world application information, generates training task packages with evaluator-side rubrics from these worlds, and iteratively validates and refines both through agent rollouts. For App World synthesis, Terrarium organizes public Web information and in-application observations into structured app specifications that guide the construction of self-contained runtimes with callable operations and mutable, resettable state. For task synthesis, Terrarium constructs tasks grounded in App World state together with evaluator-side outcome rubrics that assess success without prescribing reference trajectories. We construct a training suite of 275 App Worlds and 13,344 tasks for outcome-based reinforcement learning across three Qwen3 model scales (4B, 8B, and 14B parameters). Across these scales, models trained with Terrarium outperform the corresponding Qwen3 models by an average of 18.34 percentage points on the $\tau^2$-bench and 10.94 percentage points on the AppWorld bench. These results suggest that app-grounded world and task synthesis offers a scalable path toward general-purpose assistants capable of operating across broad application ecosystems.

### [667] [World2TS: Real-World Event Context for Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14861)
*Zhiding Liu,Jiqian Yang,Mingyue Cheng,Zhi Li,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Time-series forecasting plays a vital role in a wide range of real-world applications. Recent approaches have achieved strong performance by modeling temporal correlations and cross-channel dependencies, yet most forecasting benchmarks still represent time series primarily as numerical histories. In practice, time series are observations of complex real-world processes, and their trajectories may reflect events, interventions, disruptions, and changes in measurement or reporting that cannot always be inferred from past values alone. A central barrier to studying context-aware forecasting is therefore the lack of large-scale datasets that align real-world events with the individual series they affect. We present World2TS, a scalable construction framework and large-scale dataset for time-series forecasting with real-world event context. We first develop world2ts-core, a reusable tool that combines agent-led semantic reasoning and Web search, command-line execution and validation, and human review within a feedback-driven discovery workflow. Given heterogeneous time series with semantic descriptions, the workflow discovers candidate events, consolidates retrieved evidence into verified events, and links them to relevant series under explicit temporal and semantic scopes. Using this framework, we construct world2ts-data, which contains 31 datasets across six domains, comprising 4,179 series, 97.1 million observations, 1,159 events, and 56,846 event-series links. We further conduct extensive data analyses and controlled comparative experiments to characterize the dataset and demonstrate the utility of the collected context for improving forecasting accuracy. World2TS provides a reusable data foundation for developing and evaluating context-aware forecasting models and agents. The project homepage is available at this https URL .

### [668] [Blending experimental electron density information to protein-ligand interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14862)
*Seonghyun Park,Shuan Chen,Jun Jin Choong,Noboru Kuno,Gyubok Lee,Kaushalya Madhawa,Keisuke Ozawa,Hikaru Shindo,Sungsoo Ahn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Machine learning models for protein-ligand interactions commonly rely on atomic coordinates, which are constructed by fitting molecular models to experimental electron-density maps. However, most models represent each complex as a single fitted structure, which can omit information about conformational heterogeneity, positional uncertainty, and local density support for individual atoms at binding interfaces. To fill this gap, we present CoDE, a Coordinate and Density Encoder, pre-trained on experimental density maps. We represent each binding site on a shared three-dimensional voxel grid combining atomic occupancy, experimental electron density, and its gradient magnitude. Using approximately 100K curated complexes, we pre-train a channel-wise vision transformer to jointly reconstruct masked atomic and density channels, learning a representation that integrates structural and experimental information. We evaluate the frozen encoder on two downstream tasks: (i) binding-affinity regression under leakage-controlled splits and (ii) pocket-conditioned ligand generation. Across these settings, CoDE improves over an identically pre-trained coordinate-only encoder and remains competitive with task-specific baselines, showing that density complements fitted atomic coordinates for protein-ligand interaction modeling and that the density-blended representation is useful for structure-based ligand generation.

### [669] [Contrastive Linearized Laplace: Loss Geometry, Valid Repairs, and Reliable Cores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14875)
*Francisco J. Sáez-Maldonado,Luis A. Ortega,Andrés R. Masegosa,Thomas D. Nielsen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: While contrastive learning is widely used to learn deterministic representations, it does not inherently provide estimates of uncertainty. Post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods, such as the Linearized Laplace approximation (LLA), offer a way to quantify uncertainty without retraining the encoder. However, we show that directly using the LLA induced distribution over the contrastive embedding does not yield reliable pointwise uncertainty estimates for downstream tasks: embedding variance alone does not reflect whether decisions such as nearest-neighbor retrieval or cluster assignment are stable. To address this limitation, we develop a post-hoc framework based on LLA that propagates encoder uncertainty through the downstream task. We characterize the curvature of contrastive objectives and introduce positive-semidefinite repairs where needed to obtain valid local Gaussian approximations without retraining the encoder. We test the proposed approach in metagenomic binning and image classification tasks. For metagenomic binning, posterior coassignment probabilities support consensus partitions and the selection of reliable cores, leading to improvements over existing baselines. Additional image classification experiments show calibration improvements on standard benchmarks and real histopathology datasets.

### [670] [Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14894)
*Zhikang Xu,Jiarui Xing,Jian Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: this https URL .

### [671] [Prediction with Expert Advice under Heavy-Tailed Losses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14904)
*Yuki Shibukawa,Shinji Ito*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We study prediction with expert advice over $T$ rounds with $K$ experts under heavy-tailed losses whose $(1+\epsilon)$-moment is bounded by $\theta>0$ for some $\epsilon\in(0,1]$. In this setting, existing algorithms designed for the case $\epsilon=1$ can be suboptimal when $\epsilon<1$, suffering an additional polynomial dependence on $K$. We characterize the minimax pseudo-regret rate as $\Theta((\theta T)^{\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}}(\log K)^{\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}})$ and establish gap-dependent lower bounds in a self-bounded environment. To attain this minimax rate without prior knowledge of either $\epsilon$ or $\theta$, we propose Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL, which uses robust data-dependent scale adaptation together with truncation. We further develop Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD, which likewise requires neither $\epsilon$ nor $\theta$ and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees in both adversarial and self-bounded environments. Finally, when $\epsilon$ and $\theta$ are known, an FTRL algorithm with Shannon-entropy regularization achieves optimal regret guarantees in both environments.

### [672] [Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14921)
*Hao Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.

### [673] [TLA-Verus: Generating and Solving Temporal Proof Obligations with LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14923)
*Kseniia Strelbytska,Balázs Szilágyi,Anna Mészáros,Ferenc Huszár*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The TLA+ (temporal logic of actions) formal specification toolkit has seen widespread adoption in modeling modern distributed software systems including databases, storage systems, ledgers and coordination protocols. This popularity is despite its two significant limitations for software verification: Firstly, TLA+ offers no way to detect drift between software implementation and mathematical specification; secondly, TLC and TLAPS cannot provide satisfactory proofs of arbitrary temporal logic properties. We take a step towards addressing these shortcomings by translating TLA+ specifications into Verus, an auto-active verifier built for Rust, via both a deterministic transpiler and an agentic translator. We demonstrate that our LLM-based pipeline is able to generate proof obligations from TLA+ specifications at scale, and to produce fully machine checkable proofs of both safety and liveness properties. Since temporal logic reasoning in Verus is a largely new task for LLMs, our work yields a valuable evaluation dataset, which we use to map out current generation model capabilities in Verus theorem proving.

### [674] [Compositional Average Velocity Modeling for Efficient Diffusion Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14941)
*Thanh Nguyen,Abu Hanif Muhammad Syarubany,Hwanhee Kim,Chang D. Yoo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.

### [675] [Exact Phase-Type Point Processes for Certified Measurement and Prediction of Event Streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14948)
*Sayak Dutta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Temporal point processes are used both to measure market mechanisms, for example how fast prices absorb news and how much of the reaction is the market responding to itself, and to predict the next event. We show that one algebraic object, the phase-type (Erlang-chain) state space, serves both purposes with exact likelihoods. For measurement, we build a multiscale phase-type Hawkes process whose parameters all enter linearly. Its log-likelihood is concave, and we compute the global maximum together with a Fenchel duality-gap certificate. A Markov embedding gives the response to an exogenous shock, echoes included, in closed form, and this response is stable if and only if the spectral radius of the branching matrix is below one. Applied to six markets around 670 scheduled macroeconomic releases (2022-2026) with a built-in placebo test, the model shows that the direct reaction to CPI, payrolls, PPI and the FOMC statement is absorbed in about a second, while the market's own echoes stretch half of the response to 16-137 s. For prediction, we introduce EPT-X, a neural point process that adds a history-dependent mixture-of-Erlang renewal channel to a linear Hawkes backbone. Its intensity and compensator remain in closed form, its states follow an affine recursion that trains with a parallel scan, and it can start from the certified fit of the measurement model. EPT-X has the best test likelihood on all five LOBSTER order-book streams and on Retweet and Taobao, and is level with the best published model on StackOverflow. We also find that the EasyTPP implementation of IntensityFree clamps short inter-event times before scoring, and that the gaps of the EasyTPP Amazon data are uniform on two fixed intervals.

### [676] [HiPAD: A Unified Gait, Audio-Visual, and Personality Fusion Network for Depression Detection, with a Hierarchical Personality Ablation and the Calibration Limits of Domain-Adapted LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14961)
*Karol Chlasta,Piotr Struzik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We present HiPAD, a single fusion network submitted to all six sub-tracks of the MPDD-AVG 2026 depression-detection challenge, covering the Elder and Young cohorts and three modality sets (gait, audio-visual, and both), each combined with personality descriptions. The network encodes each available modality with a shared BiLSTM, zero-pads absent modalities, and applies cross-modal attention only when at least two of gait, audio and video are present. Personality, which dominates our results, is kept out of the attention and fused by concatenation. Because the architecture is identical in every sub-track, differences between them reflect the data rather than the model, and we use this to study three questions. Our main finding is that the personality description, roughly 150 tokens about who the subject is, carries more depression signal than audio, video, and gait combined: gait plus personality alone (TLS 0.647) beats every configuration that includes audio and video. First, a four-level ablation of the personality description (L0-L3) quantifies this: removing every personality-derived feature, including the Big Five scores that earlier MPDD ablations keep, lowers the Track-Level Score by 0.499 to 0.507 and leaves the model at chance. Second, domain-adapting the personality encoder with LoRA (7B) or QLoRA (72B) on PHQ-8/9 data raises binary Cohen's $\kappa$ by 0.13 but lowers the overall score by distorting the PHQ-9 regression; a frozen RoBERTa-large encoder does better at this sample size. Third, at fixed architecture, handcrafted clinical features (eGeMAPS, OpenFace action units) outperform generic deep features (wav2vec2, DenseNet) on the audio-visual tracks. The unified system reaches a cross-track G-Score of 0.482; with under 100 subjects per cohort, the limiting factors are the size of the representation and the calibration of the outputs, not the choice of architecture.

### [677] [Cross-Material Magnetic Core Loss Prediction via Operating-Condition Matching and Partial Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14964)
*Cong Yao,Yu Zheng,Zehao Hou,Rui Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-material magnetic core loss prediction requires adapting to new material responses with limited measurements. Global feature alignment overlooks differences in source and target excitation coverage. This motivates selecting comparable samples and controlling each source measurement's alignment contribution. This paper proposes T-PCOT, a Transformer transfer method based on condition-supported partial optimal transport. Frequency, flux excursion, temperature, and waveform descriptors define a sparse graph of comparable operating conditions. A capacity-constrained transport plan distributes alignment across source measurements and leaves costly target mass unmatched. The plan is constructed from measured inputs before training and guides local waveform-feature consistency. An importance-weighted sampling scheme preserves both uniform source regression and the transport objective during minibatch optimization. Experiments on three material pairs and three target label budgets show that T-PCOT reduces mean relative error (MRE) and 95th-percentile error (P95) relative to Transformer-based multiple-kernel maximum mean discrepancy (T-MKMMD) in all nine comparisons. Macro MRE decreases from 12.60% to 9.65%, and macro P95 from 30.94% to 25.06%, corresponding to relative reductions of 23.41% and 19.01%. Controlled comparisons and ablations examine the roles of input processing, condition correspondence, and source capacity. The results demonstrate the predictive advantage of organizing cross-material alignment through operating-condition support over the compared global alignment method. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance in magnetic core loss transfer learning.

### [678] [HodgePhaseNet: Discrete Hodge Decomposition of Semantic Flows in Transformer Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14971)
*Kiyotaka Kasubuchi,Kazuo Fukiya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WavePhaseNet introduced frequency-resolved semantic representations, QuantumPhaseNet introduced gauge-covariant phase connections, and ModularPhaseNet made a finite cyclic phase channel and its cycle holonomy computable in an ordinary Transformer. These constructions are complementary, yet they do not by themselves separate an observed collection of pairwise relations into a globally consistent direction, circulation around local compositions, and circulation that persists around a larger unfilled cycle. HodgePhaseNet addresses this separation by representing semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on a finite oriented simplicial complex. With vertex-edge incidence matrix $B_1$ and edge-face incidence matrix $B_2$, every such field has a unique orthogonal decomposition $\Omega = B_1^T\Phi + B_2\Psi + H$, where $B_1H=0$ and $B_2^TH=0$. The three component fields are unique even when their potentials are not. We give explicit projectors, a sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, a verified numerical example, and a redesigned attention interface. The attention bias is defined on allowed ordered query-key pairs, remains consistent under arbitrary choices of edge orientation, and preserves a decoder's causal information boundary by constructing its complex from the visible prefix. Gauge invariance of the attention output is conditional on using invariant or appropriately compensated features. A simple difference of vertex embeddings has no coexact or harmonic component; a genuine relation encoder is therefore indispensable. Local circulation is not automatically contradiction, and harmonic flow is not automatically missing knowledge. These interpretations and any reduction in factual error require controlled empirical evaluation. This paper presents a mathematical and architectural proposal, not external natural-language performance results.

### [679] [Characterizing the Separability Gap in Prior-Data Fitted Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14989)
*Julius Kobialka,Manuel Hülskamp,Thomas Nagler,David Rügamer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are transformers pretrained on simulated datasets to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive distributions. Standard PFN theory assumes a separable task prior, under which the feature distribution and the mechanism generating labels from features are independent. We show that common PFN priors are non-separable, even in simple settings. Consequently, standard pretraining targets a predictive distribution based on a task posterior updated using both the labeled context and the query features. We characterize its difference from the predictive based on the context posterior alone and show that this difference vanishes under posterior concentration. Under misspecification (i.e., when the true joint distribution lies outside the prior's support), however, prior non-separability can favor better feature fit at the expense of conditional label fit. We illustrate the consequences for feature attribution, Bayesian optimization, and martingale checks of Bayesian behavior. The same dependence also enables PFNs to learn from additional unlabeled observations. We demonstrate this with SemiTabICL, a PFN explicitly pretrained to use these observations, which improves accuracy over a matched supervised baseline. Our findings highlight the need for explicit rules on unlabeled data use in PFN evaluation and establish the dependence between feature and label distributions as a consequential prior design choice.

### [680] [Conformal Sequential Decision Making With Cost and Sublinear Policy Regret Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15011)
*Jayadev Naram,Giuseppe Durisi,Matteo Zecchin,Osvaldo Simeone*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Automated decision makers, such as AI agents that control robots or network devices, must often satisfy hard cost constraints while maintaining competitive performance. In such settings, a cost measure, such as a safety violation rate, energy consumption, or a distortion level, must stay within a given budget in every episode of operation. Furthermore, a cumulative reward metric, accounting for per-step performance, must stay close to the reward of a meaningful reference policy. We formulate this setup as an episodic sequential decision problem in which the state sequence is arbitrary, and the reward and cost may depend on past actions within the same episode. We propose the online conformal episodic agent (OCEA), a policy that selects one candidate action per episode using a regret-controlled algorithm, and switches to a zero-cost action when the remaining budget cannot absorb the maximum cost of one more round. We prove that OCEA satisfies per-episode cost constraints for every state sequence and for every realization of its internal randomness, while achieving a sublinear expected policy regret with respect to the best action sequence in hindsight from a comparator class satisfying the same per-episode cost constraints. We apply OCEA to risk-averse control and online compression with distortion guarantees.

### [681] [Algorithmic Fairness Over Time: Advances & Prospects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15015)
*Miriam Rateike*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In the presence of feedback loops, algorithmic decisions at one time step can influence observed data in subsequent steps, potentially introducing selection bias or shifts in data distribution. Research has demonstrated that ignoring these effects can lead to unfairness, which may worsen over time as the model remains deployed within society. This raises important questions of how to measure and ensure fairness of algorithmic decision-making models over time. In this short paper, we present a taxonomy that distinguishes between different types of static and temporal fairness notions in recent advancements. We then suggest prospects for future research by identifying common implicit temporal assumptions, open questions to enhance our temporal understanding of fairness, and other open challenges.

### [682] [PATTERN Can Be Solved from Memory: Generator-Aware Baselines for Synthetic Node Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15020)
*Amin Najafgholizadeh,Mohsen Afsharchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PATTERN, a synthetic node-classification benchmark still used to rank graph networks, plants a random subgraph in a random host graph and asks which nodes belong to it. Its generator draws 100 patterns once and plants the same ones in every split, so each test graph carries a pattern that also appears in 100 training graphs. A matcher that reads these patterns off the training labels and looks them up in each test graph reaches 99.2 class-weighted accuracy with no trained parameters, against 89.8 for the best published model. Inference under the generator without the patterns reaches 86.8. Two published models, CKGConv and GRIT, score lower on patterns they have not seen: on new graphs with fresh patterns both fall below this pattern-blind predictor, and withholding patterns from CKGConv's training lowers its accuracy on the test graphs that carry them. Training CKGConv with a new pattern in every graph raises its accuracy on fresh patterns by about 2 points, to the level of the pattern-blind predictor, at some cost on the reused patterns. The same kind of inference under the generator matches the best published result on CLUSTER and, without any training, scores above every published result we found on Minesweeper's released board. We recommend that synthetic benchmarks report scores on fresh templates beside reused ones, publish baselines built from their generators, and state how their metric is weighted and pooled.

### [683] [Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15039)
*Sagar Ghosh,Huy Nguyen,Alessandro Rinaldo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_\Delta$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

### [684] [Information-Theoretic Foundations of Online Temperature Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15043)
*Jin Sima,Nikolaos Papagiannis,Ananth Grama,Wojciech Szpankowski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $\Omega(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.

### [685] [The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15058)
*Nikolaos Papagiannis,Ananth Grama,Wojciech Szpankowski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{\eta V}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.

Abstract: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{\eta V}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.

### [686] [Toward a Multimodal Foundation Model for Plasma State Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15076)
*Bin Xia,Chuanfei Dong,Boting Li,Yilan Qin,Zikang Xie,Sung Hyun Son,Adam J. Stanier,Jongsoo Yoo,Hantao Ji,Ahmed Diallo,Han Ding,John Wise*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Plasma experiments observe coupled physical states through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. We present a proof of concept toward a multimodal foundation model for plasma state reconstruction during magnetic reconnection, motivated by the Facility for Laboratory Reconnection Experiments (FLARE). Using 250 synthetic VPIC simulations at fixed reference electron beta $\beta_{e0}=0.2$, with 225 training runs and 25 disjoint validation runs, we train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net to reconstruct three magnetic-field components and electron density from incomplete observations. The model combines spatial-only pooling, which preserves all 24 temporal frames, with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding. Independently masking magnetic and density modalities across random, grid, block, and temporal patterns enables sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion with a single set of weights and no task-specific retraining. With density fully hidden, just 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility reduces median density NRMSE from approximately 0.9 to 0.1. Conversely, observed density improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. With no magnetic observations, roughly 1% density visibility approaches the density reconstruction accuracy achieved with fully observed magnetic fields, although current structure remains more dependent on direct magnetic measurements. Full magnetic conditioning also stabilizes completion of missing future density frames. These results demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal predictive coupling within this simulation regime. Generalization across plasma regimes or to experimental measurements remains untested.

### [687] [On the Theoretical Limits of Learning Unconstrained Interatomic Potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15078)
*Prajwal Ananth,Shuwen Yue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) accelerate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by learning the energies and forces that govern atomic motion. Recent work has shown that relaxing physical inductive biases can improve computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, raising the question of whether energy-and-force matching alone is sufficient to ensure accurate sampling. We show that, for unconstrained hypothesis classes, the relationship between prediction error and sampling accuracy is exponentially ill-conditioned in dimension. In particular, prediction errors that decay exponentially with dimension can coexist with nearly maximal total variation distance between the learned and target distributions. We identify two failure mechanisms. The first is kinetic trapping, where relaxation to an accurate learned equilibrium requires exponentially long times, even when simulations are initialized from training configurations at which energies and forces are matched exactly. The second is equilibrium mismatch, where the learned stationary distribution itself remains far from the target. Under explicit assumptions, we show that equilibrium mismatch can persist even in local, symmetry-preserving models, where small per-atom errors coexist with a distributional discrepancy that approaches its maximum as system size increases. Finally, we establish global energy-control conditions that guarantee equilibrium accuracy and identify additional conditions required for rapid relaxation.

### [688] [Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15095)
*Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem,Irene Tenison,Yang Zhang,Yada Zhu,Boris Katz,Dan Gutfreund*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.

### [689] [Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15097)
*Feiyu Qu,Zheng Huang,Andrea Zanette*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.

### [690] [Random Feature Pruning for Multi-Class Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15101)
*Mohammad Amin Omidi,Babak Seyfe,Shahrokh Valaee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Weighted sums of random kitchen sinks (W-RKS) is a commonly used feature extraction technique for supervised learning tasks. A major drawback of this method is the redundancy and ineffectiveness of many extracted random features. This paper investigates efficient methods for reducing such redundancy in multi-class classification problems. We specifically formulate feature selection as a variant of the sequentially nested model selection problem and introduce the Successive Empirical Excess Risk Difference Maximization (SEED-MAX) algorithm. It recursively computes empirical risks to identify the most parsimonious yet informative set of features. We derive an analytical lower bound for the probability of correct feature selection by the SEED-MAX algorithm. This lower bound on the probability of correct feature selection can be made arbitrarily close to one by increasing the training dataset size. To further enhance the rate of pruning, we evaluate the features retained by SEED-MAX using the Fisher test (F-Test). Empirical evaluations on UCR time-series classification datasets show that the sequential application of SEED-MAX with the Fisher test achieves approximately 92 percent rate of pruning with negligible degradation in classification accuracy. Implementations of the SEED-MAX and SEED-MAX-F-Test methods are available at this https URL .

### [691] [RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15106)
*Vladimir Kirill Bickov,Neil Yorke-Smith*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. An output head maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, from which an autoregressive decoder constructs a feasible solution. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.

### [692] [When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15139)
*Yuhang Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.

### [693] [Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15146)
*Dan Saunders,Benjamin Ren,Catherine He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.

### [694] [Sensor-Aware Joint Data Fusion and State Estimation under Sparse Multi-rate Distribution Grid Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15156)
*Pooja Algikar,Stefano Fenu,Kumarsinh Jhala,Siby Plathottam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Distribution-system state estimation is a growing necessity for the modern power grid as the addition of local storage and generation add system complexity that an operator or aggregator is not able to directly monitor. Classical methods work well when all system elements are time-synchronized and at least partly observable, but multi-rate monitoring of sparse heterogeneous sensors typically relies on machine learning approaches. It is a common practice in the literature to structure this task as a two-stage pipeline, first fusing data from disparate sensors and then feeding the fused pseudo-measurements to a separately trained state estimator. We propose a heterogeneous latent graph ODE in which measurement functions and sampling processes are typed and localized on specific buses, paired with a graph- transformer state estimator solving DSSE specifically for multi-rate heterogeneous sensor placements, and demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple IEEE standard topologies as observability degrades.

### [695] [Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15159)
*Muhammad Usama,Yeoreum Jung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. ### [696] [LexiCan: Lexicographic Canonicalization of Point Clouds for Machine Learning Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15171)
*Daniel Sanchez,Djordje Mihajlovic,Federica Valeau,Luka Benić,Raghuwansh Raj,Soutrik Sarangi,Snir Hordan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.

### [697] [Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15177)
*Michael Cardei,Anjun Hu,Chenrui Ma,Francesco Pinto,Chawin Sitawarin,Chulin Xie,Ferdinando Fioretto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.

### [698] [Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15183)
*Pooja Algikar,Stefano Fenu,Kumarsinh Jhala,Siby Plathottam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.

### [699] [DeltaNet-PC: Test-Time Memory Without Backpropagation Through Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15185)
*Todd Morrill,Richard Zemel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $\Delta S_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.
