### [700] [Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning of LLMs in Learnable Low-Rank Subspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15225)
*Chuang Tong,Ling Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). However, ZO optimization suffers from high variance in high-dimensional parameter spaces. While recent methods restrict perturbations to random low-rank subspaces, these subspaces often misalign with task-specific descent directions. We propose AdaSub-ZO, a novel forward-only fine-tuning framework in learnable low-rank subspaces. Instead of relying on fixed random matrices, AdaSub-ZO iteratively learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback to track task-aware descent directions. Furthermore, AdaSub-ZO incorporates a subspace momentum acceleration mechanism to smooth noisy gradient estimates across evolving subspace bases. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding tasks demonstrate that AdaSub-ZO outperforms existing ZO baselines, substantially reducing gradient estimation variance and accelerating convergence.

### [701] [ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15246)
*Kyle Montgomery,Wang Zhang,Chenguang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at this https URL .

### [702] [Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15250)
*Md. Johir Raihan,Zahra Zamanzadeh Darban,Yueyang Liu,Flora D. Salim,Levin Kuhlmann,Mahsa Salehi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Reconstruction-based detectors for multivariate time series anomaly detection typically learn a single entangled representation of normal behavior and flag anomalies based on reconstruction error. However, real-world anomalies are not only isolated spikes in a single channel but also disruptions in the relationships between channels, where each sensor individually appears normal, but their joint behavior deviates from the norm. Because these models compress both temporal evolution and inter-channel structure into this single space, they lack an explicit mechanism to isolate such inter-channel dependencies from normal temporal dependencies, leading to lower detection rates for cross-channel anomalies. We propose CARMA (Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection), which is a reconstruction-based variational autoencoder with two complementary latent spaces: a temporal latent that captures sequential dynamics, and a correlation latent that is trained to reconstruct the window's pairwise Pearson correlations. Both representations are fused in the signal decoder, and anomalies are detected from the reconstruction error. We evaluate CARMA on the TSB-AD-M benchmark suite (17 datasets, 180 series) against 29 baseline methods, and show that it significantly outperforms all of them across multiple threshold-free and range-aware metrics, achieving a VUS-PR of 0.4929. Ablations show that removing the correlation branch degrades performance, that adding a second latent without supervision recovers only part of the gain, and that supervising the correlation latent with an explicit correlation target accounts for the rest and produces a sharper error response at anomalies.

### [703] [Imperfect Verifiers, Exact Targets: Inference-Time Scaling for Continuous Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15281)
*Kijung Jeon,Molei Tao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Verifier-guided inference-time scaling uses additional computation to score intermediate states and steer generation toward better outputs. However, imperfect intermediate verifiers can distort sampling, and repeated refinement alone does not ensure recovery of the desired reward-tilted distribution. We introduce Continuous-State Verifier-Guided Backtracking (CS-VGB), an inference-time scaling method for sampling from reward-tilted distributions with continuous generative models through repeated denoising and renoising. With correctly paired denoising and renoising transitions, the stationary distribution of CS-VGB at the clean checkpoint equals the desired reward-tilted target, even when intermediate verifiers are inaccurate. Under stated regularity conditions, CS-VGB converges exponentially to the target despite verifier error, and the expected number of updates needed to reach a clean sample grows only linearly with the number of checkpoints. In analytically tractable settings, we empirically demonstrate that CS-VGB recovers the desired reward-tilted distribution despite verifier error, whereas the compared verifier-based sampling methods fail to recover the target under the same verifier errors. We also instantiate the framework with diffusion models and one-step stochastic posterior maps. Across prompt-guided ImageNet generation, facial-attribute generation on CelebA, and multi-robot planning, recurrent CS-VGB search improves reward and task success as inference budgets grow, with image-generation rewards continuing beyond the observed plateaus of denoising-only baselines.

### [704] [FragFlex: Fragment-Based Flexible Molecular Generation for Exploring Vast Chemical Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15284)
*Sihyun Park,David Ryan Koes*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Drug discovery requires efficient exploration of an astronomically large chemical space. Molecular graph diffusion models offer a promising approach to this task, but many require graph size to be fixed before generation. Although atom-level insertion and deletion can enable flexible-size generation, jointly modeling molecular size, atom types, and bonds while maintaining chemical validity remains challenging. We introduce FragFlex, a flexible-length discrete diffusion model that performs node insertion and deletion at the fragment level. During denoising, FragFlex jointly learns the size, fragment identities, and inter-fragment connectivity of the fragment graph. A neural attachment-site predictor and valence-aware assembler then convert the generated fragment graph into an atom-level molecule. In large-scale experiments generating 10 million molecules, FragFlex achieves near-perfect chemical validity while maintaining high uniqueness, demonstrating a strong balance between the two.

### [705] [FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15307)
*Yifeng Mao,Yuze Feng,Yutong Shen,Liyang Gao,Zhixiang He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($\tau$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.

### [706] [CIViC: Evidence Gates for Audio-Conditioned Visual Prediction on Proxy Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15327)
*Mengzhe Geng,Max W. Y. Lam,Yuewen Cao,Shoukang Hu,Jing Xu,Marc Tessier,Xu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Removing audio can shift a visual predictor's output without showing whether the task uses the intended audio information. We introduce Conditional Input and Visual Interpretation Checks (CIViC), a four-gate protocol that links an interpretation to an intervention, held-out task comparison, or endpoint control. We demonstrate CIViC on actor-disjoint face-raster tests, a synthetic audio-feature mixture, and source-video-disjoint SpeakerVid proxy tasks. In the static face-raster test, cross-actor audio replacement meets the registered detection rule with a small effect; on a separate temporal endpoint, constant-audio fits score better than audio-trained fits in four matched seeds. In the synthetic mixture, the condition-augmented fit has higher 1,000-step RMSE than the audio-only fit (0.1807 vs. 0.1707), with the gap shrinking during training. In the SpeakerVid proxy, the five-feature-zero fit (five low-level audio summaries zeroed; identity, dialogue, and condition inputs retained) has lower whole-frame grayscale RMSE than aligned audio across four held-out conditions and five paired seeds, while aligned audio has lower segment-drift error. The results show that output activation, held-out error, and endpoint controls support different interpretations across these proxy tasks.

### [707] [Full Waveform Inversion with a Learned Preconditioner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15331)
*Jeongjin Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful approach for reconstructing subsurface velocity models, but its practical performance is limited by ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the high cost of curvature-based methods. In this project, we investigate whether a neural operator trained on reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can provide a useful learned preconditioner for FWI. We compare projected FWI against neural-preconditioned FWI using either a standard Fourier neural operator (FNO) or a Jacobian-informed FNO (JI-FNO). The neural preconditioner applies the normal operator of the learned RTM map to modify the true Devito FWI gradient. Our experiments show that the JI-FNO preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while maintaining data-residual decay comparable to baseline projected FWI. In contrast, the standard FNO preconditioner is unstable and gives worse model recovery, despite using the same neural-preconditioning framework. We also identify a failure mode of a nonlinear neural Gauss Newton-type inner solve: directly matching the neural RTM output to the FWI gradient creates an objective-space mismatch and does not yield a reliable descent direction. These results suggest that forward RTM-image prediction alone is insufficient for learned preconditioning; accurate learned derivatives and objective-consistent use of the neural operator are critical for producing useful inversion updates.

Abstract: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful approach for reconstructing subsurface velocity models, but its practical performance is limited by ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the high cost of curvature-based methods. In this project, we investigate whether a neural operator trained on reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can provide a useful learned preconditioner for FWI. We compare projected FWI against neural-preconditioned FWI using either a standard Fourier neural operator (FNO) or a Jacobian-informed FNO (JI-FNO). The neural preconditioner applies the normal operator of the learned RTM map to modify the true Devito FWI gradient. Our experiments show that the JI-FNO preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while maintaining data-residual decay comparable to baseline projected FWI. In contrast, the standard FNO preconditioner is unstable and gives worse model recovery, despite using the same neural-preconditioning framework. We also identify a failure mode of a nonlinear neural Gauss Newton-type inner solve: directly matching the neural RTM output to the FWI gradient creates an objective-space mismatch and does not yield a reliable descent direction. These results suggest that forward RTM-image prediction alone is insufficient for learned preconditioning; accurate learned derivatives and objective-consistent use of the neural operator are critical for producing useful inversion updates.

</details>


### [708] [ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute -- Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15368)
*Yi Ge,Kangrui Ruan,Jifan Chen,Manish Prajapat,Christian Bock,Xiaoyang Wang,Rein Houthooft,Aritra Sengupta,Varun Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.

### [709] [Approximation in Contrastive Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15388)
*Yuanfan Li,Zihan Zhang,Yiming Ying,Ding-Xuan Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Contrastive representation learning (CRL) is a fundamental paradigm for learning transferable representations. Recent work identifies its population target as the pointwise mutual information (PMI) $\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)}$ between two modalities $X,Y$, where $p$ is the joint density function and $p_X,p_Y$ are the marginals. However, it remains unclear why standard inner-product scores $f(x)^\top g(y)$ can effectively approximate a generally nonseparable population target PMI. In this paper, we address this question from the aspect of approximation for CRL. By linking PMI to a compact operator, we show that $D$-dimensional inner-product models perform rank-$D$ spectral approximation, with error controlled by the spectral tail. We then study neural network realizations: in general settings, we show that deep neural network scoring functions are universally consistent, and the approximation error rates depend on the smoothness of the PMI function; under structured low-rank data models we obtain improved rates attained by moderate-width encoders. Finally, we establish a fast calibration rate from contrastive excess risk to downstream retrieval error under a density-ratio Tsybakov noise condition.

### [710] [DC-Flow: Target-Conditioned Cyclic Peptide Design via Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15391)
*Yitian Wang,Minjie Cheng,Yaning Cui,Maohua Yang,Dongdong Wang,Hongteng Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Target-conditioned cyclic peptide design requires coordinating interfacial side chains with macrocyclic closure. Existing end-to-end generators concurrently update geometric and chemical variables from noise, assigning residues to disordered coordinates. Meanwhile, predictor-assisted workflows often get stuck in local traps because they lack feedback in the propose-and-filter stage and ignore 3D structural proposals during sequence search. To overcome the drawbacks of these two paradigms, we propose DC-FLOW, a staged generative framework built around Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching. In principle, DC-FLOW postpones sequence and side-chain activation until a target-conditioned backbone takes shape, resolving structural ambiguity before chemical assignment. Then, it feeds delayed activations back into the backbone, achieving co-evolution of backbone geometry and emerging residue identities by coupling their flows. This mechanism enables more reliable macrocyclic closure and favorable interface packing. For predictor-assisted workflows, DC-FLOW supplies 3D proposals with in-trajectory guidance, enabling cascaded test-time scaling to prune redundant backbones and terminate unpromising refinement early. Extensive experiments show that DC-FLOW improves cyclization fidelity, diversity, and interface energetics, substantially increasing the yield of confident cyclic peptide binders under a fixed final-candidate budget. Our code is available at this https URL .

### [711] [WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15394)
*Shengkun Tang,Dan Alistarh,Zhiqiang Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.

### [712] [GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15398)
*Shengkun Tang,Cong Zeng,Zongfang Liu,Dan Alistarh,Zhiqiang Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.

### [713] [Harnessing VLM in Embodied RL: From Reward Regressor to Success Detector via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15401)
*Xin Liu,Yutong Jiang,Jian Su,Ziheng Wang,Chuang Wang,Haoran Li,Dongbin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VLMs provide promising solutions to embodied reward design. Most current methods that train VLMs as reward regressors not only require extensive annotations but are also primarily designed for finetuning pretrained policies, and perform less well in the more challenging from-scratch RL setting. This issue stems from a fundamental mismatch: regressing precise rewards is misaligned with what VLMs naturally excel at. We posit that it is more aligned with VLMs' inherent multi-modal VQA capabilities for the models to function as success detectors, and propose VLM success reward via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating (VLMeg) to well harness VLM for embodied reward design. As the core of VLMeg, the proposed exploration-augmented key-observation gating first determines whether the current RL episode is judgment-worthy based on its similarity to a generated success trajectory. Then, the key observation with the lowest confusion from the judgment-worthy episode will be selected for VLM evaluation as episodic reward. This gating mechanism not only avoids redundant calls but also enables higher detection accuracy of VLM. Considering the sparsity of judgment-worthy episodes, the advanced exploration incentives based on the generated trajectory are introduced, enabling more efficient exploration toward judgment-worthy trajectories for more VLM reward triggers and thus gaining higher RL efficiency. Extensive experiments in MetaWorld demonstrate VLMeg achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL, outperforming advanced VLM-based baselines on 12 challenging reward-free tasks. Furthermore, VLMeg also enables effective RL without any ground-truth reward in 3 challenging real-world experiments. Code will be open after acceptance at this https URL .

### [714] [Riemannian Graph Tokenizer for Structural Knowledge Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15427)
*Qimin Zhou,Haibo Liu,Yujie Wang,Li Sun,Chuan Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Foundation models are at the forefront of artificial intelligence. A tokenizer, converting the raw input into discrete representations that the model can understand, plays an important role to the success of foundation models. Unlike the text tokenizer that is well studied in large language models, graph tokenizer is still at its early stage, facing the challenges of tackling the non-Euclidean structures and capturing the structural semantics. How to design a graph tokenizer for structural knowledge transfer? To this end, we propose a Riemannian Graph Tokenizer (RGT) that bridges the structural knowledge and quantized representations to support cross-domain structural knowledge transfer. The connection is established by Riemannian geometry. Specifically, we first define the geometric vocabulary (trees, cycles and sequences), which captures fundamental structural patterns and reflects the intrinsic geometry of graph. Second, we construct a Riemannian quantizer with Riemannian Straight-Through Estimator to tokenise graph structures across multiple domains into discrete tokens. To ensure consistency and transferability across diverse geometric spaces, RGT further incorporates a geometry-aligned decoder that projects manifold-specific tokens into a unified tangent space. The theoretical analysis and geometric interpretations are provided to support the effectiveness of our proposed method. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that RGT significantly enhances structural knowledge transferability across graph domains.

### [715] [Split Conformal Interval Length under Huber Contamination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15458)
*Xiao Zhang,Bowen Zhang,Lie He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Existing analyses of interval length in split conformal prediction largely focus on clean data. However, how contamination at the training and calibration stages alters interval length relative to the corresponding clean population oracle remains understudied. In this paper, we consider Huber contamination and derive a finite-sample upper bound that holds uniformly over contaminating distributions, with leading terms scaling as $L(\delta_1+n_1^{-1/2}) +(n_2^{-1/2}+\delta_2)/((1-\delta_2)r_0)$, in addition to a clean-sample estimation term. We further establish a minimax lower bound matching the upper-bound rate up to constant factors on a regular asymmetric location submodel. For calibration contamination, we obtain an exact worst-case characterization of the population interval-length deviation. We also extend the upper-bound results to conformalized quantile regression and adaptive residual scores. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets provide empirical support for our theoretical findings on training and calibration contamination.

### [716] [Revisited Support Vector Machines: A Unified Joint Optimization Framework with Nyström Approximation for Scalable Adaptive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15498)
*Nassou Gongon Benjamin,Noulapeu Ngaffo,Patrick Njionou Sadjang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The theoretical elegance of Support Vector Machines (SVMs), grounded in statistical learning theory, establishes them as a reference for robust classification. However, in the era of Big Data, classical SVMs face two major bottlenecks: the prohibitive cubic complexity $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ of training and the rigidity of static kernels. Traditional methodologies treat kernel selection as a discrete, "brute-force" GridSearch problem, effectively decoupling the learning of data representation from the optimization of the decision boundary. This paper proposes a paradigm shift with a so-called "Revisited SVM", a unified framework that recasts the learning process as a continuous %bi-level joint optimization problem. We derive a novel objective function $J(\alpha, \theta)$ that allows for the simultaneous optimization of dual Lagrange multipliers and kernel hyper-parameters. To solve this challenging non-convex problem efficiently, we introduce a hybrid Block Coordinate Ascent (BCA) algorithm, tightly integrated with Nyström-based low-rank approximation, which drastically reduces computational complexity to $\mathcal{O}(Nm)$. Extensive experiments conducted across four heterogeneous domains (Bioinformatics, Finance, Cybersecurity, and Computer Vision) demonstrate that our approach not only matches but often exceeds exhaustive GridSearch accuracy, while delivering training speedups of up to 100x. Notably, on the complex NSL-KDD intrusion detection dataset, our adaptive kernel approach achieves 96.25\% accuracy compared to a mere 50\% for standard baselines, proving its unique ability to model complex non-linear manifolds in high-dimensional spaces. We validate our results using rigorous statistical tests and provide a theoretical convergence analysis of the proposed algorithm.

### [717] [Sensitivity Fidelity Reveals Physical Dependencies Beyond Forecast Accuracy in Deep-Learning Earth-System Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15540)
*Qi Chen,Peng Zhan,Hongxing Cui,Wenqing Cui,Ibrahim Hoteit*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deep-learning models increasingly rival numerical simulation in Earth-system forecasting, yet forecast error alone cannot determine whether their learned input-output dependencies are physically consistent. Here we introduce sensitivity fidelity as an additional criterion: alongside prediction error, model responses to input perturbations should be examined against a trusted reference or established physical knowledge. In an idealized Rayleigh-Bénard convection benchmark, four surrogate architectures achieved low forecast errors yet encoded markedly different sensitivities. Quantitative comparison with a matched adjoint distinguished the models far more sharply than forecast accuracy and showed that predictive skill and sensitivity fidelity need not coincide, while finite-perturbation experiments further linked these differences to the propagation of initial-condition uncertainty. We then applied this strategy to El Niño-Southern Oscillation prediction, where no adjoint reference exists and learned sensitivities showed event-wise robustness, validity under finite perturbations, and consistency with established precursors. These results identify gradient-based evaluation as a discriminating complement to forecast-error metrics, providing a practical test of whether data-driven Earth-system models learn physically credible dependencies.

### [718] [UNISON: A Unified Framework for Learning from Scored Bags](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15564)
*Ofek Kirshenboim,Or Shkuri,Shani Finkelshtein,Yoram Louzoun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We introduce UNISON, a unified framework that bridges multiple instance learning and recommendation systems by treating both as instances of learning from scored bag collections of (item, score) pairs. Unlike traditional approaches that address bag-level classification and personalized recommendation as separate problems, UNISON decomposes learning into three interconnected stages: (1) learning universal item representations, (2) modeling bag-specific preference patterns through lightweight personalized parameters, and (3) inferring bag-level characteristics from learned preferences. We justify the architectural choice of linear bag-specific scoring through a first-order analysis: when item embeddings are sufficiently smooth in the score, a linear function approximates the score up to a Taylor remainder controlled by the curvature of the underlying preference function. For cold-start scenarios, we show that the cold-bag fitting problem reduces to ridge-less linear regression with a closed-form solution, and provide convergence guarantees for the iterative variant. Empirically, UNISON matches or outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse domains: entertainment (books, movies), immunology (T cell receptor (TCR) based classification), and microbiome, offering superior computational efficiency and interpretability. A controlled synthetic experiment further confirms that the bag-specific parameters ($w_j, b_j$) recover the latent factors that drive item scores even when the projection $\phi$ has no access to the original scoring mechanism (AUC > 0.998). UNISON is available at this https URL .

### [719] [Truncation Samplers Are Nested: Comparing Decoding Rules Is a Measurement Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15570)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Settling one comparison between two truncation samplers has cost six thousand A100-hours, and nothing says in advance how far apart two samplers can be. We observe that almost every deployed truncation rule keeps a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, so any two such rules are nested at every decoding step. Nesting yields a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which both samplers emit identical text until they first disagree. Accumulated over a generation, this gives a separation certificate that bounds the difference between two samplers on any bounded outcome, is computable from logs a comparison already produces, and equals their sequence-level total variation distance exactly when neither rule ever overtakes the other. Two consequences follow without measurement: exactness is fragile, and certifying a small difference requires the two retained masses to agree to very high precision at every step. On six open-weight models over four math and science benchmarks, the certificate for every hyperparameter grid we tested is at least 0.998, so a bound alone rarely settles a comparison, although two members of one family can be far closer. What remains useful is the coupling, which gives an unbiased paired estimator that cuts variance $1.2$-$3.8\times$ against prompt-level pairing. Read against benchmark sizes at the default pair's variance and our point estimate of its between-prompt component, resolving a one-point difference needs 8 to 32 samples per prompt on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond and about 210 on AIME 2025; at that component's upper confidence bound GPQA-Diamond needs more than 32 and AIME 2025 cannot be resolved at any sample count. Choosing a truncation sampler is a measurement problem at least as much as a design one. The code is available at this https URL .

### [720] [The Gradient That Top-k Distillation Never Computes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15589)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Many deployed distillation pipelines show the student a truncated view of the teacher: keep the top-k probabilities, renormalize, and minimize a divergence on what remains. Renormalization is assumed to account for the missing mass. We prove that it removes the visibility of tail mass, not the freedom to move it. The renormalized objective depends only on log-odds among the retained tokens, so at each position its gradient along the directions that control tail mass is exactly zero; on a real teacher that component measures $2$-$3\times10^{-15}$ of the gradient. The full-vocabulary gradient equals the truncated gradient plus a residual weighted by the tail masses, and training acts only on the first term. Without the cross-entropy term, a top-k student's tail mass drifts away from the teacher's while a full-vocabulary control moves slightly toward it; with it, the gap shrinks about fourfold but persists. On seven open-weight teachers, the retained set determines the teacher's distribution only from $k=d+1$ ($d$ the hidden dimension): recovery is exact from there on all seven, and commonly cached sizes sit below it. In our off-policy runs the practical effect is real but smaller than the choice of teacher-student pair. Renormalization is a normalization, not a safeguard. The code is available at this https URL .

### [721] [An Attention-Guided Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Boundary Integral Computation in Physical Field Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15590)
*RongZe Gao,YuWei Wu,XinRan Ji,XingYue Ren*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In practical engineering and scientific computing, a real physical system can be reduced to a boundary value problem, and the adequate boundary information to determine the interior spatial distribution and evolutionary state of the physical field can be solved with linear equations, alternatively, the the real physical problem can be treated with boundary problems with in adequate information problems in field of machine learning. This paper proposes a deep learning framework for the recovery of missing boundary information using an attention-guided graph neural network (GNN) surrogate. The framework extracts features from the physical information on the discretized boundary into a latent space, and the missing boundary quantities are then predicted by the network. Thus, the nonlinear mapping from known boundary quantities to missing boundary quantities is learned using a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture, while an attention mechanism is incorporated to better model the correlations among different types of boundary information. Furthermore, the interior physical field can be reconstructed using the conventional boundary element method (BEM) integral formulation. The effectiveness of the GNN-BEM framework is evaluated using numerical examples of the two-dimensional Laplace and Poisson equations, which demonstrate good performance in reconstruction accuracy, local detail preservation, and model stability. The results show that GNN-BEM provides a feasible computational framework for boundary information recovery and fast interior physical field reconstruction for partial differential equations under complex boundary conditions.

### [722] [ProML: Progressive Multi-label Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15614)
*Yi Kou,Jieting Wang,Yuhua Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multi-label learning typically pursues model construction through the joint optimization of label fitting, correlation modeling, and structural regularization. While empirically effective, such a coupled paradigm imposes multiple learning objectives on a single predictive parameter matrix, forcing it to simultaneously fit observed labels and encode structural priors. This coupling may induce ill-conditioned optimization geometry, increase hyper-parameter sensitivity, and complicate capacity control. To address the these issues, this paper proposes a Progressive Multi-Label Learning (ProML) framework, which decouples direct label fitting from predictor learning via the introduction of an auxiliary predictive variable. This auxiliary variable admits a closed-form solution, yielding an equivalent profiled objective in which the supervised fitting term is scaled by a trade-off parameter. This result provides a unified view of ProML and conventional coupled learning, with the latter recovered as a limiting case. We theoretically analyze the optimization geometry of ProML and show that, under quadratic positive semidefinite structural regularization, ProML attenuates the dominant curvature of the fitting term, enlarges the stable learning rate range, and provides a controllable fidelity-regularization trade-off. Further, we instantiate the ProML for multi-label feature selection task by integrating global-local label priors and row-sparse regularization. Extensive experiments and controlled optimization analyses on 12 benchmark datasets empirically corroborate the theoretical analysis and demonstrate the robust and competitive performance of the proposed method.

### [723] [Adaptive Role Assignment and Controlled Feature Reconstruction for Federated Image Semantic Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15623)
*Yuxuan Chen,Jiao Bie,Hang Qi,Jingjin Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid federated semantic communication enables user equipment (UEs) to contribute model updates or semantic features under a shared training framework. However, heterogeneous role costs and the interaction between model aggregation and feature reconstruction (FR) remain key challenges in practical radio access network (RAN) deployment. To address these issues, we propose ARC-FedSC, a RAN-aware framework that coordinates UE role assignment and server-side controlled FR under a fixed communication budget. Within ARC-FedSC, RAN Aware Role-Bandit learns the historical contribution of UEs in different roles together with current uplink conditions, while Temporal Consistency Alignment (TCA) regulates FR according to recent model aggregation directions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 with time-varying RAN channels show that ARC-FedSC outperforms baselines across all five tested role configurations in the later training stage, with the best configurations achieving about 24.17 dB average PSNR over the last 20 rounds. Component level results further show that Role-Bandit maintains an average rolling UE coverage of 85.3%, compared with about 65.7% for baseline, while TCA reduces the probability of harmful FR events from 0.245 to 0.093, corresponding to a 62.0% reduction. Ablation and sensitivity studies further support the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed design.

### [724] [The Price of Precision: A Calibrated Cost Model for Mixed-Precision LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15629)
*Mukund Athmaram,Manoj Rao,Liang Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Choosing a mixed-precision configuration for large language model (LLM) serving trades speed against accuracy. Allocators that use average bit-width or a memory budget as a speed proxy can miss changes in the resource that limits execution. We argue that served speed can be limited by compute, weight loading, or key-value (KV) cache access, depending on the phase, batch size, and context length. A byte-based proxy does not capture all of these costs, so fewer bits do not always mean faster serving. To address this gap, we build a cost model that accounts for the binding resource and use it in two ways. First, as a predictor: given a configuration and operating point, it estimates serving latency using constants calibrated for the model, GPU, and serving stack. We evaluate its accuracy across three hardware classes. Second, as an allocator: we combine modeled time costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs and use a dynamic program to select a configuration under a latency or accuracy budget. We compare its configurations against byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.

### [725] [MERIT: Scaling KG Foundation Models with Relation Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15638)
*Cosimo Gregucci,Daniel Hernandez,Antonio Vergari,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Knowledge graph (KG) foundation models (KGFMs) predict links on unseen graphs zero-shot. KGFMs have been pioneered by ULTRA which builds a relation graph from co-occurrences that match motif templates, and passes messages over it to obtain relation representations. More recent KGFMs such as MOTIF and TRIX increase the size of this relation graph, and FLOCK replaces message-passing with probabilistic random-walk ensembles. However, larger relation graphs mean more messages, and more walks mean more sequences to encode, so they improve performance at higher training and inference cost. This cost hinders their use in more complex reasoning tasks, such as complex query answering. To reverse this trend, we design MERIT, the first KGFM with a transformer relation encoder: every relation name attends to every other, and the motifs enter as a soft prior rather than as edges. Over 56 benchmarks, MERIT matches the zero-shot MRR of SoTA KGFMs while being 6x faster than TRIX and over 100x faster than FLOCK at inference. Fine-tuned for complex query answering like UltraQuery, MERITQuery improves over it at matched cost.

### [726] [Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15640)
*Mukund Athmaram,Manoj Rao,Liang Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.

### [727] [Testing Central Structure for Complex Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15659)
*Qilong Wu,Yuxiao Li,Simeng Zhang,Xinying Liu,Yan Liu,Zengyou He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Centrality measures rank nodes even when the observed differences can be explained by ordinary structural variation. We therefore study a preceding question: whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all. We formulate this question as a network-level hypothesis testing issue using the adjacency spectral radius as the test statistic and estimate an empirical p-value from randomized networks generated under a specified null model. The framework is evaluated using G(N,M), Chung-Lu, and two implementations of the configuration model on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks. Controlled experiments further vary the number and connection weights of designated central nodes while holding network size and density fixed. The results show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the empirical p-value. They also demonstrate that rejection decisions depend substantially on the structural properties preserved by the null model: the detected network sets are not simply nested across models.

### [728] [Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15662)
*Chunyu Luo,Hongyu Zhao,Guangyi Ni,Yue Song,Lingkai Kong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

### [729] [DRanker: A Transformer-Based Multi-Task Ranking Model for the Disney+ Homepage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15696)
*Priya Nirmal Singh Khokher,Daniel Nemirovsky,Benjamin P. Whitesell,Ethan Sukrae Lee,Eric Wulf,Tom Chee-Duffy,Nicholas Flores*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We present DRanker (Disney+ Ranker), a transformer-based multitask ranking model serving personalized recommendations on the Disney+ homepage. We describe the encoder-only architecture over enriched engagement-history sequences paired with a lightweight causal debiasing mechanism, and the inference stack that enables transformer-based ranking at scale. Through iterative development, we systematically evaluated more complex alternatives and found that simpler designs consistently outperformed them on offline metrics, qualitative behavioral evaluation, and in production. Deployed globally, DRanker drives over 1% lift in our key engagement metric and 0.5% lift in daily active users across all experiences powered by the ranker. We share practical lessons on data engineering, debiasing, and architectural choices that shaped our ranking system at scale.

### [730] [Generalizable Model Editing Could Be More Than Direct Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15707)
*Xiaotian Ye,Chunyao Yang,Xiaohan Wang,Junkai Chen,Yongqi Duan,Mengqi Zhang,Shu Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A central desideratum in model editing is generalization to complex tasks, which prior work formalizes under a direct generalization paradigm: treating and evaluating LLM behavior as an input-output mapping and expecting a factual update to alter outputs on reasoning tasks. Yet despite substantial empirical effort, the field consensus remains that such generalization is highly challenging and elusive. However, when we deploy the latest models in an in-the-wild chatbot-user setting, we surprisingly find that even classical editing methods exhibit remarkably fluent generalization behavior. This motivates us to revisit the obstacles to generalization and the limitations of the prevailing paradigm. We find that direct generalization is fundamentally constrained both theoretically and practically: theoretically, it suffers from an identifiability issue; and practically, existing approaches attempting to circumvent this are further hindered by the ambiguity of their constructed biases and by vulnerability to being overridden by other factors such as optimization dynamics. We instead identify compositional generalization, empowered by the increasingly strong reasoning and composition abilities of modern LLMs, as a theoretically grounded and empirically validated alternative. We validate this phenomenon across multiple models and editing methods, showing that such generalization behavior is widespread. Overall, we argue that generalizable model editing could be more than direct generalization, and call for a paradigm shift toward more generalizable and practically deployable knowledge update techniques.

### [731] [Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15709)
*Haotian Li,Liran Dong,Kaicheng Xiao,Guoliang Xing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.

### [732] [Who Sets the Pace of Judge Hacking? Judge Capability versus the Policy-Judge Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15778)
*Haosen Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: When a policy is trained with GRPO against a frozen, reference-free LLM judge, the judge accepts more of its answers, but in a post-hoc analysis we detect no gain in held-out greedy accuracy: in all 12 (policy, judge) cells, the seed-mean gain never exceeded 0.04. A gold-reward control with the same recipe raised the 1.5B policy's greedy accuracy by +0.054 [0.013, 0.096], so for this policy the flat accuracy is specific to the judge reward; for the 0.5B policy, gold reward also gave no detectable gain. In the four rising cells we checked, the early rise in training-rollout accuracy is mostly sampling sharpening, as it is under gold reward. We then ask whether the policy-judge gap or the judge sets how far and how fast RL exploits the judge's false positives. We train 0.5B and 1.5B Qwen2.5 policies against four judges at least as large (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B, Llama-3.2-3B) and the 1.5B policy against one smaller judge (Qwen3-0.6B). The depth of judge hacking (the plateau) tracks the judge: it correlates with judge AUC (Spearman -0.69 [-0.94, -0.14] over 12 cells), and within a family the larger judge is fooled less deeply. For the pace (onset), two pre-specified pairs contradict the gap account (the larger-gap cell was fooled 3.5x sooner at the pre-specified threshold). With 12 cells we cannot formally separate judge AUC from the gap for either endpoint. The smaller judge was not fooled sooner than a judge as large as the policy, though it also differs in family and template. In a blind test on three held-out judges, a hash-locked step-0 predictor did not beat step-0 AUC, but three cells cannot separate them. At 7-8B, judges from three families plateaued at 0.37, 0.67 and 0.85.

### [733] [Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15781)
*Cameron Barker,Andreas Paraskeva,Jan N. van Rijn,Elliot J. Crowley,Henry Gouk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines. A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: this http URL .

### [734] [ML-CLAPPS: A Probabilistic Framework for Imbalanced Multilabel Learning under Class Prioritization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15816)
*Priel Hazan,Nir Almog,Noam Keidar,Yael Yaniv,Assaf Schuster*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Real-world datasets often exhibit severe class imbalance, degrading the performance of deep learning models, particularly on rare classes. While imbalance is well studied in binary and multiclass settings, it is substantially more challenging in multilabel problems due to complex label co-occurrence. In clinical applications such as ECG classification, this challenge is coupled with a second critical challenge: the need to prioritize high-risk conditions, regardless of their prevalence, to mitigate the high cost of false negatives. We introduce the Multilabel Class-Prioritized Probabilistic Sampler (ML-CLAPPS), a learnable sampler that optimizes a distribution over training instances to control the model's exposure to different classes. This approach addresses multilabel imbalance while enabling prioritization of significant conditions via a user-defined importance vector (IV). Empirical evaluation on a real-world multilabel ECG image dataset demonstrates that ML-CLAPPS achieves state-of-the-art performance. We show that it aligns class exposure with the specified IV, and that increasing a class's importance leads to corresponding improvements in its classification performance, enabling explicit prioritization of clinically critical conditions.

### [735] [Guarded Block Transfers for Polytope Distance: Linear Convergence with Explicit Constants and Gap-Certified Screening for SVM Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15829)
*Mayank Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hard-margin SVM training is the distance problem between two convex hulls, which the Triangle Algorithm (TA) solves with a certified duality gap. We propose \emph{guarded block transfers}: $k$ Mitchell--Demyanov--Malozemov (MDM) transfers per scan are aggregated into one exact line search, guarded by a comparison with the single best transfer at a cost independent of the number of points $n$, and replaced by an away step when the leading transfer is capacity-clipped. On the Minkowski-difference polytope, where the objective is $1$-strongly convex, we prove global linear convergence with explicit constants and no combinatorial swap-step bounds; the per-step contraction is $k$-independent and only the drop-count bound grows with $k$, so aggregation is provably safe while the saving in scans is measured, not proved. Since the TA certificate is the Frank--Wolfe gap divided by the current distance, gap-safe screening applies, and we bound the iteration after which it has removed every zero-weight point off the optimal faces by $O\!\left(\tfrac{k}{\rho}\log\tfrac{1}{\tau}\right)$ up to logarithmic factors in the geometry, $\rho$ the rate constant and $\tau$ the optimal-face margin. On five LIBSVM benchmarks, with fairer baselines than our submission, the solver matches the baselines to four or five digits wherever both converge, ties LIBSVM on sparse-support hard margins and beats our blended pairwise conditional gradients (BPCG). But our full-cache sequential minimal optimisation (SMO) code ties or beats it on kernel $L_2$ margins, LIBLINEAR's dual solver is up to $4.5\times$ faster on the separable $L_2$ margin, and our solver is one to three orders of magnitude slower than LIBLINEAR's Newton solver on dense-support $L_2$ margins and than LIBSVM on a nearly touching kernel hull. Its edge is the certificate, not speed.

### [736] [How Shared Representations Become Specialized: Formation, Maintenance, and Latent Susceptibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15830)
*Toru Takahashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: When several predictions use the same internal representation, information about some targets can remain easier to recover than information about others. We study how this specialization forms, persists, and changes in minimal artificial learners. With reconstruction errors weighted equally during learning, changing which target is observed precisely selects the favored target and redirects an already specialized learner. Removing current support can reduce a formed bias, whereas state-following update feedback can maintain it. We then compare learners formed through different observation and update conditions but matched on specified reconstruction measurements. Both change under the same brief opposing intervention, yet their responses differ. Resetting Adam largely removes the ten-update difference; exchanging its second moment reverses which route is more susceptible. New interventions show that equalizing the mean second-moment scaling reduces but does not remove the difference: its coordinate-wise pattern also matters. With fresh Adam or calibrated SGD, smaller route differences emerge later, whereas 500 common opposing updates bring the selected allocation endpoints close. A further control produces response differences with identical acquisition and equal mean loss weights but jointly different weight variability and realized sequence. Acquisition-selected formation also extends to a symmetric three-target setting. These interventions distinguish specialization's formation, present support, and time-dependent latent susceptibility.

### [737] [What Do Sparse Autoencoder Feature Discovery Scores Identify? From Activations to Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15850)
*Yifeng Guo,Yanran Li,Xiang Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are typically discovered from how their activations co-vary with behaviour, yet they are often used through interventions such as steering or ablation. We take intervention attribution, the first-order effect of a specified intervention on the model output, as our estimand. For a broad class of response functions, we show that observational feature-discovery evidence generally does not identify this attribution, and derive an exact gradient-based decomposition of the gap between linear-probe predictions and intervention attribution. Across four model-SAE pairs, median probe-to-attribution magnitude ratios range from tens to hundreds, while attributions closely track small-step steering. For single-latent ablations with nonzero effects, gradient predictions match the realized sign in 91-97% of cases, compared with 17-35% for probe-implied changes. Attribution-selected sets also produce larger absolute mean ablation effects on held-out prompts than sets selected by correlation, rank tests or probe coefficients. Together, these results establish intervention attribution as a principled, gradient-estimable target for selecting SAE features for intervention.

### [738] [GuidanceNFT: NFT-Based Reward Fine-Tuning of Guided Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15856)
*Jiayin Liu,Zeyu Michael Li,Bingshuo Qian,Xiang Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DiffusionNFT (NFT) fine-tunes diffusion models toward task-specific rewards, but optimizing these rewards does not guarantee fidelity to the full prompt. Although classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens prompt alignment, NFT is formulated as a CFG-free method, and applying CFG to the fine-tuned velocity field can reduce the optimized reward. This motivates optimizing rewards over the guided output distribution while seeking to retain its prompt alignment. However, applying standard NFT directly to guided samples can cause reward degradation or training collapse. We trace this failure to a mismatch between the reference velocity used in the NFT loss and the score of the guided sample distribution, which biases the improvement direction. We propose GuidanceNFT, which estimates the matching reference velocity through online flow matching on guided samples and uses it to correct both regression terms. With an exact reference, the corrected objective recovers NFT's intended update. In our experiments, the learned correction sustains reward improvement under both explicit and built-in guidance. On SD3.5-M, GuidanceNFT achieves higher optimized rewards than NFT with and without CFG across GenEval, text-rendering, and multi-reward objectives, together with better overall prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. Experiments on models with built-in guidance, including Model Guidance and ELF, further demonstrate improved ImageNet generation, a better perplexity-entropy tradeoff on OpenWebText, and higher accuracy on GSM8K.

### [739] [A Hybrid Gaussian Process-Extreme Gradient Boosting Machine Learning Framework for Robust Knockdown Factor Prediction and Reliability-Based Design of Thin Spherical Shell Caps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15862)
*Budhaditya De,Rohan Majumder,Devasmit Dutta,Aman Deep Gupta,Sudib Kumar Mishra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Elastic buckling remains a critical concern in the design of deep spherical shell caps, given that experiments reveal a significant reduction of critical loads from those predicted by linearized eigen-buckling analysis. This discrepancy has been attributed to initial geometric imperfections and is often reconciled through a dimensionless parameter, namely the knockdown factor (KDF). However, conventional KDFs (NASA SP-8007; Eurocode 3) are highly conservative, as they represent the lower bound of an extensive body of experimental data. This study aims to narrow the conservatism in the KDFs for spherical shell caps through machine learning (ML) regression models trained on experimental data on spherical shell buckling. A hybrid model is proposed by combining Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and its improved performance is demonstrated over conventional ML algorithms, i.e., the Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Support Vector Regressor (SVR), Random Forest Regressor (RFR), and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting (HGBoost). Each of these models uses six input features and a single output, i.e., the KDF. The most critical feature affecting the KDF is ascertained through a sensitivity analysis. The study concludes with a reliability-based design framework that relies on the predictive ML model to obtain safety-consistent, yet less conservative, KDFs.

This discrepancy has been attributed to initial geometric imperfections and is often reconciled through a dimensionless parameter, namely the knockdown factor (KDF). However, conventional KDFs (NASA SP-8007; Eurocode 3) are highly conservative, as they represent the lower bound of an extensive body of experimental data. This study aims to narrow the conservatism in the KDFs for spherical shell caps through machine learning (ML) regression models trained on experimental data on spherical shell buckling. A hybrid model is proposed by combining Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and its improved performance is demonstrated over conventional ML algorithms, i.e., the Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Support Vector Regressor (SVR), Random Forest Regressor (RFR), and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting (HGBoost). Each of these models uses six input features and a single output, i.e., the KDF. The most critical feature affecting the KDF is ascertained through a sensitivity analysis. The study concludes with a reliability-based design framework that relies on the predictive ML model to obtain safety-consistent, yet less conservative, KDFs.

</details>


### [740] [Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15916)
*Princewill Okoroafor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $\Omega((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

### [741] [Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15921)
*Xingke Yang,Sicong Li,Lingfeng Yao,Rui Chen,Changqing Luo,Xin Fu,Miao Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.

### [742] [Mesh-Free Convolution: Learned Spectral Attenuation and Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15931)
*Niloufar Zakariaei,Manav Manav,Eldad Haber*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) requires models that can represent spatial structure across grids and scales. This becomes especially important in time-dependent problems, where the learned operator is often used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict future states. In this setting, small spatial errors can be repeatedly propagated through the learned dynamics, leading to instability and drift, vitiating long-term solution fidelity. We propose Mesh-Free Convolutions (MFCs), filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time. This allows the same learned filters to be applied across resolutions. Rather than imposing a grid-dependent stencil or a fixed spectral cutoff, MFCs learn smooth scale-dependent filtering and include directional terms for transport-like behavior. Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics. These results suggest that continuous, mesh-free filtering is a useful inductive bias for PDE operator learning, especially in autoregressive prediction.

### [743] [Error-Based Bidirectional Predictive Coding Enables Deep, 4-Bit Predictive Coding Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15933)
*Garrett Kinman,Zeljko Zilic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.

### [744] [Instance-Adaptive Online Multiclass Multicalibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15954)
*Zhiming Huang,Jamie Morgenstern,Aaron Roth,Claire Jie Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We study online multiclass multicalibration over $T$ rounds, and give an algorithm with beyond-worst-case guarantees. With $n$ possible outcomes, forecasts lie in a simplex of dimension $d=n-1$. In the worst case, cumulative $\ell_1$ multicalibration error scales with $\widetilde\Theta(T^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$, which becomes untenable once $d$ exceeds a small constant. Our algorithm adapts to the geometry of the realized sequence: if the sequence of adversarially selected outcome means lies in an affine subspace of dimension $s$, it obtains error $\widetilde O(n^{1/(s+2)}T^{(s+1)/(s+2)})$ with high probability. The algorithm adapts to this structure without knowing the subspace or its dimension. For $T\ge n\ge2$, this rate is minimax optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. For a stochastic instance with a fixed conditional mean, the bound specializes to $\widetilde O(\sqrt{nT})$, giving a square-root dependence on the horizon.

### [745] [Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15965)
*Sewon Min*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. Nevertheless, even under a fixed time budget, a smaller batch with fewer GPUs can achieve lower validation loss than a larger batch with more GPUs, challenging the common practice of increasing data parallelism to maximize GPU utilization under a deadline. Together, our results identify underexplored factors in repeated-data training and provide concrete guidance on how training recipes and resource allocation should change from single-pass pretraining.

### [746] [Softmax-Free Attention in Spiking Transformers as the Zero-Temperature Limit of Two-Level Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15968)
*Roberto C. Sotero,Pouya Taghipour,Jose M. Sanchez-Bornot*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Spiking Transformers achieve energy efficiency by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded, binary attention. However, this removal breaks the thermodynamic framework used to analyze attention networks, as the normalized measure and partition function cease to exist. We restore this theoretical foundation by proving that softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems. This correspondence places spiking attention strictly in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. Consequently, the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses, replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor governed by action-potential generation. Furthermore, this ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the optimization difficulty caused by vanishing surrogate gradients. We validate this theory with forward-relaxation experiments, placing both standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.
