### [1300] [Vesta: Queueing-Aware LLM Scheduling for Real-World Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14686)
*Lancheng Zou,Bowen Li,Wei Mao,Wenbin Ye,Lecheng Li,Kai Liu,Chao Deng,Jianchen Zhu,Bei Yu*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Agentic applications generate multi-turn sequences of LLM requests, with each new turn extending the context accumulated from prior interactions and tool calls. Prefix caching reuses the KV cache of earlier turns and avoids redundant prefill, but routing every turn to its cache-affine instance can create severe local queues while capacity remains idle elsewhere. Remote KV cache access relaxes this tension, yet migrating execution adds transfer work and is harmful when the cluster is already congested. Thus, deciding where to execute a request requires reasoning jointly about cache locality, queueing, and the current operating point of the cluster. We present Vesta, a queueing-aware scheduler for distributed agentic LLM serving. Vesta assigns each session a stable holder for its authoritative KV cache while independently selecting an executor for every request. Grounded in classical queueing theory, its objective accounts for backlog, reusable prefixes, KV cache transfer, and the queueing externality of additional service demand; it migrates execution to recover idle capacity when beneficial and favors placements that add the least prefill and transfer work as congestion rises. Vesta also migrates reusable prefixes across length buckets to avoid cold starts. On real-world agentic workloads, Vesta improves throughput by 14.0\% and reduces mean TTFT by 57.8\% over the state-of-the-art scheduler in a PD-colocated deployment. In PD-disaggregated deployments, it reduces mean TTFT by up to 18.1\% and P99 TTFT by up to 29.0\% at matched throughput.

### [1301] [Accelerating MoE Training through Expert Placement and Replica Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14798)
*Zhiqiang Tan,Maoxin Wang,Wenxiang Lin,Sijie Wang,Qiang Wang,Shaohuai Shi,Bo Li*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Distributed training of sparsely activated mixture-of-experts (MoE) models is often bottlenecked by workload imbalance and all-to-all (A2A) communication induced by dynamic token routing. Existing token deduplication, expert placement, and replication techniques alleviate these bottlenecks but do not jointly capture their distinct load semantics. Under hierarchical token deduplication, communication counts each token once per destination group at each hierarchy level, whereas expert computation processes every token-expert assignment. With replication, both costs depend jointly on physical layout and token-to-copy mapping, making separate optimization suboptimal. We present PlaceMoE to address this coupling. First, we formulate the joint optimization of expert layout and source-aware token-to-copy mapping for E experts distributed across P devices, accounting for both hierarchical communication traffic and expert-compute load. Second, we develop a solver that combines co-selection-aware expert grouping, bounded dynamic programming for replica allocation, and alternating refinement of layout and mapping. Third, PlaceMoE overlaps replica-gradient synchronization with attention backward. We evaluate PlaceMoE on a 32-GPU cluster and a 64-NPU cluster using Qwen3-VL and DeepSeek-V3. Experimental results show that PlaceMoE achieves up to a 6.94x speedup in A2A communication and 1.74-2.33x speedups in end-to-end training over the state-of-the-art training framework VeOmni.

### [1302] [AgentWeave: Efficient Distributed Agent Serving via Flow Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14804)
*Kaibin Guo,Pengtu Li,Zicong Hong,Zhiyuan Fang,Wuhui Chen,Rachid Guerraoui,Anne-Marie Kermarrec*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Agent applications are evolving into workflows composed of large language model (LLM) calls and tool invocations, termed modules. Existing distributed agent systems typically adopt a disaggregated architecture, deploying different modules on separate devices. While this enables pipeline parallelism, imbalanced module latencies introduce severe pipeline bubbles that limit throughput. A natural alternative is an aggregated architecture that co-deploys all modules across all devices, eliminating bubbles by keeping every device continuously active. However, this introduces request blocking: short requests are forced to progress in lockstep with longer ones in the same batch, and newly arriving requests must wait until the entire ongoing batch completes the full workflow. To address this, we propose AgentWeave, an efficient distributed serving system for agent applications built on the aggregated architecture. Its core mechanism, flow decomposition, decomposes long agent requests into fine-grained execution units while preserving agent semantics, allowing short and newly arriving requests to proceed without being stalled by long-running ones. Complementing this, a flow-adaptive scheduler dynamically balances the throughput gains of decomposition against its scheduling overhead. Experiments across four representative agent applications demonstrate that AgentWeave improves throughput by 1.81x, reduces average latency by 2.45x, and reduces P90 latency by 2.04x over state-of-the-art baselines.

### [1303] [KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14810)
*Jun He,Deying Yu*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.

A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.

</details>


### [1304] [Weighted Beeping Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15068)
*Dariusz R. Kowalski,Miguel A. Mosteiro*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Beeping Networks (BN) have become an established model of wireless communication and computation. They assume, however, that the communication interference caused by beeping nodes is binary (OR channel), while both artificial and nature-driven networks are based on varied signal strength and receiving thresholds. This work naturally extends the classic beeping networks to weighted beeping networks (WBN), by modeling signal strengths by weights on graph edges and receiving a beep if the accumulative signal strengths of transmitting neighbors are above receiving threshold. Under this generalized model, we study the fundamental Local Broadcast (LB) problem. Since edges with low weights may not even accumulate to a received beep, we only require that messages are delivered along sufficiently heavy edges, with weights above some given threshold $\sigma$. We design an LB algorithm that completes its task in $O(I_\sigma \log n \cdot (\mathcal{M}+\log n))$ beeping rounds, whp, where $n$ is the number of nodes, $I_\sigma$ is the maximum local interference on heavy edges, and $\mathcal{M}$ is the maximum length of messages sent locally. This result is nearly optimal, as, with probability $1$, $\Omega(I_\sigma)$ beeping rounds are necessary to solve LB. Finally, we show that any algorithm designed for the classic beeping networks and terminating in polynomial number of beeping rounds, can be emulated on any WBN with a logarithmic overhead, that is, it returns the same output as working on the classic beeping network isomorphic to the sub-graph of heavy edges.

### [1305] [DualColl: Throughput-Optimal Bandwidth-Bound Collective Communications via Fractional Tree Packing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15704)
*Namir Ballan,Reuven Cohen*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Large-scale distributed training increasingly makes collective communication bandwidth-bound. In modern GPU clusters, communication libraries such as NCCL implement collectives including AllReduce over heterogeneous interconnects such as NVLink, InfiniBand, and Ethernet, making efficient use of available network bandwidth a central systems challenge. ForestColl showed that collective communication on such fabrics can be formulated using fractional tree packing; its scalable polynomial-time construction is developed for AllGather, with AllReduce obtained by composing AllGather and ReduceScatter. We present DualColl, which targets bandwidth-bound AllReduce directly. Under the tree-based AllReduce model, DualColl applies a Garg--Könemann-style multiplicative-weights algorithm and, for any $0<\epsilon<1$, computes a feasible schedule whose throughput is at least $(1-\epsilon)^2$ of the optimal AllReduce throughput. Its key component is an exact minimum-cost collective-tree oracle that projects physical-link dual prices onto a logical graph of participating ranks, reducing each iteration to shortest-path computations followed by a minimum spanning tree. We further extend the framework to local equal-next-hop packet-sprayed routing and to networks without explicit per-tree bandwidth control. For the latter, we introduce a tree-coupled max-min bandwidth-sharing model and show that tree duplication approximates an explicit fractional allocation with a provable accuracy-complexity tradeoff. Finally, we extend the fractional-packing framework to additional collective operations and multiple concurrent collective groups.

### [1306] [Native Dual Pools or Shared Paging? Memory Organization for Concurrent Hybrid LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15755)
*Dongwook Kang*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Hybrid attention-SSM serving combines growing attention KV with fixed-size recurrent and convolution state whose allocation units, reuse boundaries, and lifetimes differ. We implement four memory organizations in a modified vLLM runtime: a coarse shared-page baseline (S0), checkpoint-internal recurrent paging (S1), paging with convolution-slot packing (S2), and native dual pools (D0). Nine evaluation questions cover storage costs and serving behavior. The cumulative S0-S1-S2 refinement improves completed-output throughput and tail completion time at the main operating point. D0-S2 performance varies with memory budget, offered load, and admission headroom. Shared-prefix workloads yield larger stepwise gains; gains also persist in a no-sharing control with equal recorded input-work totals. State traces identify recurrent-checkpoint availability as the limit on joint reuse in the tested S2 runs. Extending producer-side checkpoint lifetime increases reusable depth at a fixed page budget. A fresh-seed SHARE/ISOLATE comparison estimates a positive retention interaction, with a primary confidence interval that includes zero. Retained-state continuation correctness remains unresolved. These findings motivate evaluating physical state representation together with request admission and checkpoint lifetime when designing memory management for concurrent hybrid-model serving.

### [1307] [Multi-GPU Communication Schemes for Iterative Solvers: When CPUs are Not in Charge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15878)
*Ismayil Ismayilov,Javid Baydamirli,Doğan Sağbili,Mohamed Wahib,Didem Unat*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This paper proposes a fully autonomous execution model for multi-GPU applications that completely excludes the involvement of the CPU beyond the initial kernel launch. In a typical multi-GPU application, the host serves as the orchestrator of execution by directly launching kernels, issuing communication calls, and acting as a synchronizer for devices. We argue that this orchestration, or control flow path, causes undue overhead and can be delegated entirely to devices to improve performance in applications that require communication among peers. For the proposed CPU-free execution model, we leverage existing techniques such as persistent kernels, thread block specialization, device-side barriers, and device-initiated communication routines to write fully autonomous multi-GPU code and achieve significantly reduced communication overheads. We demonstrate our proposed model on two broadly used iterative solvers, 2D/3D Jacobi stencil and Conjugate Gradient(CG). Compared to the CPU-controlled baselines, the CPU-free model can improve 3D stencil communication latency by 58.8% and provide a 1.63x speedup for CG on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The project code is available at this https URL .

### [1308] [Learning based Scalable Multi-Objective Scheduling of Workflows across UD-IaaS-FaaS Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15886)
*G Vasantha Reddy,Ram Bansal,Krashna,Suvarthi Sarkar,Aryabartta Sahu*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Workflow scheduling in user device-centric edge-cloud computing has emerged as a challenging problem due to the need to jointly optimize execution performance, energy consumption, and monetary cost. Modern workflows consist of heterogeneous tasks, where compute-intensive components are well-suited for Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) resources, while fine-grained, event-driven tasks are more efficiently executed using the Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) model. We formulate this scheduling problem for application workflows over a hybrid User Device (UD)-IaaS-FaaS computing continuum as a multi-objective Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP). The formulation models the workflow execution mechanism by incorporating cumulative capacity constraints for IaaS resources and elastic resource provisioning for FaaS. To overcome the intractability of MILP, we propose a learning-based framework that combines graph neural networks, surrogate performance modeling, and a multi-sample REINFORCE approach. The proposed approach is workflow-aware, leveraging task pairing to improve data locality and structured task placement decisions. Agent training is organized into three stages: small-scale learning of UD-IaaS trade-offs, intermediate locality aware co-location, and large-scale handling of parallelism and aggregation bottlenecks in workflows. The proposed framework is validated through real-world experiments using the Pegasus Montage workflow on a custom UD-IaaS-FaaS testbed comprising a user device, multiple IaaS nodes, and serverless FaaS instances. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the improved trade-offs across makespan, energy consumption, and cost. Compared with the genetic algorithm and greedy scheduling approaches, the proposed approach reduces makespan by 10-17.5%, energy consumption by 3-9%, and cost by 4-10%, while remaining within 3.5-5.6% of the MILP optimum.

### [1309] [Lightweight Scheduling Policies for Continuously Batched LLLM Serving Across GPU Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15899)
*Ashman Mehra,Akshan Agarwal,Aryeh Carmi*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Large language model serving is increasingly limited not only by model size and GPU speed, but also by scheduling during autoregressive decoding, where continuous batching interleaves requests at token granularity as sequences arrive and finish. We study whether lightweight scheduling policies can improve latency-throughput tradeoffs without changing model architectures, kernels, or deploying learned schedulers. We implement a Python/PyTorch continuous-batching testbench with real Hugging Face execution and evaluate eight policies across 1,152 GPU-model-scheduler-workload runs using ShareGPT-derived traffic, six Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral models, and Modal L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs. Scheduler choice changes throughput, TTFT, completion latency, and tail behavior under fixed model, GPU, workload, batch size, and prefill budget. Aging shortest-prompt-first is the strongest practical baseline in many L40S and mixed-workload settings, while oracle remaining-length scheduling shows that job-size knowledge alone is insufficient because batching and hardware effects also shape performance. The custom dataset has been uploaded to Hugging Face.

### [1310] [Substep Linearizability: Relaxing Atomicity While Preserving Sequential Specification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16099)
*Finn Hackett,Evan Wrench,Ivan Beschastnikh,Yuanhao Wei*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Linearizability is a standard correctness condition for concurrent this http URL takes a correct by construction sequential specification of a concurrent data structure, and produces a composable specification under atomic interleavings of operations. However, some operations like atomic exchangers are not specifiable atomically, making it difficult to reason compositionally about their specifications. Interval linearizability is the state of the art in relaxing linearizability's constraints. Formally it is a powerful framework, but it requires an interval-sequential specification of the target data structure, which we show is challenging to correctly generate or understand, even for simple operations on a single concurrent register. We propose substep linearizability, which we show is equivalent to interval linearizability using X-CCorrectness, a relaxed concurrency framework we created to compare existing linearizability semantics. We show that substep linearizability's sequential specifications are suitable for previously infeasible specification tasks, while being comparable in complexity to linearizability's sequential specifications. For evaluation, we model an atomic exchanger, a popular non-linearizable queue structure, and snapshot isolation between database transactions.

### [1311] [A New Lens on Multi-GPU Communication: API-Level Memory Models for Portable Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16190)
*Johnathan Alsop,Bradford Beckmann,Brandon Potter,Jiakun Yan,Aurelien Bouteiller,Omri Mor,Tony Tye,Sameer Sahasrabuddhe*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: As network communication increasingly becomes a performance bottleneck for ML and HPC workloads, it is more important than ever to optimize multi-GPU data transfers. Recently, low-level device APIs have emerged that allow programmers to perform fine-grain optimizations via one-sided put/get operations triggered directly from the device. However, the communication libraries providing these device APIs (e.g., rocSHMEM, MSCCL++, and NCCL/RCCL GIN) currently lack a rigorous memory model defining how their primitives interact with the underlying memory systems. Without this, emerging HPC and ML workloads aggressively optimizing network communication via device APIs can be brittle, error-prone, and face compatibility and inter-operability challenges. This paper proposes the use of API-level memory models for these emerging device communication APIs. An API-level memory model defines the memory semantics of communication API calls in a way that abstracts lower-level details from the API user and simplifies development. This work defines one such model for device-side communication (implemented in AMD's recently open sourced rocSHMEM library) and demonstrates how formal relaxations to such a model can enable low-level LLM performance optimizations while retaining a well-defined standardized interface. Specifically, we describe how updating the SHMEM API implemented by rocSHMEM can properly support cache bypassing for network data, improving performance of a collective communication workload by up to 2.48x, a fused compute+communication workload by up to 1.77x, and a state-of-the-art expert-parallel communication workload by up to 1.18x.

### [1312] [HeteroVDiff: Pipelining Video Diffusion across Mobile NPU and GPU with Shared Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16244)
*Zheyu Shen,Ziyao Wang,Yexiao He,Guoheng Sun,Yuning Zhang,Yiting Wang,Wanghao Ye,Ang Li*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Video generation is moving from the cloud to phones for privacy and offline use, and applications often ask for several clips at a time, so on-device video generation is a throughput problem before it is a latency problem. Contemporary mobile SoCs carry both a GPU and a neural processing unit (NPU) on shared DRAM, yet existing on-device video diffusion systems run the denoiser on one engine while the other sits idle or only decodes the finished latent afterwards. Heterogeneous designs built for mobile LLMs do not carry over: they synchronise the two engines at every operator and partition weight tensors between them instead of sharing one stored copy. We first measure the platform limits that decide what can run on this class of SoC: how large one buffer may be, whether both runtimes can map the same buffer, and how much activation memory the NPU toolchain lets one graph hold. Guided by these measurements, we store the base weights once in INT8 in the layout the NPU reads natively; the GPU consumes the same bytes directly as integer dot-product operands, so neither runtime rearranges weights on load. We then flatten the denoising trajectory into its full sequence of block executions and cut it once at a block boundary, so the GPU runs the prefix and the NPU the suffix. The cut is placed from measured rather than modelled rates, including the decoder that only the NPU can run, and taken while both engines run together because each engine's speed changes when the other is active. We present HeteroVDiff, which serves a multi-expert video diffusion model across the NPU and GPU with 48% less weight memory than giving each engine its own copy. Generating videos back to back on a Galaxy S25 with decoding inside the pipeline, HeteroVDiff sustains 1.35x the stream throughput of NPU-only execution, and on VBench-2.0 it matches FP32 in the total score over all 18 dimensions.

### [1313] [From Nominal Capacity to Deliverable Compute: Design, Calibration and Validation of the D-PIN SCU Dynamic Metering System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16374)
*Cheng Li,Jiexiong Liu,Shikun Wang,Feiyu Ren*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Nominal chip specifications do not capture the compute deliverable by heterogeneous distributed networks under communication, runtime and verification constraints. We formalize D-PIN Standardized Compute Units (D-PIN SCU) as a dynamic metering system for deliverable compute. The system combines five-dimensional resource normalization with topology-aware and runtime-corrected metering. A cluster-scale Roofline model yields a closed-form communication ridge, while runtime factors describe thermal, fault and load effects. We show that runtime deviations cannot be identified from nominal specifications alone. Uniform re-anchoring preserves relative metering results, and a simplex-constrained calibration algorithm estimates resource weights. The framework couples Proof-of-Physical-Work verification to a no-arbitrage condition for over-claiming and electricity-aware pricing. An end-to-end recomputation on the Zhangjiang Science Gate production node covers ten heterogeneous 8-GPU servers totaling 59.5 D-PIN SCU. Billed throughput of approximately 33,000 D-PIN SCU-hours is consistent with the physical upper bound at 78% utilization over 720 hours. Derived metrics are 3.02 kW per D-PIN SCU at the supply-and-distribution design boundary and 0.26 D-PIN SCU-hours per delivered kWh. Empirically calibrated chip values differ materially from datasheet projections; the published calibration is not independently reproducible from vendor specifications. Validation is limited to one production node, and the originality claim concerns the integrated system rather than the SCU terminology or individual components. The framework provides a basis for scheduling, verification and pricing of deliverable compute in distributed heterogeneous networks.

An end-to-end recomputation on the Zhangjiang Science Gate production node covers ten heterogeneous 8-GPU servers totaling 59.5 D-PIN SCU. Billed throughput of approximately 33,000 D-PIN SCU-hours is consistent with the physical upper bound at 78% utilization over 720 hours. Derived metrics are 3.02 kW per D-PIN SCU at the supply-and-distribution design boundary and 0.26 D-PIN SCU-hours per delivered kWh. Empirically calibrated chip values differ materially from datasheet projections; the published calibration is not independently reproducible from vendor specifications. Validation is limited to one production node, and the originality claim concerns the integrated system rather than the SCU terminology or individual components. The framework provides a basis for scheduling, verification and pricing of deliverable compute in distributed heterogeneous networks.

</details>


### [1314] [SP-Allreduce: Symmetric Tree Schedules for Tori and Beyond](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16387)
*Mikhail Cherniavskii,Andrey Kupavskii,Georgy Mironov,Stanislav Moiseev*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Allreduce is a fundamental communication primitive in large-scale distributed training, and torus interconnects remain widely deployed in high-performance systems. We introduce SP-allreduce, a new allreduce algorithm for $d$-dimensional tori that exploits the symmetry of the topology and routes only along shortest paths. We call an allreduce algorithm \emph{fully bandwidth-optimal} if it incurs no bandwidth overhead, no multihop-induced traffic inflation, and achieves perfect per-round load balance. SP-allreduce is based on a family of carefully symmetrized shortest-path trees that guarantees full bandwidth optimality in the $\alpha$--$\beta$ model. We prove that it uses the minimum possible number of rounds among all fully bandwidth-optimal allreduce algorithms on $d$-dimensional tori, and therefore the minimum running time in this class. In this sense, SP-allreduce refines Bucket allreduce: it preserves Bucket's key strengths while reducing the number of rounds by a factor of two. We further extend our approach to broader symmetric topologies and to communication trees of prescribed depths. Experimentally, the resulting algorithms improve over the best compared state-of-the-art algorithms for tori by up to $1.19\times$ on square tori and $1.65\times$ on rectangular tori across the tested configurations. On HyperX and spine-leaf networks, we demonstrate gains of up to $14.82\times$ and $1.72\times$, respectively, over the best evaluated baselines.

### [1315] [Space AI Infrastructure: Where the Edge Meets the Orbital Cloud](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16395)
*Zhanwei Wang,Jianhao Huang,Min Sheng,Kaibin Huang*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) and space technologies is extending spaceborne intelligence beyond onboard payloads toward a global infrastructure, here termed Space AI infrastructure (SpaceAI-Infra). Its promise rests on two distinctive advantages of space systems: abundant solar energy in orbit and the global reach of satellite constellations. Realizing this promise hinges on a fundamental systems question: How should satellite constellations be designed and orchestrated to deliver data-center-scale AI services competitive with their terrestrial counterparts? This article develops a roadmap-oriented answer. We first chart the evolution of SpaceAI-Infra through three progressive stages: onboard AI, Space Edge AI, and Space Cloud AI. By revisiting the space-constrained fundamentals for end-to-end token services, we derive enabling design principles and translate them into an integrated space edge--cloud architecture. The communication-centric space edge comprises free-flying LEO constellations that provide user-proximate computing and form the access and backhaul fabric for cloud AI services. Complementing the edge, the computing-centric space cloud comprises formation-flying satellite constellations organized as space data centers in dawn--dusk sun-synchronous orbits. A case study demonstrates that the proposed architecture can support data-center-scale foundation-model inference for millions of concurrent users worldwide.

### [1316] [Federated Coreset Subsampling for Distributed Memory Banks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16425)
*Jason Witzemann,Daniel Pröll,Sebastian Hegenbart*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: In real-world scenarios, industrial processes can span multiple factories and goods are often produced at multiple sites, leading to a shared yet non-identical distribution of data across locations. To address this, we propose two federated approaches for i) combining existing coresets (Double Subsampling) and ii) creating new coresets (Federated Subsampling) in a distributed anomaly detection setting. In particular, we adapt the memory bank based PatchCore algorithm to a federated setting, resulting in increased cold-start performance, resilience to domain- and sensor-shift, and resilience to unreliable actor participation, a common problem in classical, network based federated learning strategies.

### [1317] [Revisiting Fast Tendermint: An Agreement Violation and Two Repairs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16442)
*Alejandro Ranchal-Pedrosa*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Fast Tendermint reduces Tendermint's good-case latency to two communication steps for n>=5f+1. We show that its published round-change rule violates Agreement: one Byzantine process suffices for every f>=1, and for f>=2 two Byzantine processes suffice without double signing. The failure occurs when a process advances past a round without recording the value that may have been decided there. The Quint specification that accompanies the protocol does not allow this kind of round skipping and is not affected; the violation lies in the published pseudocode. We present two repairs. Walk requires a process to leave each round on a quorum of that round's precommits and to precommit before leaving. It keeps the recorded valid state and removes the wait after a precommit quorum. Justify carries the evidence needed to accept a proposal in the proposal itself, removing both the recorded valid state and the proposer's synchronization wait. Both satisfy Agreement and Validity under asynchrony and Termination under the partially synchronous gossip model of Tendermint and Fast Tendermint. Both retain proposal timeouts. The main text presents the executions that violate Agreement and explains the two repairs. The appendices provide proofs, a brief comparison with other round-change designs, and an extension to chains.

### [1318] [Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16592)
*Chiheng Lou,Xiangwei Deng,Bangjun Xiao,Xiaodong Ji,Yikai Zhao,Xin Jin,Hailin Zhang*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.

### [1319] [StageBreaker: Shifting Video RL Post-Training Scheduling from Stages down to Data Dependencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16691)
*Li Peng,Chenghuan Huang,Ziyang Ma,Jing Lyu,Xiang Chen,Jie Zhang*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has emerged as the key paradigm for improving autoregressive video models. Emerging vision-language reward models further strengthen post-training with accurate rewards, but their long chain-of-thought inference substantially raises the associated costs, while the pursuit of long videos prolongs policy training. Despite these rising costs, existing video RL systems still adopt coarse-grained stage-centric execution, which stalls policy training until all reward evaluation finishes, replays every trajectory twice due to a further barrier within policy training, and induces load imbalance across GPUs. To address the challenges, we propose StageBreaker, a fine-grained data-dependency-driven scheduling framework, which schedules the true dataflow of an RL step rather than its stages. Specifically, StageBreaker overlaps policy training with reward evaluation by exploiting reward-separable policy training, and merges the two trajectory replays into one by leveraging loss-independent back-propagation. It further balances GPU load by scheduling computation at the finer granularity. Our evaluation results show that StageBreaker achieves a speedup of up to 1.41$\times$ over stage-centric execution.

### [1320] [Improved Massively Parallel Shortest Path Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16787)
*Yi-Jun Chang,Shaun Quek*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: We present new algorithms for approximate shortest path computation in weighted undirected graphs within the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Specifically, we construct an $a$-approximate Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP) oracle: Given a query consisting of a source vertex $u \in V$, the oracle returns $a$-approximate distances $\delta(u,v)$ for all $v \in V$. Fix an $n$-vertex weighted undirected graph. We consider two regimes of the MPC model: the near-linear regime, where each machine has $\tilde{\Theta}(n)$ memory, and the heterogeneous regime, where all machines have $\Theta(n^\gamma)$ memory for some constant $\gamma\in (0,1]$, except for a single machine with $\tilde{\Theta}(n)$ memory. We develop randomised algorithms that construct $O(1)$-approximate SSSP oracles in $O(\log\log n)$ rounds in the near-linear regime and in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds in the heterogeneous regime. These oracles answer distance queries in $O(1)$ rounds. Our results improve upon the recent work of Dory and Matar (SPAA 2024) which, for the same total memory, requires $\left(\log\log n\right)^{2+O(1/\gamma)}$ rounds and applies only to unweighted graphs in the heterogeneous setting. We say that $\tilde N_k(u)$ is the approximate $k$-nearest neighbourhood of a vertex $u$ if there exists an approximate distance estimate $\delta$ such that $\tilde N_k(u)$ consists of the $k$ vertices closest to $u$ according to $\delta$, breaking ties by vertex ID. The main technical ingredient is a new method for efficiently computing approximate $n^{O(\gamma)}$-nearest neighbourhoods in the heterogeneous MPC model in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds.

### [1321] [Beyond the Boundary: Optimal Grid Dispersion by Spread, Reverse, and Collect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16935)
*Manish Kumar,Anisur Rahaman Molla,Debasish Pattanayak,Subhajit Pramanick*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: \emph{Dispersion} requires a set of mobile agents to occupy distinct nodes of a graph such that each node contains at most one agent. We study deterministic dispersion of $k\le n$ agents on an $n$-node oriented square grid, where each node has globally consistent North, East, South, and West port labels, from arbitrary initial configurations. This includes both \emph{rooted} configurations, where all agents are co-located initially, and \emph{general} configurations, where agents are initially distributed arbitrarily across the nodes. On oriented square grids, Kshemkalyani, Molla, and Sharma~\cite{KMS20} gave an $O(\min(k,\Side))$-round algorithm in the local-communication model, where only agents on the same node can exchange information, and an $O(\sqrt{k})$-round algorithm in the global-communication model, where any two agents can communicate regardless of position, both using $O(\log k)$ bits per agent. The bound in the local communication model is optimal when $k=\Theta(n)$, but it remains open whether local communication alone can match the $\Omega(\sqrt{k})$ time lower bound when $k=o(n)$. We solve this by presenting \textsc{Spread--Reverse--Collect} (SRC), a deterministic algorithm that disperses any $k\le n$ agents in $O(\sqrt{k})$ synchronous rounds using $O(\log k)$ bits of persistent memory per agent, matching both time and memory lower bounds. SRC is based on a geometric primitive, a \sharpS-shaped parallel sweep, together with a simple priority rule. Unlike earlier grid algorithms that gather agents at the boundary and spread out from there, each SRC sweep starts from the agents' current position, and when it reaches the boundary the group simply reflects its sweep back inside and continues. SRC therefore needs no knowledge of the grid size and runs unchanged on an infinite oriented grid.

### [1322] [MODAIC: Coordinated Asynchrony for Decentralized Multimodal Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16987)
*Yanhang Shi,Xiaoyu Wang,Houwei Cao,Jian Li,Yong Liu*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Multimodal decentralized learning enables collaboration across heterogeneous edge devices without sharing raw data, but differing modality sets create coupled computation and communication bottlenecks. Multimodal agents support cross-modal alignment while training more model components and sharing bandwidth across multiple modality overlays. Under bandwidth limits, these agents can become hot spots: transfers miss aggregation windows, and their updates become stale or underrepresented, degrading worst-agent accuracy. Asynchrony removes global blocking but does not by itself coordinate local cross-modal interaction with timely peer-update exchange. We present MODAIC (Modality-Decoupled Asynchrony with Interleaved Coordination), a wait-free system that coordinates local modality progress, peer-to-peer update delivery, and aggregation under heterogeneous compute and bandwidth. Hierarchical asynchrony lets modalities progress independently while enforcing reciprocal feature exchange; load-aware update fetching overlaps training with communication, limits concurrent serving load, and reuses late arrivals; and consensus-aware peer selection uses lightweight metadata to account for update availability, peer participation, and loss similarity without active probing. We implement MODAIC as a containerized multi-agent framework and evaluate it on local and cross-region cloud testbeds. Across AVE and KU-HAR, MODAIC improves average accuracy and multimodal worst-agent performance. On AVE at 200 Mbps per agent, it improves multimodal worst-agent accuracy by 11.0 percentage points at 1000 seconds over the strongest baseline. On the cloud testbed, it reduces time-to-accuracy by up to 30%. Ablations show that simpler load-balancing and delayed-aggregation variants leave a worst-agent accuracy gap, and stress tests show tolerance to WAN variability and partial tracker unavailability.

### [1323] [FlashT2S: GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators for Heterogeneous Neuromorphic LLM Backends](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17035)
*Rongyuan Guo,Haotian Wang,Yufeng Zhang,Wangdong Yang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Artificial intelligence faces two growing challenges: computational bottlenecks and energy inefficiency inherent to the von Neumann architecture. Neuromorphic computing offers a promising alternative, yet its immature ecosystem still relies on conventional systems for data supply, requiring efficient conversion between tensor and spike dataflow. We observe a clear mismatch, where data conversion is slow while downstream computation is fast. As data size grows quadratically with large language models, this mismatch becomes a major bottleneck. In this work, we examine the data-conversion components that appear on the critical path of training and inference in neuromorphic LLMs. The work presents FlashT2S (Flash Tensor-to-Spike): GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators, which applies architecture-aware and data-centric optimizations to reduce conversion latency. Experimental results show that FlashT2S delivers an average speedup of 850.78x over the native operators across individual operators and 802.83x in realistic workloads. Additionally, compared with GPU kernels automatically generated by this http URL , our kernels achieve 5-11x speedups. Notably, it achieves near-optimal absolute performance: large-scale conversions are reduced to tens of microseconds (10-99 us), while small-scale conversions reach single-digit microsecond levels (less than 10 us). Furthermore, its standardized output enables seamless integration across heterogeneous backends, including diverse neuromorphic hardware.

Notably, it achieves near-optimal absolute performance: large-scale conversions are reduced to tens of microseconds (10-99 us), while small-scale conversions reach single-digit microsecond levels (less than 10 us). Furthermore, its standardized output enables seamless integration across heterogeneous backends, including diverse neuromorphic hardware.

</details>


### [1324] [GPU Goldmines: Tunable WebGPU Kernels for Edge LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17321)
*Rithik Sharma,Reese Levine,Zheyuan Chen,Ananthajit Srikanth,Yanwen Xu,Tyler Sorensen*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: As demand for LLM inference grows and consumer GPUs grow more capable, edge deployment is becoming increasingly attractive. WebGPU is compelling in this setting because it offers cross-platform portability and browser accessibility. However, these same strengths also make high performance difficult to achieve, as an implementation that performs well in one context may not perform well in another. To address this, we present GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and tuning WebGPU kernels. We instantiate GPU Goldmines with kernels for key LLM building blocks: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention. We characterize performance across diverse devices, shapes, and browsers, and use the resulting database to accelerate subsequent autotuning and configuration selection. On shapes drawn from Llama and Qwen models, our matrix multiplication kernels outperform ONNX Runtime and this http URL WebGPU kernels by 7.0x and 1.41x geometric mean, respectively, and deliver end-to-end improvements of 1.48x in the prefill stage of this http URL for chat workloads.

### [1325] [ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17528)
*Leo Fan,Hongyang Wang,Wenbo Chen,Jingguo Liu,Xian Li,Xuan Wang,Ruochen Wen,Yiming Yan,Hao Wu,Zheshen Wang,Benoit Dumoulin*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at this https URL .

### [1326] [FLAI Protocol: Decentralized Federated Learning with On-Chain Rewards and sPEG-Based Contribution Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17546)
*Eli Yune,Mahesh Balan*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without data centralization but struggles with incentive alignment, accountability, and robustness under heterogeneous non-IID data. Existing decentralized FL (DeFL) systems leverage blockchains for coordination yet face high on-chain overhead, unverifiable self-reports, and weak fairness guarantees. We present the FLAI Protocol, a trusted execution environment (TEE)-backed DeFL framework that integrates enclave-validated aggregation, sparse Peer Evaluation Graph (sPEG) scoring, and on-chain settlement. sPEG incorporates peer-based quality, class coverage, promptness, effort, and reputation into composite contribution scores. The protocol formalizes contribution evaluation and tokenized incentive distribution, ensuring verifiable fairness and resilience against free-riding and collusion. We evaluate FLAI on image, text, and healthcare datasets and demonstrate parity with FedAvg in utility while improving fairness and accountability. A case study in consumer eHealth (aggregating wearable and electronic health record data for real-world evidence generation) illustrates the protocol's applicability to privacy-critical domains where equitable rewards, auditability, and data sovereignty are essential.

### [1327] [Capacity over TFLOPS: Memory-Centric Deployment of Large Clinical Language Models on Consumer CPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17551)
*Eli Yune,Umer Majeed,Mahesh Balan*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The dominant barrier to running large clinical language models at the point of care is not arithmetic throughput but graphics memory: consumer GPUs cap at 4-16 GB, while the working set of a 27-billion-parameter model in 4-bit precision is 17-25 GB. We argue that the edge node should be treated as capacity-enabled (system RAM) rather than compute-limited (GPU VRAM), and we test this on commodity hardware. Using an INT4 build of a 27B open model as an architecture-faithful stand-in for a 27B medical model, we measure the memory footprint, inference latency, energy, and federated communication cost of a fully CPU-based pipeline driven by synthetic Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) prompts. On two independent consumer machines (a desktop-class machine with 67 GB of RAM and a 6 GB GPU, and a mobile workstation with 34 GB of RAM and a 4 GB GPU) the model loads entirely into system RAM (37% and 60% utilization, respectively) while both GPUs are out-of-memory before the first step. Inference runs at overnight-batch speed (0.6-2.4 tokens/s for the 27B model), and federated fine-tuning would transmit only a 22.6 MB low-rank adapter, a 99.96% reduction over full weights. The capacity result is independent of CPU microarchitecture, RAM size, operating system, and GPU. We further identify an open, CPU- and NPU-optimized inference runtime as the natural production path for this approach, indicating a privacy-preserving and broadly deployable route for on-premises clinical AI. All data is synthetic; this is a research artifact and not a medical device.

### [1328] [A Minimum Exact Disjunctive Basis for Two-Robot Solvability Profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17677)
*Tsukasa Ninomiya,Shota Naito,Naoki Kitamura,Yuichi Sudo,Koichi Wada*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: We completely characterize the solvability profiles of tasks for two autonomous mobile robots in the plane under variable disorientation, chirality, and rigid movements. The four standard capability models and the schedulers considered here have a known quotient order Q of thirteen computational classes. A task's solvability profile is the set of classes in which it is solvable, and is necessarily an upset of Q. We prove that every upset is realizable and construct a minimum exact disjunctive basis of thirteen concrete tasks. The basis contains one task for each principal upset. For every antichain of Q, the disjunction of the corresponding tasks has profile exactly equal to the union of their profiles. This exactness is not implied by the individual profiles: an algorithm may satisfy different disjuncts in different executions. We establish it by constructing, for every algorithm in each maximal class outside the target union, a single admissible fair execution violating all selected predicates simultaneously. Consequently, the realizable profiles form the entire finite distributive lattice Up(Q): there are exactly 54 profiles, counted by the antichain polynomial 1 + 13z + 24z^2 + 16z^3, and each has a canonical disjunctive representation using at most three principal tasks. We also identify six tasks whose solvability signatures recover every inclusion and incomparability in Q, and prove that six is minimum even among arbitrary separating tasks. Their profiles are precisely the principal upsets generated by the join-irreducible elements of Q. In contrast, any task family generating every profile by exact disjunctions must contain all thirteen principal profiles. Thus our exact disjunctive basis has minimum size and is unique at the profile level.

### [1329] [Quota-Based Aging for Prediction-Guided Scheduling in LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17795)
*Hanzhi Zhang,Anxuan Che,Hang Qi,Qiyue Li,Jingjin Wu*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Large language model (LLM) serving systems use token-level continuous batching to improve resource utilization, but heterogeneous response lengths complicate request scheduling. Prediction-guided short-first scheduling reduces average latency but can severely delay long requests, while unrestricted aging may over-promote delayed long requests under congestion. We propose Quota-Based Aging (QBA), a lightweight policy that combines predicted short-first admission with quota-bounded, debt-enforced promotion of aged predicted-long requests. We also use a reduced M/G/n queueing surrogate, calibrated from simulator traces, to explain first-order mean-latency trends. QBA is evaluated using a serving-aware event-driven simulator that models decode-priority batching, chunked prefill, token-budget constraints, and KV-cache-safe admission. We compare QBA with FCFS, predicted short-first, and aggressive aging under asymmetric prediction errors on synthetic and production-derived workloads. The evaluation considers queueing delay, throughput, utilization, and class-conditional tail performance. Results show that QBA provides a controllable middle ground between aggressive short-first prioritization and unrestricted aging, substantially reducing long-request tail latency while retaining much of the mean-latency benefit of prediction-guided scheduling.

### [1330] [A Distributed View from a Single GPU: RankLens for Distributed Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18009)
*Yufan Wang,Yihao Zhang,Yi Liu*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Modern distributed training is costly to debug, tune, and analyze because faithful analysis often requires repeated target-scale executions. We observe that many analysis tasks depend on the original distributed execution path, but not on full all-rank execution. We present RankLens, a single-rank emulation system that runs one survivor rank on a single GPU while preserving the target job's distributed semantics. The survivor rank executes the original training program and performs real local computation. At communication boundaries, the system replaces real multi-rank communication with task-dependent semantics, selectively restoring recorded communication results and recorded or estimated completion timing while preserving the asynchronous dependencies required for analysis. This enables replay from real executions and supports analysis, debugging, and tuning with existing debuggers and performance analysis tools. We evaluate the system on DeepSpeed and Megatron-LM across 8-64-GPU target configurations. RankLens achieves 100% training-tensor communication-structure match, keeps emulation timing error below 5%, supports local anomaly reproduction and execution analysis, and reduces the resource requirement of these analyses from target-scale clusters to a single GPU.

### [1331] [LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18393)
*Yuanchang Zhou,Mingzhen Li,Chen Wang,Xiangyu Zhang,Guangming Tan,Weile Jia*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.

### [1332] [FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18451)
*Yunfei Feng,Jingkai He,Shiqi Liu,Cheng Zhang,Dong Du,Erhu Feng*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Large-scale expert parallelism (EP) has become the standard deployment configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in production. Meanwhile, the highly dynamic nature of LLM workloads requires providers to continuously adjust serving capacity to match fluctuating demand. Scaling MoE serving cannot be efficiently achieved by simply adding or removing serving instances; instead, it often requires resizing the EP group within an existing instance, which we refer to as intra-instance this http URL inference engines primarily rely on instance-level scaling, which destroys and reconstructs entire serving instances, incurring substantial scaling overhead. We present FastEEP (Fast Elastic Expert Parallel), a fast intra-instance scaling system for MoE serving based on the principle of Partial Reuse. FastEEP reuses existing runtime state across worker execution, GPU memory, and communication by separating reusable execution structures from the resources activated by the current EP configuration. This separation enables coordinated resource reclamation and reconfiguration while preserving costly-to-reconstruct state, allowing fast EP scaling without full instance teardown and reconstruction. Our evaluation shows that FastEEP achieves 4.5x--11.7x faster scaling than the existing vLLM-based approach across different models, enabling efficient, fine-grained scaling of MoE serving.

### [1333] [Tremulant: Latency in Serverless Platforms beyond the 99th Percentile](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18532)
*Linus Gustafsson,Trever Schirmer,David Bermbach*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) increases developer productivity by removing operational concerns such as managing hardware and software runtimes. Because function instances are started on demand, some requests must wait for a new instance, called a cold start. These are a common obstacle to more widespread adoption of FaaS, as they lead to unpredictable latency spikes that are not acceptable for some use cases. To solve this, many cold start optimizations have been implemented. However, comparatively little attention has been directed towards the slowest warm starts. With improvements in cold start times, slow warm starts emerge as a new problem for extreme tail events. By analyzing a dataset of several million requests across seven FaaS platforms, we show that the long tail of slow warm starts can be hundreds of times slower than their median performance, while a virtual machine we use as a baseline is substantially more consistent. We confirm this across four independent public datasets spanning 2020 to 2025, so the effect is neither new nor specific to one platform. Moreover, the warm share among the slowest calls starts to rise again at the highest percentiles: the most extreme latencies are not only cold starts, and cold-start mitigation alone cannot remove them.

### [1334] [Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18557)
*Anton Altenbernd,Dylan Everingham,Philipp Wiesner,Odej Kao*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths. Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated dense linear layers while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting dense linear layers in LLM inference, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths. Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated dense linear layers while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting dense linear layers in LLM inference, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.

</details>


### [1335] [Orrery: Modeling and Simulation of GPU-direct MPI Communication with SimGrid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18565)
*Ahmad Moh'd Saleh A. Belbeisi,Amir Raoofy,Josef Weidendorfer,Majid Salimi Beni*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Simulation of HPC applications is an essential tool for analyzing system design trade-offs and enabling effective hardware--software co-design. As modern supercomputers increasingly rely on GPU acceleration, MPI implementations have evolved to support GPU-aware communication, enabling direct GPU data transfers. Modeling these mechanisms is therefore critical for simulating HPC applications on current systems. In this paper, we introduce Orrery, an interposition layer built on SimGrid's SMPI to model GPU-aware MPI communication using existing collective implementations and flow-based simulation. Orrery intercepts GPU memory allocations, kernel launches, data transfers, and MPI operations, and models their execution in SimGrid according to target system specifications, enabling simulation without requiring physical GPUs. We validate Orrery using CUDA-aware MPI microbenchmarks and a Jacobi solver on up to 32 nodes of the MUSICA supercomputer and demonstrate that it reproduces key GPU-aware MPI mechanisms.

### [1336] [A Distributed Energy Relay Framework for Sustainable Drone Missions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18772)
*I-Ling Yen,Farokh Bastani,Akeem Mohammed,Agastya Bose*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Limited battery endurance remains a major obstacle to persistent UAV missions. Existing energy-replenishment approaches typically rely on battery-swapping/charging infrastructure or on ground vehicles with accessible road networks - assumptions that may not hold in infrastructure-less regions (ILRs) such as remote wilderness, mountainous terrain, and disaster-stricken areas. We formulate energy resupply in ILRs as a distinct logistics problem, in which energy itself must be projected into a region with no pre-existing infrastructure, and proposes a Distributed Energy Relay Framework that enables cooperative energy delivery using porter drones. The framework introduces a Transportation-by-Relay-and-Cache (TRC) mechanism, in which drones relay battery resources toward a mission location. Additional models are developed to characterize battery transportation capacity, relay amplification, energy-delivery capability, operational cost, and reliability. Based on these models, stations independently evaluate their delivery capability and submit bids to a mission coordinator, which selects an energy-delivery coalition that satisfies mission requirements while minimizing cost. Analytical evaluation illustrates the impact of battery characteristics and drone capabilities on energy projection and demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework for sustaining UAV missions in ILRs.

### [1337] [SlideDP: Scaling Host-Resident LLM Fine-Tuning Across Multiple GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34162)
*Ruijia Yang,Shiyuan Lin,Yulong Ao,Zhiyu Li,Yingli Zhao,Xianduo Li,Yonghua Lin,Zeyi Wen*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Host-resident layer streaming enables full-parameter LLM fine-tuning beyond GPU memory, but data-parallel ranks compete for shared host resources. Replicated transfers amplify traffic, while strong scaling can expose host work as computation windows shrink. We present SlideDP, a synchronous data-parallel runtime for shared-host multi-GPU systems. It maintains one authoritative host state, decouples communication routes from state layout, and pipelines parameter delivery, gradient aggregation, and CPU updates across ranks and chunks. An analytical step-time model characterizes resource bottlenecks and pipeline exposure; runtime measurements guide communication, chunking, and activation policies under a GPU memory budget. In matched-batch sweeps, SlideDP achieves geometric-mean throughput ratios of 1.46-2.64$\times$ over SlideFormer, MegaTrain, and ZeRO-Offload. On four H100s, SlideDP approaches GPU-resident FSDP2 throughput for Qwen3-14B at a smaller batch size. With a larger batch, it processes over 1M tokens per step and exceeds FSDP2's measured peak throughput by 11.2%. Separately, it supports 256K-token sequences for the same model and fine-tunes Qwen2.5-72B on four RTX 4090 GPUs. Project page: this https URL .
